Beach, M.P., at Keevil, 10 per cent. was returned on the last half-year's rent.—The Duke of Newcastle has again returned his tenants 20 per cent, of their rents on the hal ayear.—The Earl of Rosebery has again remitted to the tenants on his Rackinghanashire estate 15 per cent. of the rents due at Lady Day.—lt is announced that Earl Beauchamp will again return 20 per cent, to his Gloucestershire tenants. GITENON'S Mean OF a MILKING Cow.—The extent and form of the "escutcheon" of reversed hair on the udder and above it on the hinder part of the cow is said to oe indica- tive of milking yield. Mr. Heaton, of Fifeshire, in his "Row to Choose a Cow," says " The conclusion arrived at, in regard to M. Guenon's rest Of judging of the milking pro- perties of a cow by the development of the ecussent is that, in a very large majority of cases, it is borne out by facts. In a London dairy belonging to Mr. Biggs, 31, Edaeware- road, where about 400 cows were kept, and where nine-tenths of them were far above average milkers, tke development or upward growth of the hair on the posterior part of the udder, thigh', and perinzam was too remarkable to be ac- counted for by accidental causes." FATALITY AMONG LAMBS.—The Veterinarian states that a great fatality prevails among the lambs in the eastern counties, more especially in Norfolk and Kent. In the latter the disease known as "rickets," swayback, dm., is very rife. That journal says :—" This congenital affection is evidently dependent originally on want of tonicity, or atrophy of the muscles of the haunch in particular, by which, as a cones- (pence, an elongation of the ligament= tens and partial relaxation of the hip-joint takes place. The probable origin of this disease, and others affecting young lambs, is the character and condition of the food supplied to the ewes during utero-gestation. It is well known that in consequence of the wet and mild winter, many flocks lived almost entirely on watery and unripe grasses, turnips, dm." POTATO EXPERIMENTEL—I have been for several years trying small experiments with these; and the results, this season, are so very marked that I feel convinced I have hit upon a method which is of value. Everybody knows the favour with which "greened" seed is regarded by growers of early kidneys. I have proved that all kinds acquire con- stitution, and a disposition to form tubers earlier by having the seed taken up very early indeed, and when not above a quarter of its size; and that the produce gathers increased vigour in proportion to the length of time in which it has been so treated, and seed treated so one year is say, a week forwarder in consequence. If the seed is then treated a second time, the produce in the third season will be a fort- night earlier; and a third season of similar practice will confer vet more of vigour and precocity. I have just raised six kinds. Of some the seed has had three seasons of this treatment, of some two, and some only one. In each calm seed treated in the usual manner was grown side by side with the special seed; and in every case the rule held true, the earlier the seed was taken up, the forwarder the crop of 1884.—f1. S. L. THE DAIRY Fearanect Coemennsrcm—The report of the cammittee of the Gloucester Dairy Farming Conference contains a paper in which are embodied suggestions for the consideration of the committee which was formed at the Conference, and which is to miserable in the large tent on the second day of the Royal Show at Shrewsbury. Among these are propositions for a national conference to be held once a year. and to be followed by a second conference in London during the Dairy Show. It is also proposed that similar organisations should be promoted in particular counties or districts, and conducted in connection with the national one. In addition, it is suggested that a dairy school should be started, together with a model collection of appliances and objects illustrative of the dairy industry, and that the instruction in the theory of dairying should be conducted in a similar manner to that carried on at Copen- hagen under Professor Segelcke. If these ideas can be carried into effect something will be gained; but in the Danish educational system it is rather on large farms that the system is learned by students, who are sent to them by Professor Segelcke mad not absolutely taught by the Pro. 'tenor himself in dopenhagen. The model dairy, it is sug- gested, should be similar to the Station Latiere at Lausanne, conducted by M. Schatemann. This station has also the Danish system of education. ARTIFICIAL MANURIX.—FAIKKRRS CHRATIM.—At the last monthly meeting of the Council of the Royal Society of England, Mr. Wells reported that the Chemical Committee had received the report of the Woburn Sub-Committee, which recommended, with a view of carrying out further experiments on the manurial value of cotton-cake, a diviaion of each acre of the rotation experiments into two equal halves, and the sabstitaticn on one-half acre of peas for clover. Dr. Voelcker had been desired to institute some • direct experiments on the same subject in Lansome Field. —Dr. Voelcker reported cases of cheating farmers in the supply of artificial manure.—Mr. P. M'Gregor' of Crowton Hall, near Northwich, bought some dissolved bones at £8 55. per ton delivered, warranted made entirely of pure bones. Doubting the genuineness of them, he sent a sample on Metall 13th. The analysis showed that this it not made entirely of pure bones, but is an ordinary super-phosphate containing aboat 10 percent. of bone. Such a manure can in most places be bought at £5 105. to £6 a ton.—Mr. W. Adams, joint manager. Barrett PEESERVING.—kt the present season of the year, when batter is so cheap, it Is advisable that farmers should lenow the best systems of salting and packlog for winter use, , for it is far preferable to preserve it and so obtain higher prices than to sell at the ridiculous figures which are now too generally offered by the dealers and grccers. It should not be forgotten that if butter is well made it may be pre- served under a good system so as to come oat at the latter end of the year in almost 83 fine a condition as it is when put Into salt, and the price obtained for it being twopence or threepence per pound more. There is one which espe- cially deserves mention. Fine muslin bags are prepared, these heing made in a cylinder form. They hold about two pounds, and being filled tightly, are packed incrocks or tubs , wkich aro filled with brine, the %easel when fall being ' covered with a thick layer of salt. In other words, the sys- tem somewhat resembles that of pickling pork. In this way ' the ..lnitter is entirety preserved or shielded from the atmo- sphere, and it will not be found to absorb more salt than if salted in the ordinary way. But, what is more than this, however heavily it may be salted that can be rectizied when the butter is required for sale or use by working upon the improved butter-worker either with cold /spring water or new milk, s-hon this greater portion of the salt can, if necessary, be eliminated,and a delicate flavour imparted by.the milk. In this brine, which may be described as an antiseptic II aid, It is quite' -safe although, as is well knawn, there is a de- •velopment in bolter which is due to the action of the milk- er:gar int* ilactic acid and thence into hatyric acid. The change, however, instead of destroying any portion of the butter, sinaply alters its flavour, which becomes more power- fal and, as some consider, more agreeable. In some parts of Cheahire and the neighbouring Welsh districts butter is largely made and pecked in crocks after-each making, these crooks holdingabout 80Ib., and •a slight cone being formed at the tom A layer of emit is spread over, and it then remains at the call of the butter merchant; but the marvellous por- tion of the business is that seldom n:ore than 1.2 d. is given, and this just when it best sniM the dealer. The butter le not well made, and consequently of but moderate quality, and very little energy is displayed either in its manufacture or sale. 'Until the butter maker realises the faot that it is just as necessary Is take trouble in marketing as in making he will never make his dairy successful. Well.made butter of the summer which has been properly preserved should turn out for winter sale and realise at least sixteenpence a pound.

THE ROYAL COMMISSIONERS' REPORT ,ON AGRICULTURAL EDUCATION. NO. VII. "Great Britain" is file heading of the seventh reoort of Mr. Jenkins, the Royal Commissioner on Agricultural Educa. tion. In that part of our country called Great Britain, says the Commissioner, very little is done by the Govern- ment towards encouraging the teaching of agriculture ex. cept by payment for results obtained, and that may be summed up in two lines: (1) The recent establishment of a chair of agriculture at the iVormal School of Scienec, South Kensington. (2) A grant of £l5O a year towards the endowment of a chair of agriculture at the University of Edinburgh. The few institutions where agriculture and the veterinary art are taught are either self.supporting, or depend for their existence upon voluntary subscriptions or money advanced by philanthropic individuals, unless, in- deed, one may include a few elementary schools in which the "Principles of Agriculture" are taught as a apecific subject. The Science and Art Department, the Royal Agricultural Society of England, and the Highland and Agricultural Society of Scotland, all act as examining bodies; but whereas the principle of the Government Da- s partment is to give its chief pecuniary rewards to the teachers, , the eh a view of stimulating them to impart in. principle of the societies is to reward the taught for their previous exertions, and with a view to stimulate the acquisition of farther knowledge by them- selves and by others. A description is given first of the colleges and schools where agriculture is taught in Great Britain, and afterwards of the operations of the institutions iwhich act as examining bodies so far as their action is directly educational. Dealing briefly with the National Agricultural Societies, he expresses the belief that through their annual shows, and their periodical meetings for pur- poses of discussion, the action of •!licee associations i,. in the large sense of the term, distinctly educational lie observes that the opinion Is spreading more rapidly that the money spent in a needless, and indeed mischievous,

special agricultural articles—that of Cirencester. In a re- view of what has been attempted and what has been accom- plished in Great Britain to promote the agricultural educa- tion of landowners, land agents, and large tenant-farmers, the Royal Agricultural College of Cirencester deservedly takes precedence. Previous to its establishment no institu- tion existed in England having for its object the technical instruction of agriculturists of any degree; but a school of agriculture existed in Ireland at Templemoyle, London- derry. The Cirencester College owes its origin to an address delivered by the late Mr. R. J. Brown to a meeting of the Cirencester and Fairford Farmers' Club, in 1842, on the ad- vantages of a specific education for agricultural pursuits. By the efforts of Mr. Brown, Earl Duels, and others, a capi- tal of £12,000 was raised; a charter was obtained in March, 1845, and afterwards the capital was increased to £24,000. The college soon found a balance of £lO,OOO owing at its bankers and a supplemental charter was got and another £20,000 obtained. Mr. Jenkins describes the arrangements for instruction which we have beforetime given, the pro- gress of the eollege and its system down to the minutest de- tail. Generally speaking, the students are the sons of land- owners, large farmers, estate agents, and professional and business men, and they have generally been educated in large public schools. The itflaence of the college teaching has for many years been largely felt in agricultural circles, not only in the United Kingdom, but in foreign countries and the colonies, and especially in India.—Another college described is one that we have often dealt with in these columns—the College of Agriculture at Downton, opened in May, 1880. This is purely a private undertaking, and commercially has been a great success. The building itself is an old farmhouse, and the requisite accommodation for about 40 indoor students has been obtained by a large ex- tension of the original building backwards. Instruction is imparted by lectures, field clamss, practical work and catachetical lectures, and the results of the teaching are tested by weekly examinations conducted on the farm, in the laboratories, and by means of printed papers. The eubjects of instruction include agriculture and dairy and pastoral farming; estate management, land agency and forestry, and the best results are expected from the educa- tion given.—The Commissioner gives some particulars of the Chair of Agriculture at the University of Edinburgh. It was founded in 1790, with a stipend of £5O per annum, and in 1888, by the exertions of the Highland Agricultural Society, the endowment was raised to £3OO. The fees paid ' by the students are four guineas for a course of 100 lee- ' tares. The Highland Society endeavours to stimulate young farmers to attend these lectures by offering annually ten bursaries of £2O earth towardetheir 'expenses. Exam- ' inations are held, and the lectures have had a perceptible effect on the agriculture of Scotland. Agricultural in- structian is also given at various county schools in the king- dom. Although these are not agricultural schools in the pruner eerie of the term, some of them have so far shown the possibility of the elements of agriculture being taught to the senior pupils as to justify the Commissioner in giving a notice of their existence and capabilities. The Royal Agricultural Society of England has made various attempts to induce the headmasters of these and other middle-class schools to teach subjects connected with agri- culture to their pupils by offering rewards for proficiency, but only ten schools have responded to the Royal Society's invitations, none being in Lancashire. By far the most successful of these county schools is the Surrey County School at Cranleigh, where 350 boys are boarded, lodged, ' and educated.—Good work has been done in Veterinary education in England. The Royal. Veterinary College, London, was founded in 1791, and is a private educational , establishment, being the only Veterinary College in Eng- land and Wales.—Assistance to instruction in agriculture is given by the English Government through the Science and ' Art Department in two ways :—(1) The higher instruction ' is aided by the delivery of a course of lectures at the Normal School of Science and the partial endowment of a Chair of Agriculture ;a the University of Edinbargb. ' (2) The lower instruction in the "principles of agriculture" is encouraged by the payment of fees to teachers in elementary schools and science classes. Mr. Jenkins gives ' in detail the course of instruction in the Normal School of Science, observing that the curriculum seems to him to ' require considerable modification ; the main lines of the teaching of the Principles of Agriculture in elementary ' schools, the chief features of which our agricultural readers have been made acquainted with in the admirable series of articles written for us by Professor Tanner; the class sub- jects, elementary subjects, and specific subjects taught; the regulations and grants, and he quotes a lengthy extract from the Regulations of the Science and Art Department applicable to the teaching of the Principles or Agriculture In science schools. He also gives Professor Tanner's report as to the assistance rendered in the promotion of agricul- tural education by the Education Department and the Government Department of Science, a report which em- braces some very interesting reading. From 50 to 10 teachers obtain qualifying certificates in science every year, and so far as their services as science teachers are concerned their chief emolument is derived from the Government grant, the fees paid by the pupils being generally very small, One well-known teacher has summed up the effect of hie teaching upon the agriculture of his district as follows (a) Tendency to adopt six or seven years' rotation, so as to leave land longer under grass. (b) Chaff-cutters and palper, are much desired ; impetus is given to keep up with the times in reapers, lec. (c) Subsoiling and draining, and avoid working land when wet, are approved of, and give Increase of produce. (d) Cutting of hay enables more ani- mals, as cheep, to be kept on less turnips in proportion, and more stock is carried through. (e) Tendency to utilise water•power wherever it is available. He also notices indirect results of great importance, such as the interchange of ideas among those working on land, the eager reading of works on agriculture, and the patting of suggestions to the test of experience for the common benetit.—The Commissioner goes on to refer to the desirability of educating men as farm bailiffs. No class of men is more wanted on large and moderate-sized farms than in- telligent and instructed farm bailiffs. At present the men who are made of the necessary material migrate to the towns while still young, so as to earn higher wages than an or- dinary farm labourer. With the prospect of being able to quality as a bailiff, with the higher pay and the many other advantages belonging to such a position, many of therm young men would remain in the country, much to the benefit of themselves and their employers and of the coun- try generally. The Commissioner holds that there should be greater inducements offered to pupils by the Science and Art Department, and he urges the importance of the teachers being thoroughly efficient. Leaving the work of the Science and Art Department, Mr. Jenkins launches into a task which must have been moat congenial to him—the history and work of the Royal Agricultural Society, of which he is the able secretary. To this we shall devote a special article in another issue, in connection with the visit of the Royal to Preston next year. After giving a few facts as to the examinations in agriculture in connection with the Society of Arts, the Commissioner narrates the history of the incorporation and establishment of the Insti- tution of Surveyors which has done a useful work in ins. portant branches of technical instruction. He next gives the history of the Highland Agricultural Society, and goes on to give a sketch of the marvellous experimental station at Rothamsted. This was founded by Sir J. 13. Lewes nearly 0 years ago, and has throughout been maintained by him at an expense amounting to some thousands a year. What Sir J. B. Lawes has done for the advancement of agriculture and the benefit of the farmers cannot be described, for most important results have followed the enormous range of his experiments. In conclusion, Mr. Jenkins devotes a chapter to the attempt by Mr. Allender to found a British Dairy School, an enterprise which it will be remembered was pro- jected with promises of support which seemed certain to ensure success, and yet was a conspicuous failure. It is futile to speculate on the measure of success which this Dairy School might have achieved if it had been founded, but it is hoped that before long the effort will be renewed to successfully found a school which is bound to have a very healthfulinfluence en the Dairy interest of Great Britain.

Fogg, Unitarian minister, of Groaskirk, who is an octogenarian, writes with zespect to the old Hermit of Lathom :—" Robert Swars- brick, the hermit, was born in 1740, and died in the year 1624. When a young man he was deeply in love with a damsel, who jilted him and married another. He declared he would never marry, but would be a hermit for the rest of his life. There is a pleasant green walk that leads from Cross Hall to Blythe Hall on the left, and to Lathom Hall on the right. This is called the Ladiee' Walk, and on a beautiful evening it is much frequented. At the bottom of this walk Robert Bwarebrlck chose his first hermitage. There are oil paintings of it in existence. It was a thatched octagon building, with only one rcom. Here he lived for some time. There are now twenty tall trees growing where the hermit once had his residence. After a while the family at Lathom House granted him an acre of ground opposite the Wood LI the New Park, and a house was built called Bachelor's Whim or Hermitage. It had only two rooms, one below and one upstairs, but behind there was a hot- house with the Passion Flower, the Clematis, and the Vine. At the entrance of the cot there was an oil painting of a Pilgrim, life size. In the interior were framed pictures of several saints, for Robert was a Roman Catholic. The Hermit had a flute more than a hundred years old. He once bad a tame redbreast in his garden that would parch upon his shoulder and eat out of his band. It was his wish to be buried in his garden beneath a favourite tree, and a gentleman composed an epitaph and had it painted on a black board. It began with the words:— Beneath these lofty oaks and towering pines, Swarsbrick, in peace, thy mortal part reclines. Another epitaph was written by another poet, beginning : Here lie the ashes of Robert the Hermit. If you won't believe It his friends will confirm It. Robert had a quarto printed book with large margin, on which he scribbled his remarks and his poetry; but he was a mach better gardener than poet. After the tlermit's death in 1824 some of his relatives were opposed to his being theb buried Churchi a the gt rk, d a consequenceaordremns.kilnan Stone ten that h ewa: interredtthe behind e was a hermit, aged eighty-four years. The Hermitage has long been pulled down, the fruit trees are gone, and the acre of ground is added to the neighbouring farm."

• The Boston Advertiser of Jane 20 has another article on Mr. Charles Toppan's new bleaching process by means of a preparation of petroleum. The Old Canton Cotton Mills, near the Providence Railroad, have been fitted up for the purpose of workbyt the process. Other patents of Mr. Top- . . . _ .

pan's will be worked, it Is expected, by the Canton Mills Company, the most important being one for bleaching paper pulp. A series of papers on "Early New Church Worthies," written by the Rev. Dr. Bayley, and appearing weekly in the Dawn, include a number of names and topics of special interest to local readers. Amongst them we may name Samuel Dawson (Bolton), Crompton, the inventor of the mule; Mr. Agnew and Cheap Day Schools; Mr. Mottram and the immediate Friends of Mr. Clowes, Francis Marcella. Hodson, of Manchester; Mr. George Howarth and the La- erington Society, Mr. John Broadfield and the Peter.street Society,. Manchester; Mr. William Cordin, of Salford; Childers, the Astronomer; John Saxon, called John the Beggar; and Mr. Richard Boardman, of Middleton. STAR MAGNITUDES DETERMINED BY PHOTOGRAPHY:. We have received from the Rev. J. E. Espin, the indefatl- gable observer to the Liverpool Astronomical Society, a printed catalogue of the magnitudes of 500 stars in Auriga, Gemini, and Leo Minor, all determined from photographs taken with the equatorial stellar camera at the society's ob- servatory. The instrument was presented to the society by Mr. Howard Grubb, and it has been turned to excellent ac- count. The magnitudes obtained agree fairly well with those of Argelander, and this result augurs well for the future usefulness of a method almost untried and necessarily beset with the difficulties incident to a new line of research. Science Monthly.

ANCIENT Euirr.—M. Maspero writes to M. Renan, thank- ing him for the subscription for Egyptian Archie°logical re- search. M. Maspero adds :—" My campaign at Saqqarak ended with the discovery of an untouched tomb of the sixth dynasty. We found in it five funeral boats, with all their gear, a great wooden coffin covered with iascriptions, and a sarcophagus," which M. Renan was just about to open. This is the oldest tomb that ever was discovered and violated by any European. The articles in the sepulchre were arranged as in those of Thebes. Still more important, the inscrip- tions on the coffin prove that the ritual of the dead was already in use in the time of the sixth dynasty. M. Renan believes that parts of it are prehistoric. So unchanging was the religion of Egypt. MEDICINA.L VALUE OF LEMONS.—Most people know the benefit of lemonade before breakfast, but few know that it is more than doubled by taking another at night also. The way to get the better of the bilious system without blue pills or quinine is to take the juice of one, two, or three lemons, as appetite craves, in as much ice water as makes it pleasant to drink without sugar' before going to bed. In the morning, on rising, at least half an hour before break- fast, take the juice of one lemon in a goblet of water. This will clear the system of humour and bile with efficiency, without any of the weakening effect of calomel or congress water. People should not irritate the stomach by eating lemons clear, the powerful acid of the juice, which is always most corrosive, invariablyproduces inflammation after a while, but properly diluted, so that it does not burn or draw the throat, it does its medical work without harm; and when the stomach is clear of food, has abundant opportunity to work over the system thoroughly. AN INDUSTREAL USE FOR ELECTRICITT.—M. Henri de Parville calls the attention of wine-growers to the services electricity might render them in protecting their vines from the disastrous effects caused by a sudden fall in tempera- ture. For several years past vines in France have been pro- tected from the effects of cold winds or sudden changes in the temperature by artificial clouds of smoke, produced by the burning of tarred straw and other combustibles. Vine- growers have learned to appreciate the benefits of this sys- tem, but to light the fires at the right moment in the night time, it is indispensable to have a thoroughly reliable watcher. By the aid of electricity the safety of the vines I would be ensured. A vine-grower has only to place in his vineyard one or more electric batteries similar to those used to fire mines, the wires being connected with the fires pre- pared at regular distances. When the thermometer falls towards zero, by means of a very simple arrangement it causes the electric current to pass along the wires, the fires are lighted, the air being filled with the protecting smoke- clouds. M. de Parville cites one or two instances in which his system has been most successfully employed, with very little outlay to the vine-grower.

div.head: SEASONABLE HINTS.
div.p: SEASONABLE HINTS.

It is difficult at this Beason of the year to keep the fowls from drinking too much water, which is in itself apt to be warm and unrefreshing. The best way is to put a little lump camphor in the fountains, if they are used, and to make some provision for keeping the water cool, which may be done by placing them under trees or other shelter so as to keep them from the sun. It must be remembered that a large body of water keeps cool much longer than a small one, for it takes longer to heat, and this would appear to be an argument against fountains. We have no objection to large vessels, if the water is renewed often enough, and one of the great points in favour of the fountains is that they must be constantly refilled. Such places as have a ,con- stant supply of running water are fortunate indeed, for that Is almost sure to be pure and fresh. A good plan we recently heard of was to stand a large barrel upon a raised platform with a dish or trough below, and allow the water put in the barrel to drop into this latter by way of a very small hole. A few pails of water each day kept the thing going, and the water was always fresh and pure.

REKHDY FOE SMALLPDX.—A correspondent writing to a London contemporary, says:—An effective mean. was found some years ago by a friend of mine while resident in South America for stamping oat an epidemic of smallpox in the village where he lived, and as it proved so effective I am prompted to suggest, through you, that our local authorities should try this remedy in some of the crowded localities where smallpox is now so rife. Bonfires of old creosoted railway sleepers were made in the streets, and gas tar was added when necessary; wherever a death occurred, or a patient recovered, the houses were immediately white- washed inside, and smallpox disappeared from among the people in a short time after the remedy was tried. Creosote being a powerful disinfectant. I think that good results would follow if similar bonfires were lighted close to the smallpox hospitals and camps. It was efficacious in the Instance above referred to in stamping out the disease, and why may it not be equally so in this country? lam not aware that a single case of smallpox has been reported in proximity to the creosoting works either in Stivertown or Rotherhithe, and if those particular localities, in which the houses are of a very poor class, are freer of the epidemic than other parts of London, a check to the eoread of small- pox, I think, is not far to seek. The effect of creosote might be fluickly tested if some old" lumber" well saturated with it was stacked in sufficient quantities in the streets and alleys where smallpox is known to exist, and as the expense would not necessarily be great, I hope some of the local authorities and the Metropolitan Asylums Board will accept this suggestion. If it were found inexpedient or dangerous to burn creosoted wood in the courts and alley, it might be stacked and kept there for a time as a disinfectant. Gomm's " anCTIVE Avvrxtries."—lt would be almost impossible to enumerate those with whom Goethe carried on love, flirtation, or courtship. In the latest "Life of Goethe," by Heinrich Dantzer, portraits are given of Anna Katha- rine Schonkopt, a Leipsic wine-seller'e daughter, who after- wards married Dr. Kanne, an advocate; Frederik° Oeser and her sister, daughters of Goethe's drawing-master ; Charlotte Buff, who was already engaged to Kestner, a Brunswick Sec. retary of Legation; Lili Sehtlinemann, a cultivated and fas- cinating blonde of sixteen, to whom Goethe was formerly engsged, but who (herself the daughter of a Frankfort banker) married a rich banker of Strasburg; Charlotte von Stein (wife of the Master of the Horse and mother of seven children), with whom Goethe carried on an intimate and carious friendship for nearly thirteen years; Corona SchrUter, whom he would probably have married but for Frau von Stein; the fascinating Marchesa Brancoui, a Venetian lady, secretly wedded to the puke of Brunswick; ChristianeValpins,with whom Goethe lived as husband since 1788, but to whom he was not legally married till 1808; and Bettina Brentano, who when seventeen sent a message to the poet, then fifty-three, that she burned with love for him! These are, however, but a few out of the many between whom and the poet there existed amatory relationships. In his fifteenth year he, in great ardour and earneetness, be- came engaged to Gretchen, the daughter of an Offenbach innkeeper. When fifty•seven he fell for a time desperately lin love with Minnchen Herzlieb, a beautiful young girl of seventeen. In 1823, at Marienbad, when he was seventy- four, his love for Ulrike Levesow (a ')ewitching young lady, also just seventeen) reached the height of passion, and it was PO open and remarkable that the visitors at the baths talked of marriage; but her mother broke every thir,g off Dv leaving suddenly. Indeed, he seemed scarcely able to exist unless his head, if not his heart, was filled with some woman. This must be remembered in order to understand his writ- ings, many of the scenes of which are based on what he him- self passed through.

:PT AND THE SOUDAN. SITAIIM, SATURDAY.—Order has been restored at Agig. The gunboat Condor has left here no a cruise. Stream, SUNDAY.—The steamer Damanhour has arrived here from Massowah. She reports that some Abyssinian chiefs were expected there in a few days, en route or Bag land, with the present of an elephant from the King cf Abyssinia for the Queen. Canto, MONDAY.—A telegram received from Korosko this afternoon announces that Lieut. Van Koughne has arrived there, with two war steamers, on his way to Wady Haifa.— it is impossible, at present, to obtain news at Dongola, the Mudir having compl-te control of the telegraph lines. The rebels are in possession of the town. CAIRO, MONDAY.—No official news of the fall of Dongola has been received, though the report is believed, as the Mudir's movements have been so mysterious. The wire is not cut between Dosgola and Wady Halfa.—Daily News. CAIRO, TUESDAY.—The citizens of Dongola have wired the Khedive imploring the assistance of troops and offering to pay expenses.--1-30 P.M.—Turkish soldiers of the Egyptian Army ordered to Assouan deserted yesterday. ADEN, TUESDAY.—Tha British political resident here, ac- companied by the gun vessels Arab and Ranger, has gone to Berber to annex that place. ALEXANDRIA, TUESDAY—The British military authorities intend sending a British officer to Dongola, accompanied by one of the Khedive's aides to ascertain the truth regard- ing the attitude of the Governor.

MUTINY OF TURKISH TROOPS. ALEXANDRIA, WEDNESDAY, 11-45 P M.—PriVate letters from Abyssinia state that since Admiral Hewitt's mission King John, feeling assured of the friendship of a Protestant Power, haS taken up a hostile attitude towards the French Catholic mission, long a thorn in his side. The mission- bosses at Akrour and feur other places have been sacked and the missionaries expelled. The mutiny at Aseiot of native troops had to be quelled brforce and the mutineers sent to Cairo lancer arrest. A small detachment of English soldiers on the road to Keneh were ordered to remain there for the present to preserve tranquility amongst the somewhat excited population.— Daily Telegraph. . CAIRO, WEDNESDAY NlGHT.—Ttlirty•three Of the Bashi- . Bazmks have been captured, and will be brought to Cairo for c mrt-martial under the escort of Egyptian troops. The remainder are ordered up to the front.—Daily News. RAVAGES OF THE CHOLERA. PARIS, SATURDAY.—The Temps states that the death which occurred yesterday in the Rue des Saints-Peees was occa- sioned by severe colic. A death frern cholera occurred tbis morning at Lyons. In the Chamber of deputies to-day, M. Wa:deck-Itosseau, Minister of the interior, introduced a de. !nand for a credit of two million francs for the relief of the cholera-stricken towns. Urgency was declared for the pro- posal, the discussion of which was postponed until the end of the sitting, when the credit was unanimously adopted, together with a further vote of 500,000 francs to defray the expenses caused by the epidemic. Tou,ote, SATURDAY.—Seyenteen deaths from cholera oc- curred here last night in the city and suburbs. Since ten o'clock Cele morning five more deaths have occum d.— Sunday.—Since nine o'clock this morning eight deaths from cholera occurred in the city and suburbs, making a total of 36 fatal cases during the 24 hours ending half-past four this afternoon. According to official statistics, 10,691 have left here by rail since the outbreak of the epidemic.--Mon- day.— I here were 11 deaths from cholera here last night, two of which occurred in the Civil Hospital, and the others in the city and suburbs.

MARSEILLES, SATURDAY. To-night's official bulletin gives the number of deaths during the last twenty-four hours as 100, of which 05 were from cholera. At the pre- sent time there are 81 cases under treatment in the Pharo Hospital. The Bishop of Marseilles visited the hospital to- day, and let 500 francs for distribution amongst the poorest of the sufferers.--Sunday, 7-35 p.m.—Since the record was made up at nine o'clock this morning 32 fresh deaths from cholera have been registered. This gives a total of 53 since eight yesterday evening. A kitchen for the supply of relief to the indigent, the expense of which will be borne by the Municipality, was opened this morning.--Monday. —The official bulletin issued this evening gives the number of deaths during the last twenty-four hours at 112, G 6 being from cholera.

MARSEILLES, MONDAY.—The cholera bas made it ap- pearance in the Alps, taken there by fugitives flying from tie disease. Several cases have been declared. Other cases have occurred on the Loire, the Isere, and the Rhone. In the Spanish Pyrenees the rigid quarantine established by the Spanish Government has been the cause of the death of a Frenchm in, who was shot while attempting to cross the lines. At Toulon four nurses and three medical students have died from cholera.—Standard.

LYONS, SUNDAY.—Dr. Koch, who arrived here yesterday from Marseilles, has stated in Ids opinion that the cholera will extend to this town. He thinks, however, that in view of the excellent system of drainage and measures of precau- tion already taken, the visitation will bee mild one, and will prob iblv aff,ct only the suburbs. BERLIN. MONDAY—Two cases of cholera, one of vrbich ended Wally, are reported from Solotonecha, in the govern- ment of Poltava. The Siberian plague is raging in the govern- ment of Pleskoff. Twenty deaths have ,already occurred. The measures taken by the authorities for stamping out the disease are said to be inadequate. ALEXANDRIA, MONDAY.—A case of cholera has occurred here, but it is of a European sporadic character. The person attacked is a woman of low class. No death has occurred.

MARSEILLES, TUESDAY MORNlNG—Thirteen deaths from cholera were registered here last night. TOULON, TUESDAY MORNING.—Since 4-30 p.m. yesterday 13 deaths from cholera have occurred in the city and suburbs. The Mayor of Toulon is still sufferiug fiorn the choleraic symptoms by which he was attacked yesterday. The disease gams ground in the neighbouring districts. CONSTANTINOPLE, MONDAY. The Austro-Hungarian Government has seat a Note to the Porte asking co-operation in measures against the cholera.

The United States Consul notifies that clean bills of health will be refused to all vessels clearing from London and Liverp4ol unless approved by the health inspectors attached to the American Consulate. Tuntorr, WEDNESDAY, 6-30 P.M.—Eleven deaths have oc- curred since the .last report.
MARSEILLES, WEDNESDAY, 9-20 P.M.—During the last 24 hours the deaths registered number 103, of which 53 were from cholera.

PARIS, WEDNRSDAY.—The Due de Chartres left Paris this evening by the 7-15 express for Toulon and Marseilles. It is believed that he takes with him the sum of 50,0001., the donation of the Comte de Paris for the relief of the sufferers from cholera.

SIARSHILLSS, THURSDAY:BetWeen eight o'clock last night and eight o'clock this morning twenty-three deaths from cholera were reported, makinea total of fifty-seven in twenty-four hours. There are ninety-four cholera patients under treatment in the Pharo Hospital.

FRANCE AND CHINA. SHANGHAI, SATURDAY—Sir Robert Hart is endeavouring to negotiate with M. Patenotre at Shanghai. The Teung-h- Yemen seems blind to the dangers of war and rebellion. Prince Chung trusts to boastMg fanatics and officials, who conceal the defenceless condition of the coast. Ignorance, confusion, and treachery render the situation most critical The British officials have left the Ch'nese fleet.—Times. TmersiN, SATURDAY.—AII foreign officers, except two, have fer the present left the Chinese fleet, which is just now at Porteli. The rumours of war being imminent between France and China are believed to be exaggerated. PARIS, WEDNESDAY.—A formal semi-official denial is given to the report telegraphed from Shanghai that the Teungli Yawen had rejected the demands of the French I Government. On the contrary, the belief is expressed that France and China will shortly arrive at an agreement. FRANCE—THE FETES. Paws, Seroisoar.—At a Cabinet Council held this morning at the Elyebe M. Gravy signed decrees reducing the punish writs for various political crimes and misdemeanours. Louise Michel, Prince Krapotkine, and M. Gauthier are not included in this act of clemency. Paws, Morroar.—The national/etc was celebrated to-day in the same manner as in former years. The military re- views held this morning, and particularly that of the Battalions of Scholars, attracted large crowds. A regret- able incident occurred about noon in front of the Hotel Continental. Some collegians perceiving a German flag among those of other nationalities used to decorate the building, shouted loudly demanding its removal. A crowd of gamins then assembled and tore down the flag. They also broke several panes of glass in the entrance door to the hotel in the Rue Castiglione, but were immediately dispersed by the police. ACCIDENT ON MOM' BLANC. GENEVA, MONDAY.—M. Gottinger, a distinguished Al- pinist from Zurich, was making, with two guides, the ascent of the Grande Jorasse, one of the summits of Mont Blanc, when the party was surprised by an avalanche of stones. After a few minutes the guides, coming out of their hiding places, found M. Gottinger with a foot cat off and badly wounded on the head. He expired skortly afterwards. As- sistancs was speedily rendered, but it was of no avail. The general opinion is that the unfortunate man left his shelter too soon.

div.head: EGYPT.
div.p: EGYPT.

_ - - ALEXANDRIA, MONDAY:A conflict has arisen between the Egyptian Customs authorities and the French Post- office, owing to the former, on the occasion of the fumintion of the mails, having made an extensive seizure of valuables which were being forwarded through the post in order to avoid payment of Customs duties. The acting French Diplomatic Agent has protested against any interference with the French mails on the part of the Egyptian authori- ties.

DYNAMITE PLOT AGAINST THE CZAR. CRACOW, THIIRSDAY.—The Nowa Reforma publishes in- telligence from Warsaw reporting the discovery of a plot against the E.nperon of Russia. It is added that M. Barkotski, justice of the peace, has been arrested, and that a number of arms and a quantity of dynamite have been found. Tbe conspirators are represented to have intended to blow up the palace at Warsaw during the Emperor's stay in that city.

THE LATE PRINCE OF ORANGE. THE HAGUE, THURSDAY.—The funeral of the late Prince of Orange was celebrated with great pomp here to-day. The coffin was covered with wreathe, including one specially Sent by the Prince of Wales and the Freemasons.
TILE DEMOCRATIC CONVENTION. OHICAGIO, Steroansy.—The Convention adjourned after having nominated Mr. Ifeddrieha for the poet of Vise-Preei• dent of the United States.

div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

- o'Donovon Rossa has arrived at Skibbereen from the United States. The appointment of Major-General Lyon Freemantle to be brigadies general upon the staff of the army serving MEM& is gazetted. A Cabinet Council was held on Wednesday, at which all the Ministers were present with the exception of Earl Spencer. An explosion occurred at the Vauxhall Colliery, Ruabon, on Wednesday afternoon, by which four miners were seriously injured. Dr. Henry Morris, of Sheffield, has died from the effects of an overdose of chloral. He took three d-achms to induce sleep, and never recovered therefrom. The Lord Mayor of London presided on Wednesday at the Mansion House over a meeting held in connection with the National Smoke Abatement Isistitution. Upwards of eighty excursion trains, besides several spech special trains, arrived at Shrewsbury on 'I hursday ahG landed, it is said, nearly 60,000 visitors to the Royal Agri- cultural Show. Mr. Mundella, M.P., visited Sheffield on WednesdaV and laid the foundation stone of a new hall, to be called the Montgomery Hall, which is to be devoted to work of a re- ligious cbarcter. At the Food Reform Society meeting held in New York the other day, the Rev. Dr. Troy declared that not only he had never tasted flesh meat, but his father and grandfather had never tasted it. During the festivities in conaection with the Kte Yaliona , ale, at Pondicherry, a rocket set fire to a building contaisihg fireworks. A fearful explosion followed, 15 persons being killed and several injured. A woman, named Margaret Robinson, living in Brocco- street, Sheffield, and a man named James Robinson, liviet in Woodbinceroad, Sheffield, were both killed on SaturdaV night by falling downstairs. At Sheffield, on Wednesday, Samuel W. Kitching. late secretary to the Attercliffe Burial Board, was charged with having embezzled £1,400, the money of the ratepayers. The , prisoner was remanded for a week.

. ..„.. r THE PREMIER.—Mr. Gladstone, who was not looking al well as usual, left Dawning-street on Saturday afternoon for Coombe Wood, near Kingston, the residence of Lord Wai- verion, where be remained until Monday. A gold watch sod other articles were stolen from the ser- vants' apartments at Windsor Castle early on Wednesder morning. Two of the sentries have been arrested on sus- picion, and part of the stolen property has been recevered. At Sligo Assizes, on Wednesday, Michael Muldownev, as ex-policeman, was found guilty of the nawder of Peter Doherty, near Craughw 11, in 1881. His lordship sentenced the prisoner to be hanged at Sligo Jail on the 12th of Aa- gust. MIL WOODWARD WALLIS, barrister, sole trustee of the marriage settlement of Hobart Pa 7 sha was on Tuesday ur- dered by Justice Chittv to pay £7,000 jot' Court, which bad come into his bands as trustee. Justice Chit,y sail the ease was disgraceful. A NEGRO NOVELIST.—Tbe first novel ever written by a coloured man is being prepared for the prase by Mr. Georg' W. Williams, of Boston, United States. Mr. Williams WO also the first coloured man ever elected member of a Northern Legiel ature in the United States. At Leek Polio, Court, on Wednesdiy morning, Samuel Morris was fined for assaulting Mary Whittaker, a school- mistress. The complainant had chastised defendant's daughter, and he wen to the schoolroom and struck her ./0 the face, stunning her, causing her nose to bleed, and 'nibs- ted severe bruises. BURGLAR V. POLICEMAN,—At Maidenhead, about 1-30 a.m. on Tuesday, a man named William Jones was detected In the act of attempting to force an entrance into Walhatil House, and was arrested after a desaeree struggle, in the course of which both the prisoner and the policeman were injured. Proceeds of five recent burglaries were, it is stated, found upon the matt, MINERS' CONPERENCE.—Oa Tuesday, at the Miners' National Conference at Manchester—Mr S Wood (Lanca- shire) was appointed chairman, and Mr B Pickard (Wigan) secretary—lt was resolved to give all possible support to the Lancashire miners on strike against a 10 Der cant. reduction of wages, and to invite subscriptions throughout the country to the strike fund. SMOCKING MURDER.—A. coroner's jury at High Hill, Sussex, on Wednesday, returned a verdict of wilful murder against Thomas Hen' Whitcombe, a bottle dealer. The evidence showed that the prisoner had ill-treated and starved his wife and daughter. Theformer, when admitted into the infirmary, where sue died, could not stand, had not a par- ticlu of fat in her body, and the organs were bloodless. The prisoner's cruelty Was described as heartrending. THE OLD TESTAMENT REVISION.—The o.d Testament Company of Revisers has finished its labours. The preface has been finally revised and approved. As the work has to be submitted to Convocation before its issue to the public, it is not very likely to be published before next Easter. During the course of the revision two have re- signed and ten have died out of twenty-seven members of the Old Testament Company originally appointed by Con- vocation. KILLED ON THE RAILWAY.—On Monday a shocking accident occurred at Marsh-lane Station, near I iverpool. One of the workmen engaged in the construction of the new station had gone on to the four-foot way for a bucket which he had left there, and was returning to the siding when a train approached at full speed, and the front of the encioe struck him on the side of the head, knocking hint A considerable distance along the line. He died a few minutes afterwards. A MOTHER STARVING HER CHILDREN.—At Dartford Sessions, on Sa urday, Mary Fordham, of Bexley Heath, was charged with not providing sufficient food and clothing for her children. It was stated that the accused had left them 24 hours without any food. When removed to the Dartford Union the children were weighed, and it was found that the girl, aged ten, weighed 421 b., and that the three boys, aged seven, six, and three, weighed respectively 371 b., 201 b., and 181-Ib. They were clad in a few rags, and covered with vermin. The accused was committed for six weeks' hard labour.

Tun Duartti SCANDALS.—County Inspector Frencl4of the Royal Irish Cmistabulary, who was arrested in Cork on Tuesday morning, charged with having committed abomin- able offences, mriv,d in Dublin on Tuesday evening in cus- tody. More arrests are expected. At Dublin. on Wednesday, James Ellis French, late inspector of the Royal Irish Constabulary, was charged with immoral practices. Formal evidence was given, and the prisoner was remanded for eight days. James Pillar, tea and wine me chant, Rathmines, was afterwards cbarged with a similar offence. Mr. Pillar was arrested on Wednesday afternoon, and was remanded for a week. "GENERAL" BOOTH AND A RECENT RIIMOIJR.—GeneraI Booth visited Wrexham on Saturday and Sunday. Ad- dressiuo a meeting in the Public Hall, he said the members of the Salvation Army were the Radicals in religion. They wanted everybody to have the right to vote and speak on earth and a seat in heaven. Concerning a charge of irre- verence, he asked his critics to consider the people the Army had to deal with. It was impossible to make tap- room sinners into drawing-room saints in a moment. He denied the report that he had purchased Madame Patti's Welsh residence, nor bad be drawn one shilling from the Army funds since he started the movement 19 years ago. DE. JACOBSON. the ex-Bishop of Chester, died at the palatal early en Sunday, in his glst year. Hs was in fall posseesien of his mental faculties to the last moment. He leaves a widow, three sons, and two daughters. The funeral of the late Bishop took place en Thursday morning at Chester Cemetery. The body was taken from the Bishop's Palace to the ancient Abbey Church of St. John the Baptist, where the first portion of the service was read. There was a large attendance of the clergy of the diocese, who robed in the Warburton Chapel, and afterwards occupied seats in the choir and transept. The funeral service was as simple as possible, in accordance with the deceased bishop's special request. Tars WEarntatnow MEETING.—The ptize shooting at Wim- bledon began on Monday, when the Humphrey Challeng• Cup, shot for by Oxford and Cambridge University teams, was won by the former with 634 points against 549. The average of the day's shooting was low, owing to the high wind which prevailed. On Tuesday the Alfred Prize was won by Private Elambley, 2nd Cornwall, with a score of 32 points. Shooting in the first stage of the Queen's Prise commenced at 200 yards, but, except the Alfred, no compe- tition closed before evening gunfire. On Wednesday, Private Day, Btu Lancashire. Quarter-master Beeching, of the St. George's Rifl.s, and Private Ellett, Ist Somerset, each made highest possible scores for the Queen's Prize in their seven shots at 500 yards, and the s.moting generally allowed con- siderable improvement. On Thursday the shooting at Wimbledon was mainly confined to the 600 yards range of the Queen's Prize. Private Macbon. Guernsey Artillery. and Sergeant Ritchie, Ist Regrew, head the list with ag- gregates at the three ranges of 92. STOCKPORT GLEBE LEASES —The town clerk of Stock- port (Mr. Walter Hyde) has just presented to the Corpora- tion of that town an important report respecting the unfor- tunate dispute between the rector of Stockport (Rev. W. Symonds, M.A.), and the glebe leaseholders. At the outset, a petition,authorised by public meeting, was presented, ask- ing the Town Council" to assist the lessees of the glebe in obtaining a declaration, by Act of Parliament or otherwise, as to the rights of renewal in the existing glebe leases and of intending lessees to obtain statutory powers for the grant- ing of glebe leases or conveyances for building purposes on equitable terms, and for the renewal of existing leases upon the terms that the rent payable shall be such ground rent as is now or at the time of taking shall be payable as ground rent for like property in the town and district." The peti- tioners contend that.the rector is not acting in accordance with the spirit and intention of the Stockport Glebe E-1- change and Leasing Act in refusing to renew leases "on the best and most improved ground rents," and that he is "seek- ing, in effect, to introduce a system ot rack rents." To the simple question—" Shall the Corporation interfere 7" the Town Clerk returns an answer decisively in the negative. "The number of the glebe leaseholders," he says, "is in- significant, compared with the population, and to spend the borough funds for the protection of the private interests of a few individuals would not only be improper, but illegal." The Town Clerk does not think that the glebe lessee win derive any relief from the action of Parliament. Even in the event of a new statute, "the promoters of the bill would undoubtedly be called upon to compensate the rector in Come way for the riglits and property the Act would take away from him, as the Howie would never sanction e uch a gre_at injustice as to deprive him of his property, as it would be doing by extending a 99 to a 999 years' lease without eowi- pineation."—The report was passed without comment at Ice last meeting of the Town Council.

GREAT LIBERAL DEMONSTRATION AT WARRINGTON. ENTHUSIASTIC RECEPTION OF THE LIBERAL CANDI DATE. SPEECHES BY THE EARL OF DALHOUSIE, MR. MoMINNIES, M.P., AND MR. W. CROSFIELD. On Wednesday evening an enthusiastic meeting of the Liberal party in Warrington was held in the Public Hall, and also a crowded overflow meeting in the CO-operative Elalla There have in times past been many large and im- Posing demonstrations of the strength of Liberalism in War- rington, but there has not been in the recent political annals of the town a greater display of enthusiasm than that of Wednesday night. The meeting was advertised to com- mence at a quarter to eight o'clock, but more than an hour Prior to that time a large number of people had gathered in the street opposite to the Public Hall obviously eager to ob- tain seats, and on the doors being thrown open a living stream Poured continuously into the hall till shortly after seven o'clock, when every seat was filled and almost the whole of the standing space was taken up. The influx of people was then of necessity stopped, hut on anouncernent being made that an overflow meeting was to be held in the Co-opera- tive Hall the later arrivals made their way to that place, and were there addressed by Earl Dalhousie, Mr. W. Cros- geld, and other gentlemen. In the Public Hall the time from he being filled to the commencement of the proceedings was Pawed in a quiet and orderly manner, Mr. F. R. Roberts breaking the monotony of the long wait. by playing several ,_Popular tunes on the organ. The body of the uoll had been suitably, decorated with mottoes and gags. The words " Crosfield for ever" were placed in a prominent position immediately in front of the organ. and by another inscription in front of the ' Platform Liberals were invited to remember their majority "529" at the last election. Around the panels of the gallery tbe mottoes "The Bill, the whole Bill, and nothing ' hut the Bill," " No surrender," and "Long life to our Worthy member" wers hung, and it was clearly indicated by the expression. of opinion which came from the audience that the sentiments conveyed by these insciiptions were ' thoroughly endorsed by the vast majority of those present. ' Another indication of the pervading political feeling of the gathering was given by the large sale of a pamphlet, en- titled, "A History of Parliamentary Reform," by H. J. Leech, which were being sold by a lad from the Boys' and Girls' Refuge, Strangeways, Manchester. Promptly at a quarter to eight o'clock the speakers and their supporters on tbe platfom made their appearance, which was the signal for aft enthusiastic outburst of cheering, the advent of Earl Dalhoueie, Mr. W. Crosfield, and Mr. MeMinnies being spe- cially marked by an increased enthusiasm. (Loud cheers). Mr. WILLIAM CROSFIELD, who was received with loud and enthusiastic cheering, then rose to address the meeting. He said—lf you will excuse me for saying so, I think that Mr. Rigby is a man of limited vision. He has only—and it is certainly a good quality—confined himself to looking straight before him, and has given you the text, which many of you no doubt are enabled to see, of " No surren- der." (Cheers.) If he had followed the line a little bit longer, he would have found a sentiment which is quite as grateful to me—namely, "Long life to our worthy mem- ber." (Hear, hear, and loud cheers.) I regret that Mr. McMinnies, with that long life which we all hope for him, should not have seen fit to remain your member after the next general election; but such not being the c tee, I am thrust into the prominent position of first addressing this great meeting. Mr. Rigby has told you the circum- stances under which it was intended to hold this meeting when it was first spoken of now something like one mouth ago. We were fortunate in arranging for this meeting to have the presence of the noble earl, who has just left to ad- dress an overflow meeting—(cheere)—and who is a member of tier Majesty's Government, and is an enlightened member —(cheers)—of the House of Lords. (Loud cheers.) His presence this evening has given a different complexion to the demonstration which it had been intended to hold. I wish, therefore, with your permission, to immediately leave the personal element of this meeting and deal with wider questions which have recenely come to the front, and trust that you will not regret that I have made such a change in the intended programme. But before I leave the personal question entirely, I mast not forget that I am given to understand that Warrington is thirsting and yearning— (laughter)—for my private opinion upon an important political measure. (Cheers.) I am told by one of your public leaders that you are exceedingly anxious to know howl would deal with the proposed scheme of endowment of the Eet tblished Church, should such a thing come forward. (Hear, hear.) I presume that the Rev. Mr. Carle- ton as one of your prominent clerical leaders—(laughter) is well informed upon the questions upon which you would like to hear answers from me; and let me tell you a

long time to come if we deal in that way with that bright jewel of India—(cheers)—if we cultivate it, reset and make it better than it is. The Indian Budget is a very large and very important question, but it is one which always comes on in the House of Commons when very many of the mem- bers have gone out of town for their shooting and other matters, and thus this great question of finance in India is discussed in a House of about a score of members. The In- _ _ .

dime Budget is described as the annual annoyance of the House of Commons; but surely that is not a position for such a great country to be left in by the British Houses of Parliament. We need time to assimilate other na- tions into our national life. (Cheers.) We have injected our military system into India, as well as our commercial system, but there is one influence we Englishmen always look to as the most powerful element in moulding races we come in contact with to our methods and ways of thought. Now in India, family life, from peculiarities of climate and other peculiarities, is • loose, and this quiet influence of which I speak is therefore more feeble than it is in other parts of the world, where our colonists are settled with their families, and slowly permeate the nations amongst whom they dwell. They say we are not a continental nation, but with all these responsibilities F claim we are one of the greatest of Continental na- tions. One question you will wish to hear more about— that is, the events which have come up during the past few weeks, more particularly referring to the conduct of the House of Lords in the recent crisis. (Cheers.) The House of Lords are acting with characteristic obstinacy. (Hear, hear.) Obstinacy, you will often have noticed I dare say, is the strongest weapon of weakness. (Cheers.) When the question of the Franchise Bill was last before the House of Lords the dominant majority—not so large as their lordships hoped—had decided that the bill should not be treated as the representatives of the people would have liked it to be. (Hear, hear.) From what has taken place during the past few hours one would think that we are too severe in c•iticising the House of Lords as we have done. (A. voice : We as too lenient.") It would rather seem they were deserving of pity, for as I read they are under the heel of a single man. He would scarcely dare to suggest it, but if a vote on the sabject was taken by ballot in the House of Lords to-night, Lord Salisbury would find himself ai a very Small minority. (Cheers.) The question has been dealt with by many authorities, and in considering it we are bouod by the opinion of those who are better intormed than we are. Our great leader Mr. Gladstone—(loud cheers) —tells us, "We believe that there is sufficient power in this country legally and peacefully to secure the attainment of the ends which the nation has in view." He says for him- self and his colleagues, "We sleall calmly, quietly, aad firmly cirry through this great measure." (Cheers ) Chris- tian charity such as that of Mr. Gladstone, I am afraid, is scarcely possible for most of as in this room, and that to as weaker mortals some stronger measures ought to be permitted. Let me turn to a more ar- ardent spirit. Sir Charles Dilke is not usually rlle fly-mouthed, and this is what he has said: "Treat the circumstances in the calmest language; look at it in the quietest way." (Hear, hear.) I think there have been few harder things said of the House of Lords then were said to I the House of Lords by the noble earl whom you are going to hear speak presently. (Cheers.) Closing a speech of great power and breathing the true spirit of Liberalism, ne told their lordships that the spirit of the age was against them. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) And what is the spirit of the age? Ft is industrious, and we in Lancashire recognise the spirit of the age. We feel that the spirit of the age is that spirit which makes to-day better than yesterday. (Hear, hear.) The spirit of the age is now—thanks to the Liberal measures —becoming educated; it knows what it wants, and it knows how to get what it wants. (Cheers.) The spirit of the age is historical; it studies the past in order that it m ty improve the future. (Hear, hear.) The s irit of the age is inventive—if it cannot get what it wants by one method, it waits quietly and thinks over how it can be ob- tattled by some other method. The spirit of the age Is practical, and will allow no drones in the social hive. (Hear, hear.) The spirit of the age is progressive; it may be slow, but it is sure. (Hear, hear.) And why should any man or I class of men in England live outside these influences that I have spoken of? (Hear, hear.) It is a wilful self-isolation if any class or cast put itself without the pale of the spirit of the age, and I say " Woe to these who wilfully stand aloof." Their lordship, to whom the spirit of the age is in opposition, are obstructive. (Hear, hear.) But obstruction is no new thing. I will read you a description of the Re- form Bill, and in order to give it greater paint I will tell you by whom it was, and when, said. If I omitted these par- ticulars I could readily read this and you would consider, I believe, that it would be the most effective part of my own speech in dealing with the questioa before us. I quote the speech of Sydney Smith, delivered in the year 1831, and I ask you to listen—"l feel most deeply the event which has taken place, because, by putting the two Houses of Parliament in collision with each other, it will impede public busin-es and diminish the public prosperity. I feel it because I believe it will sow the seeds of cleacay hatred between the aristocracy and the great mass of the people. The loss of the bill I do not feel, and for the best of all possible reasons—because I have not the slightest idea that the bill is lost. I have no more doubt that before the expiration of the winter this bill will be pessed than I have that the annual tax bills will be pissed, and greater certainty than this no man can have, for Franklin tells us there are but two thiags certain in this world—death and taxes. As for the possibility of the House of Lords preventing ere long a reform of Parliament. I hold it to be the most absurd notion that ever entered into human imagination!' He then goes on to relate the story of a great storm in the neighbourhood of Sidmoath in the year 1824, and of an in- habitant of the shore of Sidmouth whom name has come down to us on the stream of history, who was found at her cottage door, with her pettens on, and broom in hand. It was the venerable dame Partington, of whom we have heard before trying to prevent the Atlintic ocean coming through her cottage &kir. The Atlantic was roused. Mrs. Partington's spirit was up • but the contest was unequal. 'The Atlantic 'beat' airs. Partington. She WAS excellent at a slop or a puddle ; but she should not have meddled with a tempest. Gentlemen, be at your ease—be quiet and steady. You will boat Mrs. Partiogton." (Laugh- ter and loud cheers.) Mr. CHARLES BROADBENT, who was received with cheers, said he had the honour to move a very important resolution but he saw from the way in which they had received the speaker who had just sat down, that it would not want very many words of his to recommend it to them. The eesolu'- tion ran as follows:—. This meeting is of opinion that Mr. William Crosheld, J.P., is a fit and proper person to repre- sent th s borough of Warrington in the House of Commons, and pledges itself to use every possible legitimate moans to secure his triumphant return at the next general election." (Loud cheers.) Mr. William Crosfield, Mr. Broadbent con- tinued, was not a stranger to Warrington. He was connec- ted by many ties of interest and sympathy with Warrington already, and those ties would increase every day. He was also, as they knew, nearly related to a family which was held already in very high esteem in Warrington. (Cheers.) That family was held in high esteem by those in that room for their staunch adherence to Liberal principles, and not only that, for they were held in high esteem in the town generally for their numerous acts of kindness and benevo- lence both private and public. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) In addition to Mr. Crosfield's local connections he had had the great advantage of a training amongst the etaunch Liber- als of Liverpool, where he had as they knew, taken a leading part. The Liberals in Liverpool used to be in a minority, but he (Mr. Broadbent) thought the time was come when they would soon be in a majority. (Hear, hear.) That city had generally taken a leading part in the councils of the Liberal party and of the nation. A few years ago they chose as their- candidate a gentleman not now known by that name, Lord Ramsay—e(cheers)— and although that contest was unsuccessful it was carried on in a way which did honour both to them and to him. He had new been raised to another place, and he (Mr. Broad- bent) would only say one word, and that was that if there had been more Peers like Lord Dalhousie the Franchise Bill would now have been passed, and the country would have been in a more comfortable and peaceful state of mind. (Hear, hear.) They had heard Mr. Crosfield's speech, and he had seen in what spirit they had heard and how much ' they thought of it. It seemed to him to be a straight- forward exposition of his political principles, which he was cure would be satisfactory in that room, and which were the result not of yesterday or to-day but of long thought and deep rejection; and he believed they might rely upon Mr. Crosfield as being the most suitable candidate for the borough of Warrington. (Cheers.) They bad need to send a. Strome man up to Parliament at the present time. (Hear, hear.) There was a great deal of work (or them to do. They had to meet not only their old friends the Conservatives, who had an objection to any change whatever, but they had to meet the Tory democrats, who had no objection to change, but wished to change in the wrong direction— (laughter and loud cheers)—and who appealed to the pas- sions and prejudices of the people rather than their reason, land though the leader ef that party did not feel able to meet the electors of Birmingham a little while ago in consequence of the great heat of the weather—(laughter)—still he (Mr. Broadbent) thought there was a strong element of danger in that direction, and he had the greatest possible confidencein urging upon them the resolution which he had read. It Walt no slight thing to ask a man to become a candidate fora borough in these arduous times, but he was sure Mr. Cros- field deserved, and he would get their most heaety support. (Loud cheers.) Mr. E J. GrEST said that be rose to briefly bui cordially second the resolution. He did so because he believed that Mr. Crosfield, as the Liberal candidate for the borough of Warrington, was the right man in the right place. (Ap- plause.) What they bad seen and heard of Mr. Crnsfield's opinions, his character and his position, led them to believe that they might have perfect confidence in bins. He had expounded his views to them that night and on a previous occasion, and he (the speaker) thought that as a politician, a social reformer, and a Christian, Mr. Crosfield moved on the right lines. He was no mere theorist. He could give a good exposition, a clear, concise exposition of the faith that was in him. But he was eminently a practical man also. The record of the last twenty-five years of his life testified to the good deeds that he had done. Asa true-hearted Liberal Mr. Crosfield had won the esteem, the respect, and the affection of the Liberals of Liverpool—(appleuse)—and he (tbe speaker) believed that the Liberals wanld have I secured him as a candidate at the last election if he would have been willing to accept the invitation. As a social re- former Mr. Crosfield was to the fore. He had done a noble, • work in connection with temperance reformation. (Ap- plause.) He had not closed his eyes to the fearful evils that resulted in the wake of the drink traffic, and he had not only tried to prevent drunkenness, but he had acted the ; +toed Samaritan in trying to heal that which had been ' diseased, or that which had been ruined in connection with

little secret. (Hear, hear.) When I received an inquiry from Mr. Carleton in the middle of June, and I had wraten what I considered a satisfactory and a concise reply to his , question, a second thought came to my assistance, and it occurred to me that there were possibilities, of accident ; that it was not improbable that the answer which I gave might not reach the public of Warrington in the exact words in which they would fins from my pen ; that there were evil disposed induences— possibly in the printing offices of Warrington—(laughter)— which might let slip a material word which would alter en- tirely the opinion which I had given; and now I prefer under the protection of a large meeting like this to give my answer in a form in which it cannot be misunderstood.

(Cheers.) As far as I can remember in the words which I wrote a month ago, but withheld from their intended end, the WRV in which I should treat a scheme of disendow- ment of the Established Church of England is that natioaal money should be devoted to national purp )ses—(ch&ere)— and that in the case of more recent endowments for religions purposes these should be treated in an equitable spirit— (cheere)—sullicient safeguards being provided to prevent the reestablishment of any religious denomination under a , slightly altered form. So much for my own opinions 'on these questions. Since the arrangements have been com- pleted for this meeting many events have happened. It may have occurred to some of you that three or four weeks I was rather a long period to postpone a meeting of this kind, but the Government was then in trouble, and it ' was thought that the electors of Warrington, by a meeting I of this kind, might help them over these troubles, aud that, therefore, such a meeting should be held at once. But there is a vitality about a Liberal Government—a Liberal tio- vernment which was founded upon the hearts of the people has within itself a vitality which brings it through greater , troubles than those which the present Government has ex- 1 I perienced during the last few weeke. We are met to-night under a changed aspect of affairs. We are met to express our couidence—and lam sure you will do it with all your hearts—in the Liberal Government, the Government which i is so nobly led by Mr. Gladstone—(cheers)—who in all 1 his acts, whether public or private, whether political I or social, shows that he has a brilliant genius 1 which is guided by a humble spirit. (Cheers.) We 4 are reformers. It has been well said that reform is in the I air when Mr. Gladstone is in power. Reform has been in 1 the air ever since he came to the front, now so many years : ago. (Cheers 1 We who were the electors of South Lan- 4 cashire in 1865 remember the pride with which we re- turned him in that year, and yota no doubt may well re- i member the deep humiliation which we the electors of South-West Lancashire, felt when we failed again to return him as we tried to do in 1868. It was from that date till I 1874 that he carried his great measures of reform which have done so much for the amelioration of the cenditien of I Englend and her dependencies. (Cheers.) We came then under the magic influence of his power, and England is , I benefited by all the great deeds which he did during those I I years which are too numerous for me to detain 1 you in recapitulating. It was then that Liberalism swept 1 like a torn ido over the whole land, and swept before it all 1 the obstructions which then opposed themselves to the wishes of the people. Difficulties in other forms have crop- . ped up since, but the power of Liberalism and the will of the people was sufficient to carry those measures which the 1 people desired to have. (Hear, and cheers.) It was only a ( few days ago that Mr. Gladstone in very touching language thanked a number of his supporters for a vote which they had just passed to him. He thanked them in very few words, hut in very effective words. He thanked them for the confi fence, the kindness, the love with which he had been supported by those who sympathised with him in public aff drs. (Cheers.) I, as one of the younger school of Liberals, desire no more words; I desire no better words than those three which Mr. Gladstone has supplied me with, and I say I desire to follow him as my leader politically, with all the confidence, the kindness, and all the love that I can give him. (Cheers.) This Government. then, is earnest ; it is ende ivouring to do that which the peeple wish to see done, and in that we should support them. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) But there are difficulties in the way. There is opposition. In. the old days one undersmod what opposition meaet. There was a number of responsible men in opposition to the Government. Generally, these who had recently been in office and were fairly familiar with the duties of office, who formed a constitutional com- pany of critics, and passed in review the various measures which the Government of the country proposed. But those days are gone, and we are now in the face of divided op- position. The pledges which may be given by what I be- lieve Mr. Disraeli called her Majesty's Oppoei- tion are disregarded by the followers of that Opposition be- low the gangway. In fact it seems if these affairs go on as they are at present we shall see each man fighting for his own hand. It makes the pursuit of politics very much like a hurdle race, those who are responsible for the Govern- ment and the country having to pursue their way over obstacles which are imposed by tie irresponsible members who sit opposite to them. Look at one question which has been a great deal before the country—the Egyptian Question. We have had this question bandied about until it has become almost like a game of shuttlecock and battledore. How often have we seen a skilfully-devised structure of painted feathers floating fram below the gangway on one side cf the House, in the direction of the benches upon which the Ministry sits. Occasionally by a chance win! a shuttle- cock has dawn on to the front opposition benches. As we see children on the village green excited by the game of shuttlecock, so in the excitement of this game the serious members of the Opposition have been found engaged in the game of bandying the shuttlecock back again. (Cheers.) Bat one cannot regard this treatment of the ques- tion as one of seriousness, for no sooner does some other question come up, some recent question of the Franchise, than we find that these same schoolboy politicians are diverted from the old game of Egyptian shuttlecock, and they take the Franchise, as with boys and girls the passion for one game follows another, so, as shuttlecock passes away ,we have the game of hoops and tops. In the House of Com- mons a fewr weeks ago the third rsading of the Franchise Bill was carried without any audible opposition from those who have been engaged in opposing it, and with only one visible Conservative member, who had not time to get out of the House of Commons before the division took place.
