'llia 'dkys, and If *alrtimes, ... they niedid-Christian melt. - (Applause.) - He (the sneaker) was no bigot. Were a man Church of England or Noncon• forfaist it mattered not, if he were a Christian, (Applause.) Mr: Crosfield, was, he believed, a Christian man—(hear, hear)—cloeely connected with a Christian church, a deacon of /in independent church for many years, and that gave him (Mr. Guest) increasing confidence in him. Then Mr. cr field's position was all that they could wish for. Th ugli'liiite a young man, Mr. Crosfield had attained a pos tion that would enable him to devote his time and energies to the well-being of his constituents. (Applause.) There were none of them but mast feel regret at the cause that had brought them together that night. They deeply regretted that Mr. MeMinnies felt himself no longer able to be the member for Warrington. Mr. McMinnies had served the Liberal cause in Warrington well. (Applause.) He deserved their respect and their affection and he had it. (Renewed applause.) They would gladly have given him their suffrages as in days gone by, but Mr. McMinnies felt that that could not be. They rejoiced to know that Mr. Crosfield had many, if not all, of the good qualities of Mr, McMiunies. (Hear, hear.) It would be affectation to say that Mr. Crosfield was that day all that Mr. McMinnies was to them. That could not be, but the fact that Mr. Croafield was twenty years younger than Mr. McMinnies was in his favour. (Applause.) When they returned Mr. Crosfield to , the House of Commons, as they believed they should return him—(applause)—they would feel that as he was perform- ing hie duties in the House ef Commons he would be doing it with more ease and more comfort than Mr. McMinnies ever could have done. (Applause.) They would not forget their old love in the years that were yet to come, but he trusted that they should have reason for increased confidence in their new M.P. (Applause.) _ ,

Mr. BENJAMIN( Fwansa spoke in support of the resolu- tion. He was, he said, proud to have the honourable posi- tion that he occupied that night, not simply becatiee he stood where be was, bat because he represented tne tidies and gentlemen sittiug in the body of the hall and round the gallery. He represented the working-classes. (Applause.) Great credit was due to the Committee of the Liberal As- sociation ef Warrington in that they had seen fit and proper to elect three working-men to stand upon that platform and to speak on behalf of the working-men of Warrington in support of so able a man as Mr. Crosfield. He was BIM from the appearance of that grand large meeting—a grander la-ee meeting was never seen in Warrington—be believed that they had agreed among themselves as to the resolution and that it was the opinion of that meeting that Mr. Cron- field was a fit and proper person to represent them in the House of Commons. If they had that opinion and did not carry it out at the polling-booth, if they did not carry it out by using their influence amengst the working-classes to in- fluence them to support, and to vote for Mr. Crosfield, then they would be falling far short of their duty as the working- men of Warrington. (Applause.) The abilities of Mr. Crosfield had been so laid before them by previous speakers as not to require a word from him. But with respect to the great drink question the attitude of Mr. Crosfield was of itself sufficient to bring him forward as the repreeentative for Warrington. He believed that it had been said that the Liberal candidate was going to be defeated at the next elec- tion. (Cries of "No.") But they could judge for them- selves bow excellent a man was the Liberal candidate, and in his own mind he believed that their candidate was the wan for the future representation of the borough. He would also say "Long live their excellent member Mr. McMinoies," for, when he was dead and gone his life would live whilst he was sleeping, for they should not forget what Mr. McMinnies had done,.not only for the Liberal party of Warrington, but for the whole town of Warrington. They must do all that they could to secure the return of Mr. Cros- field. They were aware that the Corrupt Practices Act had already passed, and that they would have to individually, like men and women—(laughter)—support their member. If they did their duty well Mr. Crosfield would not only be returned by a ;majority of 529 at the bead of Sir Gilbert Greenall, bot he would have nearly 1,000 majority. (Ap- plause.) He said "Long live the bon. William Evrart Gladstone' He hoped that Mr. Gladstone would live for twenty years yet, and that they, the working-men of Eng- land should continue to reap the great benefits that he bad " 80 long worked to bring about—such grand measures for the good of the masses. He hoped that Mr. Gladstone would long live, and that when he had retired from his labours he would have the pleasure of looking round him and seeing what the country was reaping from his past efforts. He was glad to support Mr. Crosftelci because he knew that Mr. Crosfield would support the grandest man the world ever knew. (Cheers.) The resolution was then put and carried with acclamation whereupon The CHAIRMAN said: I am very glad that you have so cordially supported this resolution by your shoat of hands. I think that the recommendation that you have had from the gentlemen who supported IMO tesointion is worthy of your attention. It will depend 'entirely upon you on the day of election, how each one of you shall wry himself. (Applause.) alr. T. FLOOD said he must confess that the duty that devolved upon him was rather more than he felt equal to undertake, for the simple reason that he knew the veterans which were upon that platform, and who might have been selected out of that large audience, who would have better pat forward the resolution which he had to euemit to their consideration. The resolution he bad the honour to move was to this effect :—" This meeting desires to express its unabated confidence in the policy of Her Majesty's Go- vernment both at home and abroad, and Wane recognising with gratitude the untiring zeal of the Prime Minister and his colleagues in their efforts to extend the principles of equality and justice to two millions of our fellow-country- men. further pledges itself to sustain the hands of ministers in their righteous purpose by every possible and lawful effort." (Cheers.) If, Mr. Flood continued, one might judge by' the things that had passed within' this last week, one would be inclined to think that the Government bad but one object in view during the whole time they had been in office, everything for the time being seemed to have sunk into oblivion. Ireland seemed to have sunk to where the lories had wished it long ago—(hear, hear, and labghter)— Egypt would seem as if it had been coveted by the waters of the Nile outright, which proved to him that the whole struggle for the last two or three years had beep a mere sham on the part of their Coniervative friends. There bid been n'o reality in their policy, which had been one of direct °berm- tier] to the efforts of a noble and grand career, (Cheers.) The efforts the Conservatives had put forth were not to pro- gress the nation, not to confer their rights upon the people but simply to scheme for office. And who were these aspi- rants for office? (Hear, bear, and laughter.).' They were new-fledged leaders of the Conservative party who had just hopped out of their nest—(laughter)—apd who aspired to reputatiba and a long life of glory, which he hoped would be cut short. (Laughter.) The agitation that had taken place within the last few days was such a one as had: only rarely occurred in this country. They had occurred three times within 50 years. What was the state of public feel- ing to-day? They could imagine what it was 50 years ago. Mr. Fawcett bad said on the previous day that this was an opportunity not to be lost. (Hear, hear.) If the people were wise in their generation they would grasp the opportu- nity and make use of the passing events. If they were wise in their generation, and led by that prudence and that wis- dom which was to be found in their leaders, they would be led to victory, for in the end, as Sydney Smith said, Mrs. Partington would not keep out the storm, and neither would the House of Lords stand against the will of the people. (Cheers.) But unaided by an agitation throughout the country the Ministry could not well carry out its object, but it was by the aid of that wave of public opinion that seemed to be sweeping broadcast over the land that the Ministers would be able to carry the franchise question and giye privileges to the people They were asked that night to support the resolution, which required them to weigh well its purport; it required them to pledge themselves to the Government who had been unswerving in their duty to the rights of the people from the day they went into office to the present hour. They had tiulfilled the whole of their pledges so far as it had been possible to re- deem them; and they had been unswerving in their wishes to lead the people to victory. It would be found at the eleventh hour whether it was that the people bad the power I to remove the obstruction in the way, not by rioting, not byl any unconstitutional agitation, but by their allegience and , support of a ministry who were determined to lead them to victory. (Cheers.) In the person of their intended candi- date they had a man who was pledged to that policy. He had heard a reference that right to Mr. Crosfield's years, and if he followed in the footsteps of their present member they might hope for a bright future for the Liberal party in War- rington. (Cheers.) They were not disposed to be tempted by fishing—(langhter)—or any other belt that might be thrown out to them to let them in. (Hear, hear and laughter.) As long as they gave Mr. Crosfield that unswerving encourage- ment and support so long would they be supporting a de- monstration whose one object was to carry out the wishes and the will of the people. (Loud aheers). Mr. MeMnetras' M.P., who rose to second the resolution, was received with load and prolonged cheering. He said: In the presence of, I think, the largest public Liberal meet- ing that we have ever had in this hail. I have great pleasure in saying a few words in support of the resolution which has just been moved. I command to you the support of the present Government in the first place, because it consists of the leading members and the ablest members of the Liberal party. (Applause.) We are the Liberal party. We are members of the Liberal party, however, and when I look back upon wlaat I remember during the time of the passing of the Test and Coporation Acts to the time of the pessing of the Irish Land Act last year, I feel proud that the Liberal party have done 80 much for the good government of this country. (Applause.) But 1 commend to your confidence and trust the Government of Her Majesty at the present dine, because that Government is presided over by the ablest English statesman of the day (Applause.) You may depend upon it that whatever complications and diffi- culties may wise, you may trust to Mr. Gladstone to over- come those difficulties, and to carry the country safely through those complications. (Applause.) For fifty years Mr. Gladstone has devoted himself with all his energies and with all his conscientorieness to the good government o/ this coentry, and he has been, I suppose, instrumental in carry- ing more measures that have been for the benefit of this country than perhaps any other statesman of his time. (Applause, and a voice: "Any time.") There is net a man in this room, there is not a woman in this room, who is not better, and wiser, and freer tbis day because of Mr. Glad- stone's life and work. (Applause.) And I feel great confi- dence in recommending Her Majesty's Government to your support, because Mr. Gladstone is at the head of it. (Hear. I hear.) Two or three—you haow I never could sit down with.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, JULY 19, 1884.

Liberalism in Warrington is, as heretofore, alive and hearty. There were those whose wish was father to the thought who sug- gested that, with the retirement of Mr. McMnstmEs, the present popular member for the borough, the Liberal party would have "no chance" for the return of another can- didate; but, if they say anything now, they will have to tell another tale after the magni- ficient demonstration of Wednesday night. The Public Hall crowded with some 2,+00 people, and an " overflow " meeting in the Co-operative Hall, which was filled with another 600, is an event unprecedented, we believe, in the annals of Warrington. It is on record that the Conservative party, some years ago, in the fulness of their expecta- tions, ventured to arrange for a second meet- ing on the same night, but the human stream, alas for them, suddenly ran dry; there was no "overflow," and, consequently no " over- flow " meeting. From the hour that the first speech of Mr. WILLIAM CROSFIELD, the chosen candidate of the Liberal Association, was laid before the electors, it may be said that he has been growing in favour with the constituency. The speech to begin with had the right rinz ; it was modest but manly, and displayed such a grasp of the situation and such a thoroughness of Liberalism as in- stantly commended itself to the dispassionate mind. It was natural that the electors should wish to see and hear such a man; but it is the turn of events in the rejection of the Franchise Bill by the House of Lords which has aroused the enthusiasm s'of Liberals to the highest pitch. Lord SALISBURY tells us that such expressions of opinion can be

r" produced to order;" but the wonder is, !if that be so, that his supporters do not give the order in Warrington. They have been doing their "level best" in the town for some time; have held meeting after meeting with a view to get at the working- man; but the working-man responded so badly that, on the last occasion, the small room which had been hired was half filled only. There must have been some defect about the order, or can it be that the time has arriveji when the people have resolved to take their own affairs in their own hands, with a determination not to accept " orders " of any kind? The day of mono- polies and pocket boroughs is past, and Sir GILBERT GREENALL, if he has nothing better to offer than Wilderspool ale, Walton sprats, or the handle of his name, had better, since his mind is a blank as to politics, compose himself in his easy chair and retire from a conflict for which nature never equipped him, and for which by advancing age he is now utterly incapacitated. Warrington wants a representative in the House of Commons who will be a fitting successor of our present member; a man in the prime of life, of wide information, sound judgment, and sterling character, and such a man the electors evidently believe they have found in Mr. WILLIAM CRoSFIELD. Lord DALHOUSIE, who is studiously careful not to over-praise, aptly describes him as "at once a thorough-going Liberal, and a straight- forward, manly, and sound politician," and he speaks not from a momentary acquaint- ance, but from an insight gained in the stormy period of a conflict "when men show out in their true colours." Had his lordship not had the highest opinion of Mr. CROS- FIELD, we may be quite sure he would not have left his post as a member of the Minis- try to advocate his claims on a public plat- form at a time when, as a peer, his action is so likely to be misconstrued or misrepre- sented by the Opposition. But he is an " enlightened " peer, with a high sense of duty, and a courage equal to its performance. Mr. CROSFIELD was subjected to a trying ordeal in being brought, under the circum- stances of the time, before such a large audi- ence; but he showed himself in every respect equal to the occasion. He takes a firm hold of everything that he handles, and gives the impression not only of strength, but of power in reserve. We need men in the House of Commons who have, as he has, a deep sense of the responsibility of governing an empire embracing 300 millions of people; who will demand that justice shall be done in Canada in the west as in India in the east; and who are able and willing to instruct and put in their places the unenlightened CARLETONS who may be troublesome at home. Mr. CROS- FIELD is a Liberal who has watched, who has studied, and who has therefore a reverence for Mr GLADsTONE, and no observation, let us confess, was more to our taste in the admirable speech that he made than his affectionate reference to the greatest statesman of the age. With Lord DALHOUSIE by his side, and with the risk which it involved of compromising his lordship, he could not well say all he thought as to the action of the Peers in setting themselves against the will of the people. But he was not dumb on the all- important subject, and, after expressing his own views, nothing could be more pertinent, and nothing certainly more enjoyable, than the reading of the racy quotation in which SYDNEY SMITH has immortalised Mrs. PAR- TINGTON—and the House of Lords. Lord DALHOUSIE, in addressing the audience, ' faced the issue before the country in a resolute manner; and rendered a service which may be described as national in placing the saddle on the right horse It is the object of the Conservatives from Lord SALISBURY down- wards (or should we say upwards?) to trail the herring of Redistribution across the scent in the hunt for the Franchise Bill; but Lord DALHOUSIE will have none of it, for he showed by proof upon proof that they had no love either for one measure or the other. Nay more, he carried the war into the enemy's camp when he assailed the so-called constitu- tional party for their unconstitutional con- duct in seeking to arrogate to themselves the right to force a dissolution—a dissolution which, as intended to be upon the present re- stricted franchise, would be a revelation of the want of confidence the Tories have in the toil- ing millions of the country. His speech was in the right key, at the right time, and we need hardly say that we think it was in the right place. It will strengthen Liberals throughout the kingdom in sustaining Mr. GIADSTONE, And it will strengthen the Liberals of Warrington in seeking to send to St. Stephen's a loyal supporter of the PRIME MINISTER in the person of Mr. WILLIAM CROSFIELD.

The Rev. T. R. MATTHEWS, of St. John's Church, Earlestown, is determined to see how far the force of folly can go; and it must be acknowledged that the fertility of resource which he displays in the matter is something marvellous. It was thought months ago that he must have exhausted ' himself—that he would not be able to preserve novelty in his absurdities; but in this respect it may be said of him, as was said of CLEOPATRA—age cannot wither him nor custom stale his infinite variety. It is not even yet quite clear what he is aiming at, but if his object is to quarrel with everything and everybody about the church and Sunday school, so that he may rid himself of all in- cumbrance, and have the satisfaction finally of preaching to "a beggerly account" of empty pews, we should say he is likely to be successful. Beginning with the popular organist who would not wrongfully dismiss a member of the choir to please the Vicar, Mr. MATTHEWS has managed to get rid of both organist and choir; he has "struck," too, against wardens and sidesmen ; made a raid on teachers and scholars in the Sunday school; brought about the resignation of the curate; and finally, on Sunday last, ordered both apparitor and organ-blower out of church. We don't know what he can do next, unless he quarrels;with his finger ends, or has a row with the proverbial church mouse. But then his ways are not as .the ways of ordinary mortals, for he is either above and beyond them, or a great way below them. The Rev. H. E. SMITH, the late curate, has shown throughout the proceed- ings which have brought such discredit upon the church an extraordinary amount of patience and toleration. He has been dis- posed to yield so much to secure for a moment peace—or the semblance of peace as to lay himself open to the charge of tolerating proceedings which he knew to be wrong; but, despite all this, Mr. MAT- THEWS has not hesitated to speak to and of the curate as though he were unjustly re- sisting his authority. But there is a limit to human endurance ; there is a point at which resistance becomes a din), and we congratu- late Mr. SMITH on having had the courage to speak his mind when a piece of gross injus- tice was being done, and to resign rather ,

than take part in it. He may be assured that, although it may put him to temporary incon- venience, he will not suffer in the long run. And what even if he should? Better break stones on the highway than be party to emptying church and school, and bringing all that so many men hold dear unto utter con- tempt. The people most to be pitied are the parishioners of St. .john's, who are driven from the fold which should have been a shelter and a comfort to them. They have made great sacrifices of money, and time, and labour, in order that they might have a place of worship worthy of their aspirations ; and having achieved the object of their ambition, they find that the cup is dashed from their lips by the stranger whom they have admitted within their gates. A great wrong has been done them, and yet they are power- less in obtaining redress ; they would have let bye-gones be bye-gones ; they would have forgiven unto "seventy times seven," but the olive branch is broken on their backs, and they are driven from the church by the reverend bailiff who has, unhappily, obtained possession. What are they to do? They may erect another structure of iron or of stone, but if they still retain their con- nection with the State Church they will incur the risk of a similar experience. The system is bad, and they will do well to consider be- fore making a fresh start whether it shall be on the old lines. Irresponsible authority, whether in the House of Lords or in the Established Church, is a bad thing, and it should be the business of righteous men to get rid of it at the earliest moment. "Power like a desolating pestilence pollutes whate'er it touches" when it is not under wise control. The parishioners of St. John's have felt the terrible force of this truth in the experience of the past few months ; they now see, and many of them readily acknowledge, that the remedy for the evils from which they suffer is to be found in severing the connection be- tween Church and State. Seeing this, let them be careful, whatever else they may do, not to forge fetters which will bind them in the future.

FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASH.—Foot-and-mouth disease hap again unfortunately broken out in Cheshire, there being now 18 animals under treatment, and a fresh outbreak ix reported at Blacon-cum-Crabwell.

A RIVER POISONED.—Tha River Weaver in Cheshire has again been poisoned, and fish have been found dead all along its course. Several fine trout over two pounds in weight were picked out of the river at 13.ambridge, near Nantwich. This is the third occasion this season on which the waters of this fine trout stream have been deliberately poisoned._

HERR PR/EGER'S CONCERT.—A, concert, promoted by Herr Pneger, was held on Monday evening in the Co-operative Hall, Cairo-street, Warrington, and was, notwithstanding the unfavourable nature of the weather, very largely atten- ded. A varied and well-arranged programme of vocal and in- strumental music had been prepared, but unfortunately, through one cause or another, two or three of the artistes to whom important parts had been assigned, were not able to attend. In spite, however, of this serious dsawback, the con- cert was not unworthy ef its talented promoter, the instru- mental music, and particularly those parts in which Herr Prmger himself took part, being in itself sufficient to not merely redeem the concert from failure, but even to satisfy any but the most exacting audience. The instrumental music consisted of performances by the band who were often applauded; selections on the pianoforte by Miss Baker who, by her very skilful manipulation ef that instrument, IVOR more than one recall; and pieces on the pianoforte by Miss Eckersley, Oreste Prmger, junior, Mr. Lane, and Herr Prmger. The chief feature of the concert was a violin solo by Herr Praeger which elicired quite a storm of applause. In response to this outburst of approbation Herr Praeger gave a selemion on the violin and pianoforte simultaneously. The vocal part of the programme was sustained by Miss Prmger, Miss Eckersley, and Mr. Bellian, who were each w an ly applauded. " PUFFING " EETRAORDINARY.—The Sporting alsroniele thus makes game of our "neutral" contemporary :—" A Warrington paper. which is evidently anxious to keep pace with the times, and even to steal a march, if possible, on The Times in the matter of enterprise, publishes in a recent • issue a suggestively prophetic and highly-intereeting para- graph, in the opening sentence of which it communicates the cheerful tidings that "in view of the coming General Election our reporting staff is at its full strength of fifteen members." I quote this sentence, because I think that when Mr. Gladstone reads his " Echoes " to-day he will be ,delighted to learn that this Warrington paper, at least, is quite ready for the "coming election." The advanced stage of preparedness which the selected and fully strong band of fifteen reporters has attained may perhaps dispose finally of Mr. Gladstone's objections to a dissolution of Parliament. It is more than likely that he has kept the faithful Com- mons around him so long because he feared that our War- rington contemporary might have only fourteen full- strength reporters anJ a boy, or fourteen boys and one reporter of full capacity in readiness for the campaign. Now that he is assured of their being all there, he can hesitate no longer, and the General Election must be hurried up with- out farther delay. As to the blushing candidates for par- liamentary honours who will now fling themselves at the feet of the constituencies, they will be deeply gratified to learn that in our Warrington contemporary "meetings are reported at 'great length, entirely irrespective of the poll- tics of the speakers." By way of counteracting the dazzling brilliancy of the prospect opened up to tub-thump- ing orators in this declaration, our prudent contemporary goes on to observe, "Being a purely commercial newspaper, we cannot, however, undertake to report meetings mot adver- tised in our weekly or daily columns." Were I a Cicero, or Demosthenes,or even Gladstone—which, the gods be praised, lam not--I should send columns of advertisements to this Warrington paper at once, and make sure of getting my future speeches reported therein." DARESEuRY HIGHWAY BOARD.—A meeting of this Board was held on Thursday afternoon, in the Court House, Daresbury. There were present Messrs. E Greenall (chair- man), John Mayer, John Mclntyre, W Bradford, J W Had- dock, J Parr, T Bennett, If Houghton, C T Whitley, W Long, and Major W V Fox.—Extraordinary Traffic : A letter was read from the Town Clerk of Liverpool relative te the claim of the Board for damage caused to the roads by extraordinary traffic, asking that the Board might allow Mr Walker, their contractor, to inspect the Board's books. The Surveyor (Mr. Derbyshire) mentioned that he had al- lowed the books to he seen. It was agreed that the demand for payment of extrordinary traffic should be passed. A Complaint: A letter to the chairman was read from Mr Wigg complaining of the state of the road down Halton Hill, and stating that he had taken the unusual course of writing to the chairman because of the incivility of the sur- veyor when he complained to him. The surveyor, how- ever, stated that he had never spoken to Mr Wigg in his life, and had not received a letter from him for about five years before the last one. He then simply informed Mr Wigg that the matter he complained of would be attended to in its turn.—After a little conversation the matter dropped.—There was an account amounting to £lOl for legal and other expenses incurred in connection with the Ship Canal. Some of the members expressed the opinion that this was rather a large bill, but the chairmai thought that if the ship canal was made the money would have been very well spent indeed.—Ultimately, on the motion of Mr Mclntyre, it was agreed that the account should be paid—The surveyor was instructed to report to the clerk as to the overflow of water from the canal ill Appleton township, be being also instructed to call the at- tention of the proprietors of the canal to the matter.—Tbe surveyor was further 'instructed to endeavour to keeP the roads clear from obstruction on the occasion of what were called the potato "markets," near Stockton Heath. -- The remainder of the business was not of public interest. SMALL-PDX IN WlDNES.—William Blenkhorn, a married Man living in Warrington-road, has been attacked with entail-pox. He is completely isolated, the house in which he resides being at the end of a row and the next house be- ing empty. The domestic servant, who brought the disease from Liverpool, and was conveyed back to a hospital there, is the niece of the present sufferer. TEE DISTRICT CHAPELRY OF ST. AMBROS,, WIDNES.— The London Gazette contains Privy Council orders notify- ing that the Queen has been pleased to ratify the scheme of the Ecclesiastical Commissioners for the assignment of a district chapelry to the consecrated Church of St. Ambrose, Widnes, situate in the new parish (some time district thaerelry) of Farqworth, Lancashire. in the diocese of Liver- pool, the same to be named "The District Chapelry of St. Ambrose, Whines." MILTON CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL. WIDNES.—The an- nual sermons in behalf of the Sunday schools in connection With the above chapel were preached on Sunday morning and evening by the Rev. T. Cole, of Garston. In the after- noon Mr. S. B. Stringer (Wesleyan) delivered an address to the scholars. At each service hymns specially selected for the occasion were sung by the choir and scholars under the leadership of Mr. Johnson, air. Travis being at the organ. The collections amounted to £6 18s 3i. THE FRANCHISE DEMONSTRATION AT RUNCORN. The arrangements for this demonstration are completed, and pro- mise to be very successful. Prior to the meeting on the common, several bands will parade the streets of the town, and a preliminary meeting will beheld in Devonshireaquare at 3 o'clock. Afterwards a procession will be formed and walk to Runcorn Hill, where a mass meeting will be held. Besides the Liberal candidates for the division, Mr I S Leadham and Mr T Rigby, there will be several other pro- minent politicians. MAIN OF BOWLS AT DITTON.—A main of bowls for 64 Players, open to All England, was played at the Ball Inn, Ditton, on Thursday. There was a large number ef specta- tors, and the howlieg was very good, Peter Price, of Wid- nes, especially exhibiting great skill. Owing to the dark- , ness comiag on the game could not be .finished, and the first and second prizes of £3 103 and £1 lOs respectively, were divided between Richard Price and Richard Richardson, of Runcorn. The third add fourth prize.s were divided between Ratcliffe and Stone. A BRAVE SAILOR: FORTHCOMING PRESENTATION AT RUN- CORN.—Mr. Shaw, the chairman of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners his received a letter from the Board of Trade transmitting a silver medal and diploma, which have been awarded by the President of the French Republic to Albert Palmer, late one of the crew of the Martha, for his services in assisting to rescue the shipwrecked crew of the French , fishing boat Le Gustave, wrecked in Cherbourg Roads on the 17th November, 1883. The Board of Trade requested Mr. Sbaw to present the medal and diploma in a suitable manner to Palmer, who is now serving on board the Viola, which is about to leave Plymouth for Runcorn. FIRE AT WIDNES FOUNDRY.--Ahent Seven o'clock OR Wednesday morning a fire fortunately not very serious in its results occurred at the Widnes Foundry, Lugsdale-road. In the yard of the foundry there had been erected a large pot with a wooden platform and other accessories around it for the purpose of boiling tar in which to dip large pipes. By some means the boiling tar flowed over the sides of the pot into the fire, and a fierce flame was the consequence. Two Puncheons of oil, and two barrels of varnish and the wooden 'stage also ignited, and were destroyed. The fire was sub- dued about a Quarter to eight by water obtained on the pre- mises. The damages amount to £3O. but half of this sum will be recovered through insurance. SUNDAY SCHOOL TREATS AT WIDNES —ln beautiful weather, on Thursday, the children attending several of the Sunday Scbools at Widnes, to about the number of 380 -scholars and a large number of teachers and friends of the Lacey-street Wesleyan Sunday School, went to Hough Green by the 2-23 train, and spent a pleasant afternoon in a field kindly lent by Mr. Joseph Longton. Tea was pro- vided. By the same train about 300 children attending the Primitive Methodist School also went to Hough ,Green, and were also indebted to Mr. Longton for a field, where various recreative games were engaged in. Dialing the afternoon the children bad tea at the farm, and before leaving the choir sang several hymns for Mr. Longton. The scholars of the Baptist School were conveyed to Hale in carts, the teachers driving in wagonnetten provided by Mr. Lea. Col. Black- borne, M.P., permitted them access to the grounds of the Park, where they bad tea, and various amusements. THE COLLIERS' STRIKE AND THE WIDNES CHEMICAL TRADE—The people of Widnes will he highly gratified to learn that the colliers, through their delegates, have decided not to enter upon a strike at present, as had such an event taken place the influence upon the Widnes chemical trade would have been disastrous in its results. One firm, Messrs Gaskell, Deacon, and Co, on the occasion of the last strike, lost great sums of money through continuing their men in employment, and on Thursday they posted the following notice in the works:—" Owing to the strike of colliers, all Persons employed at these works must consider themselves under a week's notice from this date, Jely 16th, 1884. Ern- Playrnent after the 23rd inst., and so long as the strike con- tinues, can only be given provided we can obtain our supply of fuel." A notice of a similar character has, we under- stand, been posted at the works of Messrs Henry Gordon and Co, and it was fully expected that the other employers would have taken similar action. As there are about 9,000 men engaged in the chemical trade in Widnes, it will be seen that there would have been great distress and destitution. TEE SALTATION ARMY AT WIDNEB.—The Widnes corps of the Salvation Army displayed great activity on Sunday And Monday, when the members celebrated the second anniversary of the establishment of the local branch. Cap- tain Cordery, who formerly had command at Widnes, and Captain Wessburg, "the converted Swede," were present, and took a prominent part in the proceedings. On Sunday Morning operations were commenced at seven o'clock in the Drill Hall; the service being characterised in the bills as "Knee drill." At various times and in various localities meetings and processions took place during the day, every- thing passing off in an agreeable and satisfactory manner, the "soldiers on parade" being very numerous. On Mon- day evening at five o'clock a reception tea meeting was held in the Drill Hall to welcome Captain and Mrs Parsons, Who have recently taken charge of the Widnes corps. Up- wards of 200 persons partook of the repast. Subsequently reinforcements arrived from Warrington' Runcorn, and St. Helens, and the members, headed by the Widnes and Run- ' corn bands of the Army, paraded the principal streets in their characteristic fashion. Later in the evening a • Hosanna meeting" was held in the Drill Hall, where there Was "a fine display of rockets, big guns, and small firing t Practice against the devil and all his work." Captains Sin- clair, Jones, and Jackson, and Lieutenants Wealthal, Rest- Amide, and Jackson, sang songs and solos, and delivered Scaoore TREATS AT Ruerconer.—The annual excursion to GraPPenhall in connection with the Mersey Missions to Sea- Men took place on Monday, when about 200 children, accompanied by the fife and drum -band, were conveyed to their destination in two boats drawn by horses. These con- veyances were provided by the Bridgewater Navigation Company, Mr Samuel Taylor, and Mr Jonathan Hossfield. The party went through the grounds of Mr John Naylor, Cuerden Hall; and tea was suosequently partaken of in the 'Church of England School, which bad been kindly lent by the Rey. Canon Greenall. An adjournment was then made • to afield, where various sports were indulged in. The band • Played selections at the residences of Canon Greenall and Mr Naylor. On the bomeword journey one of the horses Slipped into the canal near London Bridge, and dragged a second after it. The driver also fell into the water, but 'horses and man were rescued with some difficulty. The in- cident caused some excitement amongst the excursionists 'Oa Tuesday last the childrea attending the Regent-street )Primitive -Methodist Sabbath School had their annual treat, athe party being conveyed to Preston Brook in a boat be- 'Longing to the Bridgewater Navigation Company. Mr Blease 'had kindly placed a field at the disposal of the children, Who thoroughly enjoyed themselves. Refreshments were iProvided.--The scholars of Bethesda Congregational Sun- -4,43' School spent a pleasant tirne at Keckwick on Thursday La a field attached to the farm of Mr John Bennett. The jacirney was accomplished in a boat along the canal. The fhildren were regaled with buns and tea, and before leaving la the evening assembled in front of Mr Bennett'a hoarse and Sang several hymns. e Yiateroet .PRICAL.I6 FRIIINDLY SOCIRTY.—The members of ▪ his society celebrated the filth year of its existense on Iffenday afternoon. It may be well to preface that the society ie ia a.very flourishing condition. During the past year the.sabscriptions or the members amounted to atkao 17s, out af which £5l Si had been paid in allowances to sick memhers, and £4O in four amounts of £lO each for funeral meney. The balance in the savings bank is £621 148 ied, and in the treasurer's hands £26, while the sum of £615165e6d is inveated in London and North-Western Rail- way Etock. Favoneed with fine weather, no less than 260 Members assembledion the green of the Castle/Hotel on Mon- day, Mathreeo'clock, and subsequently passed through tie village in processional order to the strains of Runcorn Volunteer Barad. It was universally regretted that Lady 13r°01re, the president of the society, could not be present esiald occupy her usual position, but she had deputed Mrs. -"Ynolciento act in her behalf. Thatiadv, and the Revs. J. le.ockwood and ga. SaltCaouse, Mr. C. Reynolds, si.P., Mrs. warrant, Me. TaWright, and Dr. Carruthers accompanied '121,5 procession as It wended its way through the leafy lanes aza.': the villas, returning to the chuech, where the Rev. R. `Ulthouse, of St. James's, West Derby, preached a sermon on 'thrift. Tbe members then proceeded to the Castle grounds ky a circuitous; route, and having walked twice round the fareen in accordance with an old custom, entered a spacious 'tent, where Mr. PleiKips had provided a substantial tea. Pstore the minters diapered to enjoy themselves by danc- 'nft, ire, Mr. C. Reynolds, J.P.. delivered a short addresc, in Irhich he expressed his Palmier at the absence of 'Lady rooke, and congratulated those present mean the well-being °I the duke. He found he had done this 13 or 14 times alnico o became a trustee of the society, and he was pleased te be Itteble te state that the funds were almost £2OO more than ellen were at the time he became.connected with the club. was Tery ersy to talk about thrift, and small as the sum (4 108 gowned, it needed a good deal of self-denial and good ir:laageaaent to have the money ready when it was wanted. Was certainly a great Aource of gratification that the -"embers had brought the society by these ac's of self-denial /11,4 good maragement to its present position of prosperity. lie had been achieved by their own money and by the errnagement of their own stewardesses, and their balance ;t would compare favourably with that of any other 46°4' in England. (Applause.) At Mr. Reynold's request e thanks of the members were heartily accorded to the t Mao s, nese of the Society, to the High Stewardess, and also '!ae Rev. R. Salthouse. On the motion of Mr. Wright, a i,-,,11.1dat compliment was also passed to Mr. C. Reynolds, who h"olularibly responded. Dancing was then engaged in for some

By. JOHN'S PRESBYTBRIAN theerzz, Rurecous.—On Sunday mornindand evening, and again on Monday even- ing, the Rev. John Jones, formerly of Runcorn, preached in the above edifice to large congregations, and the callec- tions amounted to about £l2. RUNCORN VETERINARY PRACTITIONERS.—SORPEI time ago the names of Messrs Samuel Yarwood and Frederick Yar- wood were removed from the register of veterinary practi- tioners under the Veterinary Surgeons Act, 1881; but we are glad to say that they have, through Mr. Robert Davies, solicitor, Warrington, tuccesefully appealed to the Lord in Council, and the names have been replaced- TRAP ACCIDENT AT WIDNES.—MTS Wood, wife of MY Edwin Wood. house agent,was somewhat seriously injured at Widnes on Monday. She was in a trap with her husband, driving along Ditton-road, and when turning the corner at the Central Hotel, the pony stumbled, and Mrs Wood was thrown with great violence against the window of Use hotel. She fractured her ancle and also received other injuries. Mr Wood retained his seat and was uninjured. Buses WITH DRINK AT Rureconle.—At the Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. W. Bankes and Cap- tain C. W. Hazlehuret, Martha Alice Jackson was charged with being drunk and disorderly.—P.S. Walley stated that about live o'clock on the previous evening he heard a great disturbance in Cooper-street. He went there and found that the prisoner had smashed about ten or twelve panes of glass in a neighbour's house. She rolled up her, sleeves and wanted to fight several women who were in the I street. The officer, therefore, took her to the police station. I —Superintendent Leah remarked that the owner of the win- ' dows would net prosecute because it would cost a little money, and he thought it would be throwing good after bed. —The prisoner was tined lOs and costs or 14 days' imprison- ment. for THIEVES Al' WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court on Monday, Stephen Power and William Riley, lads, were charged with stealing iron worth 6s, the property of the trustees of the late Mr John Hutchinson. From the evi- dence of Thomes Dennett and PS Clarkson, it appeared that the iron was safe on the marsh on the 10th inst. On the following day Dennett found the iron in a closet in Pear- street, and he informed the police. Dennett and Sergeant Clarkson watched the place, and sew the two prisoners and another lad emerge, each lad carrying a bag in his hand. Immediately they saw the officer, triev ran away, the pri- soners, however, being captured.. The bags contained the stolen iron, and when charged the prisoners denied the theft, alleging that some other boys were the reel delinquents. Riley was ordered to receive 9 strokes, arid Power 6 strokes with the birch rod. ATTNEFTBD SUICIDE OF A. SAILOR AT RUNCORY.—About five o'clock on Sunday morning, P C Morris WAS in the Hol- loway, when he found a sailor lying on the ground with a gash in his throat, from which blood was flowing rapidly. Near him was a knife covered with blood; it being evident that he had inflicted the wound with his own hand. As the man was in an exhausted condition the officer had him re- moved to the police station where Dr McDougall stitched the wound, which fortunately for the would-be suicide is not deep. He WAS subsequently removed to a lodginghouse. The Doctor is of opinion that the man is deranged in his mind, and is suffering from the effects of a sunstroke. The in- jured man stated to the police that his name was Arend Smit, and he is a sailor on board the Tasmania, at present lying in the Runcorn docks. He alleges that he committed the rash act because the captain of the vessel would not pay him off, but the keife was not sharp enough, and he threw it away. THREATENING TO ASSAULT A WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD OFFICER.—At Widnes Police Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. G. Pilkington, Peter McCabe, a young man, was charged with threatening to assault, beat, and illtreat Peter James Rowe, an officer of the Widnes Board, whilst in the execution of his duty.—The complainant stated that on the dth July be visited the house of Peter McCafferty, 8, Walmsley-street, and spoke to Mrs. McCafferty with res- pect to the irregular attendance of her children at school. The defendant,who lodge'. with McCafferty, told the officer that if he came there again he would knock his head off, and placed himself in a threatening attitude. The officer replied that if he assaulted him he would use his stick —The defen- dant and Mrs. McCafterty alleged that the officer was the offender—Peter McCafferty was then charged with a similar offence, and he pleaded guilty, stating that he was in liquor or he would not have threatened the officer.—Mr. Denby, clerk to the School Board, said that the officers must be protected in the execution of their duty. The Board did not wish to punish the defendants but simply to have them restrained from using any violence to the officer—Each defendant was bound over to keep the peace for three months, himself in £lO and one surety of £E, or in default 14 days' imprisonment. A WARNING TO TRAMPS AT littercome.—Before Mr. W. Bankes and Captain Haziehnrst at Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, George Jakes, who said he was a labourer from Glasgow, was charged with throwing stones in Bridge- ' street.—P.C. Wallace said he was in the police office at eight o'clock on Monday evening., when the prisoner en- ' tered and applied for a ticket for lodging. He gave a ticket of admission to the workhouse, but the prisoner said he could not walk to the workhouse that night, and wanted I lodgings elsewhere. He told him he could not have a ticket for anywhere else and he went away.—P.C. Breeze stated that about half-past eleven on the previous night the prisoner went into the office and said he could not find the 1 workhouse. Witness informed him that he could not do anything for him. The prisoner replied that he could not 4 walk to the "house," and if witness would not take him into the cells he would smash the windows. Half an hour later be threw stones at the windows of the police station, but fortunately smashed none—Superintendent Leah said it had I been usual after eight o'clock at night to give tickets of ' permission to a lodging-house in the town, and in conse- quence the able-bodied tramps and vagabonds from Widnes and the neighbourhood used to swarm upon the place. This had now been altered, and able-bodied men could be I sent to and admitted in the workhouse at any time of the night.—The prisoner, in default of paying a fine of 10s I and costs, Sc 4d, was sent to gaol for 14 days. 1 Tun Rtneconer VOLUNTERES.— The F and G companies (Runcorn), of the 2nd Cheshire Rifle Tolunteera returned 1 home on Saturday after spending a week in tents on Conway Marsh, with the rest of the regiment. The anneal inspec- tion took place on Friday, there being 23 sergeants, 53 ' bandemen, and 491 rank and file, total 608, being on parade. ' The inspectingofficer was Celonel Hall, who expressed him- ' self highly satisfied with the soldierly bearing and efficient movements of all the companies. Afterwards sports were held, the Runcorn men succeeding in taking off many of the prizes. Lance Corporal Hankinson won the prize of 12s 6d for being the smartest and cleanest dressed noncom- missioned officer, The Runcorn men received a warm wel- CORM on arriving at the station on Saturday evening, hun- dreds of spectators having assembled in the neighbourhood. ' Headed by Captain Hazlehunit, who was accompanied by ' the Rev John Lockwood, the newly appointed chaplain, who made, his first appearance in uniform, the volunteers. 150 in number, paraded the streets of the town to the strains of the band. The officers present were Lieutenants Timmins, Joule, and Rhodes. At the drill ball Captain Hazlehurst briefly addressed the men. Referring to the failure of the F company to secure the company prize, he said he had no doubt they were as disappointed as he was, but he thought If they were spared until next year., they might pull it off. He hoped and trusted—and he knew theother officers would cooperate with him in gaining that end—that they would be able to-bow companies equal to any in the battalion. He could not but feel satisfied with the general conduct el the men inecamp. Of course there were one, er two exceptions which bad cast a shadow, but they must try to forget it as soon as possible. Thew could not expect to do as well as the line, but taking all things into rconsideration they had done' as well as any company on parade. The general smartnecs of the corps had been ourpaesed by none. He had had many. compliments paid to him as regarded the march- ing past, and no doubt they heard the words of commenda- tion at the close as well as himself. iThe band had played splendid-Fe while with the volunteers, and he felt satiefied in every way with their work. There was a prospect of the camp beteg held at another place next year, and he hoped the members would turn up as readily as they bad done this Tear. He asked that the old members would stick to the old companies, and that they would get ,new members so that they might get what he had always wished to see, the companies each 100 strong. The men were then dis- missed. TIM use .01 THE KNlFE.—Cstherine Burns, a married woman was brought up at Widnee Police Court, on Mon- day, charged with baying, on the 7tk July, unlawfully and maliciously wounded Ann Middleton, wife,of a litter living at 5, Carcdine-street, Widnes.—The prosecntrix -said the prisoner lived in Caroline-street. Between nine and ten o'clock on Monday night, the 7th inst., the was standing at her own door, when the prisoner psieed and threatened that what she hadn'tdone for her on the previous night she would do then. Witness replied that she had better do it in the .daylight. The prisoner's son James then.came up, and ran her (witness) to the bottom of the street. She tried to shout ,for the police, but she could not, as he held her. Whilst he held her the prisoner gave her three " prods" with a knife be saw in her hand. She had three wounda-none on the arm, one on the head, and one on the face. She lost a great deal of blood, and sneered very much. She was taken home by ,& woman named Martin, and next day Dr. O'Keeffei ,dressed her wounds. She gave the prisoner no provocatioa. She was neither drunk nor sober. She was "middling," but understood What she was doing.—Cross-exanained by Mr. J. W. Knowles, who represented the prisoner, witness stated she did not say the prieener'e husband had been buried without shirt. She never fell. She had been asked to settle the case, and told that it would be better for leer to take a few pounds and go out of the place.—Anne Brannon, wife of Daniel Brannon, who lives at 1. Margaret-street, deposed that she-saw the prosecutrie standing at her own doer,ehout- ing and making a great noise. James Burns, the prisoner's son, came and caught hold of her by the back of the neek, and ran her down the street. The prisoner followed and struck her about the face. Immediately the prosecatrix oled from wounds about the face. The prosecutrix was an entire stranger to her—By Mr. Knowles: The prosecntrix wee in a fighting position at her own door, and appeared as if challenging Mrs. Burns.—Mary Murtagh, of 19, Caroline- street, stated that the prosecetrix said she would fight any three of them, bat they must bring no weapons. She was far in drink. She confirmed the previous evidence, but added that she saw no knife.—Dr. O'Keeffe gave evidence as to dressing the woman's wounds. There was a clean cut on the forehead over the left eye an inch and a half long penetrating to the bone, and there were also two other small wounds on the forehead. There was a clean cut on the left arm, but it was not deep. The wound on the forehead was dangerous but it was healing now.—P.C. Davie deposed to apprehending the prisoner, who, when charged at the police station, said she never lifted a band to the woman.—Tlae. prisoner was committed to take her trial at the Assizes.

WIDNES STARR BOWEETT BUILDING SOCIETY. Mr. Samuel Owens has been appointed secretary of ,this society in place of Mr. W. Treacy, junr., who has resigned. WIDNES C.E.T.S.—On Tnursday evening at the weekly meeting of this society, the Rev. G. T. Duane, Mi., vicar of St. John's, Barrow-in-Furness, delivered an address on the temperance question. HALTON VIEW WANDERERS FOOTBALL CLUB.—At the first general meeting of this club the officers were appointed for the ensuing year as follows :—Captain, Walter Minton ; sub-captain, Richard Barker; hon. treasurer, Charles Ire- land; hon. secretary, Alfred Moore; committee: Walter Minter), J. Howard, T. Ridyard, J. Ridyard, G. Matthews, T. Phillips, W. Moore, and A Moore. SUDDEN DEATH AT RUNCDRN.—A woman named Ann Elizabeth Barker, who lived in English-row, died on Thurs- day evening under the following circumstances :—rhe de- ceased had suffered from erysipelas for some time, and she had been attended by Mr. Fletcher, the herbalist. On Tues- day last Dr. Bagnall was called in, and he, perceiving that there was no hope of the woman's recovery, declined to give a certificate when death occurred. The Coroner has been communicated with. WIDNES POLICE Counv.—Before Mr. Brock at Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, John Howard was fined 7s 64 and costs or 10 days' imprisonment for being drunk in West Bank-street.--For a similar offence committed in Chat- ham-street Margaret Donnelly was mulcted in the sum of 11 5s and costs.--Wm. Dwyer was charged with sleeping r on Messrs. Muspratt and Sons Works, Widnes, and as he had been before the Bench on a similar charge eight times he was sent to gaol fur 14 days' hard labour. STAR Or WIDNES LODGE,I.O.G.T.—The members of this lodge met at 56, Mersey-road, on Wednesday, when a fra- ternal visit was paid by the members of the Samaritan Lodge. The visitors filled the various offices, Brother T. Fairhurst, being in the chief templet's chair. A programme of songs, readings, and recitations was gone through in good style by Bros. J. Parker, Fairhurst, Lamb, Webb, Pearson, and Machin ; and Sisters Fairhurst and Smith. The handbell ringers, under the conductorship of Bro. Melman performed several pieces in an unimpeachable manner. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD AT WORE.—On Wednesday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, before Mr Gr Pilkington and Mr F H Gossage, the following persons were charged with ,neglecting to send their chil- dren to school :—William Edwardson (2 cases), James Leo- nard, Michael Daley. Danis Malone, Patrick Connor, James Carr, James Kelly, Thomas Spruce. John Mercer, Thomas Roach, William Jannett, William Jackson, James Hughes Elias Roberts, 'Moines McAuley (two cases), Patrick Mar- tin, Peter McCafferty, Robert Hoey, Richard Glassey, and I Henry Whitfield. The cases were proved by attendance officers Davies, Joynson, and Rowe, and the usual penalty ef 5s was imposed in each instance. • CRUELTY TO A HORSE AT WlDNES—Before Messrs. Brock and Pilkington, at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wed- nesday, James Litherland, salt dealer, Warrington, was sum- moned to answer a charge of cruelly illtreating a horse.— P.C. Clarke said that a quarter to four on Saturday, the sth instant, he saw the defendant driving a horse and cart in Warrington road. Noticing that the animal appeared to be in a weak and poor condition, he stopped it and examined it. Under the saddle he found a raw wound about the size of a two shilling piece, from which blood was oozing. The animal was not fit to work, and he ordered it to be taken out of the shafts. It could scarcely draw the cart along.—The defendant, who did not appear, was fined 103 and costs. A BRUTAL HUSBAND PUNISIIED AT RUNCORN.—At Run- corn Police Court on Wednesday John Rodford was charged under a warrant with unlawfully assaulting his wife, Alice. —The prosecutrix said she lived with the prisoner in Pen- nington's-row. About an hour after midnight on Saturday the prisoner carne home drunk and palled her out of bed; and kicked her about the body. He also threatened to throw her downstairs. On Monday she went with her stall to Halton Club. The prisoner abused her there, and when she returned home at night he again assaulted bier in a savage manner. He felled her to the ground several times. He had previously been imprisoned for illusing her. He only assaulted her when intoxicated; he was very quiet when sober.—ln answer to the Bench, witness said she could keep herself; in fact, she had to keep her husband.— The prisoner was thereupon committed to gaol for a month's hard labour, and Ike magistrates granted a separa- tion order. ALLEGED BURGLARY AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, Walter Bushell and Peter Connolley were brought before Mr. Brock on a charge of burglariously entering the house of Mrs. Margaret Mannion, 26, Water- street, and stealing therefrom half a pound of bacon, half a pound of pork, belonging to Mrs. Mannion, and two loaves, belonging to Mrs. Heavey. It seems these two families re- side in the same house, and on Saturday night they pur- chased provisions which they placed in the pantry. The next morning it was discovered that the hone had been entered lw the kitchen window and the provisions taken. On the table underneath were the marks of bare feet.— Margaret Ellen 'robin deposed that she was standing at her father's door at three o'clock on Sunday morning when she saw Bushell and Connolley, the former in his bare feet, going towards the back of Mrs. Mannion's house. In about ten minutes they returned, Connotley carrying a bundle and something in a blue paper. Information was given to the police and P.C. Laing apprehended the prisoners. They denied the charge, but the missing provisions were subse- quently found in Connolley's house, where Bushell also lived.—The prisonars were committed to the assizes for trial.

A TIOLINT WOMAN AT WIDNES. —At Widnes Petty See- I Mons, on Wednesday, Mary Ann Connor, a married woman, was charged with assaulting a young woman named Margaret Connor. The parties live in Pleasant-etreet. Lugsdale, and on the eyeing of the 14th instant the complainant had a friend in her house. After the friend left about half-past ten the complainant heard screams of murder, and on going outside found her friend on the ground with Mrs. Connor and another woman beating her. The complainant went to her mid, when the defendant seized her by the hair of the head and pulled a great quantity off. She then tore her apron off , and ran into the house. Complainant went to the I house for her apron. The defendant threw at her a quart bottle, which struck her on the head. complainant stated that she had had erysipelas for a month and had been under Dr Cooper. The defendant alleged that earlier in the evening the complainant had gent a bricki through her window, smashing three panes, and striking baron-the eye. She called several witnesses who denied that the defendant struck the complainant, alleging that the "row" was between the plaintiff and defendant's sister. The sister was called and acknowledged that she and the defendant had a row, tat stated she never struck her. She stated that the complement's hair had come off her head in consequence ef the erysipelas.—The Bench imposed a toe of in and costs, or in default In days' imprisonment. A 'VAGRANT AND DUTTON WOE6INOUSE FARE.—Edward Brooke was brought before Mr. W. Banks and Mr. James Handley, at Runcorn feline Court, on Wednesday, charged that be being an inmate of the.casual ward of Patton Workhouse, refused to perform the tasks prescribed by the Local ,Government Board. The son of Mr. Jones, the master, entered the box to give evidence, and the prisoner was asked to plead. He replied that it was no use him saying anything as they would believe all he (the witness) said. With a malignant look he added, "I will screw the young neck round:"—Trom,the evidence it appeared that the prisoner was admitted in the workhouse on Friday night, and on the following morning he was given the usual task, but refused to perform it. In consequence he was de- tained in the house, anti-on the following days he pretended to pick-some oakum, but did not do the work to the satis- faction of the officials. He also tcre to rags a pair of trousers with the object of obtaining a new pair at the ex- pense of the guardians.—The prisoner denied having re- fused to perform the task, and-stated that he was locked Dp in a room alone while Mr. Jones' son went out to play the piano somewhere. He was -kept there and given only .a small-quantity of soup, and the reason he tore his tremens wastecaase be was not provided for as be ought to have been.—The magistrates considered the offence proved, and sentenced the prisoner to 21 days' hard labour. MEE ASSAULT BY A COPDAIN AT RUNCORN. —Before Mr James Handley, at Runcorn Police Court, on Wednesday, Michael Murphy, captain of the schooner Eclipse, of Fleet-, wood, surrendered to his bail, and was-charged with doing' grievous bodily harm to William Stringer, of Portland- street,-on the 17th May.--The evidence for the prosecution! had already, been taken, med Mr ,Edmondson, solicitor, Fleet- wood, addressed the court on the prisoner's behalf. He tied' that *undoubtedly a most pitiable assault had been cam- mitted,hat the evidence chewed that there was not the slightest particle of ill-feeling, and therefore the assault had been without malice. There had been a conversation between Murphy and Stringer as to how wrestling was done in America, and the prisoner was demonstrating this. He ventured to say that had the room been larger no injury would have been caused, seed -the-" circus trick" would have been neatly done. He held -that the prisoner was en- titled to the doubt If there was one, and ought to be dis- charged. If his worship took such a course the prisoner was quite willing to make Stringer some recompense, and that would be better ter him than if Murphy was sent for trial. In the latter event occurring Stringer would not get anything.—Joseph Dawn, of Egerton-street, gave evi- dence for the defence; and theprisoner was formerly com- mitted to the assizes for trial. On the application of Mr Edmondson, the magistrates consented to take bail, the pri- soner in £lOO and two sureties of JZO eaoh.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, JULY 19. 1884.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, JULY 19. 1884.
BREAKING A BROTHER'S_ JAVir AT WIDNES.

- _ At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr. G. Pilkingten and Mr. John Brock, John and Mary Sutton were summoned to answer a charge of assaulting Samuel Sutton on the 27th June. Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared for the complainant, and Mr. L W. Wnowles for the defendants.— Mr. Swift stated that the defendants were husband and wife, and the complainant was the brother of John. The parties lived next door to each other in James-street, Widnes, the defendants living at 85, and the complainant xt 87. Though so nearly related, the complainant and the defendants had not been on friendly term together, in fact, they had considered it a wise course not to be en speaking terms. On the day in question, however, when the complainant returned home from his work about seven o'clock, he heard his brother calling out" Sam, I want to see you." The complainant went out of the back door and found his brother there. De latter asked him what he bad been saying to the landlord. The complainant replied nothing, whereupon the defendant called him a liar, and accused him of attempting to get him removed from the house. The complainant denied the charge, and the defend- ant threatening to knock his head off, struck hirn twice on the breast. He was about to strike him a third time when the complainant closed with him and a struggle took place on the ground. The complainant admitted that while his brother was belabouring him on the ground he picked up a

• stone and struck the defendant. Mrs. Sutton then appeared on the scene, and picking up a stone, she struck the com- plainant with it on the jaw. The complainant rose to his feet, but was again knocked to the ground, but he at length get into the yard, and seized an axe, but it was taken from him by a bystander, lie was then led into the house, where he was found in a state of unconsciousness by his wife. He had been seriously un well since, and htd to take all his food in liquid form.— The complain- ant, Mary Stretch, Tomas Nichols, 25, Bunk-street, and James Nerton, of Bank-street, corroborated this statement. In cross-examination by Mr. Knowles, Nicholls said that when the complainant brought the axe out he looked like using it.—Mr. Knowles for the defence contended that his client John was merely acting in the defensive, but as he appeared to be the strongest man he cams best off.—He called George Loun&s, a flatman, living at 10, Irwell-steeet, who stated that when be appeared on the scene the com- plainant was standiog up and making a great noise. Shortly afterwards he saw him go into the house, and come out with an axe, which he held in his hand in an upraised position, and asking " Where is the--." Witness slipped behind him and secured his hands, and the complainant said "Loose me, and I will cut his -- head off." Witness then took the axe off him, and he believed if he had not done so the plaintiff would have killed his brother.—Mary Webster de- posed that the plaintiff's wife was a very bad neighbour, and there had been no peace in the street sinae she came. She alleged that the complainant struck the first blow, and also struck the defendant John on the head with a clinker. When he seized the axe he swung it over his bead in a most threatening manner.—Margaret Tomlinson gave similar evidence, and the Bench after a few minutes' consideration fined each defendant 20s and costs 11s 01, or in default 14 days' imprisonment. —ln answer to Mr. Pilkington, Inspec- tor Wood stated that the defendant John had been fined 20s and costs for stealing timber.—There was no record against the wife.
RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS AND THE SHIP CANAL BILL.

A special meeting of the Board of Improvemsnt Commissioners was held in the Town Hall yes- terday, for the purpose of considering, and if advisable, to petition in favour of the Ship Canal Bill. There were present Messrs B. Shaw (chairman) P riscoe, J Pritchard, J Williams, W Fisher, W H Linaker (Law Clerk), and W Brooke, secretary. The Chairman said it was likely that if the bill passed they would have consi- derable dealings with the promoters of the ship canal, who would become the owners of the waterwave. That being the case as long as this petition did not commit the Board to anything, he did not see that it could do any harm to petition in favour of the bill in accordance with the request of the promoters. It would be well that they should seep on the best terms they could with these people.—Mr Fisher fully concurred with the chairman's remarks, and he bad great pleasare in moving that the Board petition in favour of the bill, and that the chairman of the Board be empowered to affix the seal thereto and the petition forwarded to the senior county member for formal presentation.—Mr P Speak- man seconded the motion which was carried. The petition was drawn up in general terms in favour of the bill.

div.head: FREEMASONRY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: FREEMASONRY AT RUNCORN.

The members of the Ellesmere Lodge of Freemasons (No. 755) celebrated the anniversary of St. John in the Masonic Hall, Runcorn, on Wednesday evening, when there was a large attendance of brethren. Bro. E. Marwood, W M., opened the lodge in due form ; and Bro. R. Oldbury, W.M , elect, was presented for installation. The ceremony of installation was most impressively performed by Bro. G. Moss, P.M., assisted by Bro. Coxhill. P.M. The following were then appointed officers :—E. Marwood. J P.M , the Rev. J. Lockwood, S W., George Bell, J.W Torkington (treasurer), J. Salkeld (secretary), J. Coxhill, P.M.D.C., G. Summerfleld, s.n., F. A. Lake, J.D., T. Wright, J.G., Cooper (organist), Rosenberg, S.S., Annett, 3.8., Le Coutier (almoner), W. Houghton (tyler.) The lodge was then closed in due and solemn form; and the brethren adjourned to the ante-room and partook of a cold collation. The usual loyal and patriotic toasts were given, and.the health ef the was proposed and heartily drunk. Bro. Oldbury responded in felicitous terms. On Thursday the members had their annual excursion. Llandudno was the place selected for the day's pleasure, and the party, numbering 50, travelled in a special saloon and engaged carriage. At Chester the car- riages bad to be attached to another train, and when being shunted Into a siding for this purpose they ran off the metals at the points, causing some excitement amongst the excursionists, who had to alight and travel in the ordinary way to their destination. The journey was accomplished in good time. Immediately on arriving at Llandudno, the brethren entered several waggonettes and were driven round the Great Orme's Head, the scenery both on sea and land being greatly admired. Subsequently the party partook of an excellent banquet at the Prince of Wales Hotel, every satisfaction being expressed at the manner in whin the catering was performed. The cloth having been removed, the healths of Bros. Oldbury and MOSS were drunk, refer- ence being made to tke admirable and successful arrange- ment they bad made for the comfort and pleasure of the party. In a humorous sneech Bro. Moss proposed the health of the ladies, and Bro. J. Salkeld, secretary, responded in the same vein. The party then devoted themselves to view- ing the beauties of the Welsh watering place.

He pointed out that the Franco-German war cost France 200 000 lives and 500 millions of money, and argued that if tngland spent the money on war that she spent in drink she could afford to have a campaign similar to this Ones every eight years, and lose the same number of lives that Fiance did on the occasion mentioned. In conclusion he wished success to the temperance cause in Widnes, and particularly to that hall.—Mr. T. Owens then laid the second stone, and said that the temperance workers had a a great deal to be thankful for as the country . was coming rapidly oycr to their side. It was a movement which had the broadest platform possible, and all men, whatever their crochets or opinions, ought to tight shoulder LI shoulder with what the late Duke of Albany called the only enemy England had to fear. Referring to the cause for which that hall was built, he said it would be a temperance hall, not merely for Good Templars, but where all sections of the orgtnisation might meet. The promoters would also be glad to see the Oddfellows and Foresters within its walls, because be maintained that one of the great hindrances of these orders lay in the fact of their meetings being held in public-houses. What the temperance party wished was to ask the Legislature to give the people permission to may Whether they VfQuld have public-houses in the neighbourhood in which they lived, or whether they would have any pub- lic-houses at all in their midst. (Applause.) While he Spoke he seemed to hear the tramp of two millions who were bound to be admitted to the franchise. (Hear, hear.) Let the voice of these two millions, together with the numbers already banded together, be beard with no uncertain sound on this question, upon which the House of Commons by a majority had admitted that some enactment must lee placed upon the statute book. There was much legislation on the hands of the Government, and he would be sorry as a good Liberal to accuse them of not dealing fairly with the matter. But after all he did think that there were measures of lesser importance which had had precedence over the drink ques- tion, and if temperance reformers had not spoken loud enough in the past he hoped they would do so in the future. —Mr. Robinson, after laying the third stone, expressed the hope that the building would prove permanently successful. He observed that the English people inherited their charac- teristics from their Saxon ancestors, and he exhorted those present to be careful and transmit features of character that were temperate and godly to their children.—On the motion of Mr. Swale, seconded by Mr. Harrison, and supported by Mr. Ormroyd, a vote of thanks was passed to the gentlemen who had laid the stones. A collection was then made on behalf of the building fund. Mr. Hargreaves gave a dona- tion of £5. The collection amounted to £l5, but this sum will be supplemented by several donations and sub- scriptions collected by members of the Lodge. The mem- bers hope to open the building free from debt.

A TEMPERANCE HALL FOR WIDNES: LANG OF MEMORIAL STONES..

Clea Saturday afternoon in. ce—autiful weather, and in the ,presence of a good number of spectators, the memorial stones of a Temperancediall, which is being erected on a -site in Hibbert-street, Widnes-road, by the member:sof the Hope of Appleton Lodge of Good Tempters, were laid. .Owtwardly, the building will be a plain brick structure, but thainterior will be fitted gp to accomodate 250 persons, and will ,be eminently suitable for meetings of small bodies. I Mr. T. Philips, of Gladstone.street, is the contractor. To- 'wards the cost of the building, which is estimated at about £250, upwards of LLOO has been obtained, Mr. F. H. Gos- sage, and Mr. T. S. linings laving each giyen a generous donation. Amongst those present at the opening ceremony were Messrs. James Hargreaves, F.C.S., Samuel Owens, John Robinson, Balmer, T Rely, J P Mocewood. T Baroc, Ornaroyd, Thompson, Hill, Lomas, W Reay, T Reed, and Uobineon. The proceedings commenced with singing, Mr. Ormroyd subsequently offering up a prayer. Mr. T. Reay, in introducing Messrs J. IlargreayesoS. Owens and.i. Robinson to lay the memorial stones, 'aid they had • often had the idea of building a Temperance Hall in Wid- nes, and he had had something to on with attempts to gain that end, but they had always failed until now. Tills time they did not mean to fail, and the fact that they had al- ready received liberal donations towards the building through the efforts of Mr. Morevrood, their secretary, proved that the bleesing of iGod was resting upon them. The first stone was then laid by Mr. James Hargreaves, who after, briefly referring to the purposes for which the Hall was intended, alluded to the death statistics ef Liverpool, arguing that at least 3,000 persons could be saved annually if the drink traffic was brought to an mid. He contended that owing to the squalor of many part e of that city, and to the large numbers of people living in narrow and crowded places and breathing an impure at- mosphere, nine-tenths of the deaths were due. The origin of the outbreak of cholera in Liverpool 18 years ago, when 1,700 people died, was traceable to the carelessness of a labourer named Boyle, who neglected all precautions for the sake of having a drunken spree. COUNTY ASYLUM.—Yesterday week the members of the Juvenile Choir of the Asylum, which is conducted by Miss M. Higgins, had their annual tea party and distribution of prizes. By kind permission of Dr,,, Rogers the beautiful grounds of the asylum were placed at the disposal of the children and their friends, and the weather being very pro- pitioua. a most enjoyable afternoon was spent. DEATH OF MR. JOHN Rol3Y.—Early on Tuesday morning Mr. John Roby, brassfounder, died at his residence at Rain. hill. The deceased gentleman, who was a self-made man, was born at Prescot, but for many years cirried on, at Rain- hill, an extensive business as brassfounder, employing a large Humber of workmen. His liberality was well known, although unostentatious. The funeral took place yesterday at Rainhill Church, when a large circle of friends gathered to pity the last respect to the departed.
