div.p: FRODSITAIII.

PARISH CHURCH Cnora TRIP.—The Frodsham Parish Church choir had their annual outing on Tuesday, when they went by rail to Llandudo, and, although the weather was showery, a pleasant day was spent. DANGEROUS CONDITION OF FRODSHAM CHURCH TOWER. —A special meeting of the parishioners was held in the Parish Church on Wednesday morning, to take into con- sideration the dangerous condition of the church tower. The Rev H B Blogg, M A, vicar, presided. The chairman briefly explained the object of the meeting, and expressed his regret that so few of the parishioners were present. A letter was read from Mr William Heyes, explaining that he was unable to attend, and that he would be guided by what was done at the meeting. The chairman called upon Mr Thomas Davies to give the result ef his inspection of the tower, when Mr Davies stated that he bad examined the tower, and found at the top that a joint in the stone work had opened 1.1 inches, and this fracture winds its way nearly to the bottom. From information he had received, half of this opening had taken place since the restoration; the lead roof on the tower WS in a bad state, and in wet weather the rain would get into the walls of the tower. Some of the steps were broken, and the battlements were considerably out of perpendicular. Mr Davies estimated that the tower might be bolted and the lead roof repaired for £l5O, but if taken down it would cost from £1,500 to £2,000 to rebuild. After some consideration it was decided to adjourn the meeting to the 30th inst., and the churchwardens were requested to obtain an estimate for removing the bells to a place of safety, lowering the tower, and putting a temporary wooden cap over the top, until the necessary fund could be raised for re- building the tower. 0

THE POLITICAL CRISIS- A hastily summoned Cabinet Council was held on Mon- day afternoon. A town's meeting was held in Birmingham on Monday evening to consider the action of the House of Lords on the franchise question, the Mayor presiding. The proceedings were from beginning to end of a most disordeily character; but a resolution declaring the action of the House of Lords indefensible and intolerable, and urging that their lordships should be deprived of the power they have repeatedly, ex- ercised in a manner insulting to the people's representatives in the House of Commons, and detrimental to tho best in- terests of the country, was carried by an overwhelming majority. Writing in acknowledgment of a resolution passed by the Windsor and Eton Conservative Association in reference to the action of the House of Lords on the Franchise Bill, Lord Salisbury says : "We shall have many more threats before we have done with the controversy, but I earnestly hope the House will treat them with as much disregard as It has shown to Mr. Gladstone's threat of the other day." The Hon. E. L. Stanley, M.P., writing to the Oldham Radical Association on the House of Lords, says be does not believe in the necessity for a second chamber, and that there is danger in reforming the House of Lords. By renew- ing its constitution it might be more powerful than ever. His impression is that the veto of the Lords should apply to one Session only, and any Bill sent up a second Session should pass over their veto. Wath and District North Riding Conservative Asso- ciation, and the Bury Conservative Association, have passed resolutions of sympathy with the action of the House of Lords.

At a meeting. on Wednesday night, of the Ipswich Radi- cal Association, in condemnation of the policy ot the House of Lords, a letter was read from Mr. Jessie Collings, M.P., who wrote:—" It is high time the people of this country should determine to abolish an assembly that always stands in the way of the people's will and rights. We cannot go on as we are. It is humiliating to think that this country can be cheated and thwarted by a few men who represent nobody bat themselves." The Liberals of Christchurch have appointed delegates to attend the reform demonstration in London, and have also arranged for a demonstration in the Winter Gardens, Bournemouth. Resolutions in support of the Government were passed on Wednesday by the Ashton-under-Lyne Liberal Associa- tion, a mass meeting of miners at Ashton Heath, the Preston Liberal Association, the branch of the South Durham Liberal Association, the Faversham District Liberal Asso- ciation, the Ramsgate, Bolton, North Wilts, and East Cum- berland and Carlisle Liberal Associations. A joint committee of the Nottingham, North Notting- hamshire, and South Nottioghamshire Liberal Associations met on Wednesday, and made arrangements for holding a county franchise demonstration on Saturday, the 28th inst. Steps are also being taken to hold a demonstration represen- tative of all North Wales. Mr. A. B. Forwood, the chairman of the Liverpool Consti- tutional Association, on Thursday morning received the fol- lowing letter from Lord Salisbury in reply to the resolution passed by the Executive of the Association on Tuesday last:—" 20, Arlington-street, S.W., July 16, 1884.—Dear Mr. Forwood,-1 am very much obliged to you for your letter, as well as for your kindly telegraphing to me the resolution of the Liverpool Conservative Association. Their support is exceedingly valuable, and shows that all classes of the community, including the working men in Lanca- shire, appreciate the real nature of the conflict upon which ' we have entered. Great efforts may be made to persuade the working men that we have opposed the extension of the franchise, but all the intelligence that reaches me convinces me that those efforts will be fruitless."—Yours very sin- cerely, Stussicax." iteplying to a resolution of the Lewisham Conservative Club, Wolverhampton, Lord Salisbury writes:—" Any other course would have surrendered into the hands of the Govern- ment the uncontrolled power of arranging the redistribution of seats according to their own wishes. The efforts which the Government are making to attain this illegitimate ob- ject, and the deplorable condition of our foreign policy, alike make it desirable that the judgment of the constituencies should be taken at an early date." ' Acknowledging resolutions in favour of the action of the Boum of Lords, passed by the Clackclose Conservative As. tociation, West Norfolk, Lord Salisbury writes that he deeply feels, as he believes the majority of Englishmen felt, the disgrace which is being brought upon the country, and he wishes that the power of toe Conservative leaders to arrest the evil was equal to their sense of it. Acknowledging the receipt of resolutions passed by the National Liberal Federation, last week, Mr. Gladstone writes that Her Majesty's Government rely on the efficiency of calm reasoning addressed to the awakened minds of the nation on the great question now at issue, to prevent the re- newal hereafter of the serious difficulty in the way of pas- sing the Franchise Bill. Mr. Courtenay, writing to the chairman of a meeting re- cently held in Liskeard, says it is necessary that the House of Lords should be reinforced by represmtitives of classes now practically unrepresented in it, and that its power should be restricted to a temporary or suspensive veto.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LoxlvoN, TIII?SDAY.

It is little more than a week ago that Lord Salisbury, in tbe maddest of speeches, sneered at ' the working-men, who he said might if they desired an outing congregate in Hyde Park, or march up and down Piccadilly, with much more to the same purport. It can hardly be said that the point of collision between the peers and the people has yet been touched. Up to to-night there has been a period of expec. tation. The last offering laid on the altar of peace by the Government had not been finally rejected. It was quite possible, knowing the tremor in which the Lords already existed, that even at the last moment they might yield to ' the dictates of common sense, and by accepting the moti,m of Lord Wemyss, deliver themselves from peril. Besides, since the issue is postponed till October, it would seem more useful to restrain the greatest efforts till that period is more nearly approached. But so profound is the national indignation that there is no holding the people back till October. The newspapers team with reports of indignation meetings held in all parts of the kingdom. The arrange- ments are now completed for the great demonstration to be made in London, and immediately afterwards Lancashire, which makes its voice heard at Manchester.

Lord Salisbury, it is a truism to say, is a man of great obstinacy. Be is akin with the French marquis who lives in history by reason of a single question, lightly asked. When the people of Paris, oppressed by a voluptious court, clamoured for bread, the gay marquis asked "Why can't they eat grass ? " A year or two later his head was carried through the streets of Paris with its mouth stuffed with grass. Our English marquis may or may not have refrained from uttering this brutal pleasantry, had he lived in similar circum- stances. But there is no doubt he would have been as blind to the signs of the times and as contemptuous of the people as was the Frenchman. Still he must take account 0, the rising storm, and must have formed some calculation of the proportions to which it will grow by next October. If he closes his own eyes aganist evidence, it will be brought closely under his attention by the other peers, who, to use an uncanonical but expressive term, are already in a terrible funk. "

Nobody DOW expects that whatever:course the Lords may adopt in July they would in October maintain the defiant attitude recommended by Lord Salisbury. It is a proof of how the effect of popular demonstration is underrated even by those most intimately acquainted with the people that a fortnight ago maw believed that the Lords would not only throw out the Franchise Bill in July, but would repeat the action it? October. Sir Charles Dilke, one of the shrewdest observers of public events, held this opinion. But he now takes a different view, and bAieves that surrender will be made in October. Should that view be falsified it would be rash to assume that a general election would thereupon follow. At first that WAS undoubtedly the intention of the Government as far as it was formed. Indeed, the autumn session was fixed so early as the 20th of October with the special object of bringing about a general election in time to get it comfortably over by Christmai. But even the Government were not fully aware of the strength of their position in the views of the people. They now believe that they would be justified and supported in carrying still further the conflict with the peers.

The whole beginning and ead of the struggle, as I have more than once explainedjs that the Conservatives want to have the General Election taken on the present Fran- chise, and with that object the Lords are sacrificing them- selves in the effort to force an election. It is evident that if a dissolution should follow in December or January they would to a certain extent have ga'ned their point, and may claim a victory though purchased at tremendous cost. It would be a great temptation to the Government to go to the country at a moment when it is infariated by the renewed deff trice of the Lords. Still, this would be yielding to un- constitutional dictation in the matter of forcing a dissolu- tion, and on that point the Ministry, with Mr. Gladstone as the most emphatic exponent of the principle, are not in- clined to give way. The present intention is, should the Bill be thrown out in October, to submit it again in Jan- uary, and if necessary to bring it. in a fourth time; bat on this occasion with means taken to give the Liberals a majority ist the House of Lords. - • •• •

The London hotel keepers and all others who profit by the Presence of a floating population that have put money in their purses are making a good thing out of the cholera in France. This is a time at which the second flight of Ameri- cans is reaching England with intent to spend the autumn in some of the continental resorts. Arriving ,here they find good reason not to go further afield. It is not only, perhaps not at all, the fear of cholera, but the knowledge of the in- convenience to which continental stupidity puts travellers. Anyone who has crossed the Alps knows what the Italian Custom House officer is like in ordinary times. Now, with the dreadful word " cholera " spoken, and with ofEcial in- junctions to preserve quarantine, the Italian is in his glory, and the traveller of w uatever nationality is in the depth of misery. In less degree it is the same on whatever frontier is reached from Portugal to Prusssia. Carriage loads of passengers are treated much as in this country wagon loada of sheep are dealt with where cattle disease regulations are in fall operation. In this respect, as in all others. England remains the freest country of the world. Due precautions are taken at the ports, but there is no official ruffianism such as compels travellers who have reached the frontiers of Italy to turn back, abandoning their journey rather than submit to what awaits them. The consequence is that Americans who would now be on the continent are flooding London, and do not propose to go further afield outside the three kingdoms. Vile will be a great year not only far English watering places, but for Scotland and Ireland.

It is curious how lawyers maintain to this day their time- honoured reputation for telling anecdotes. I dined the other night at the house of an eminent leader of the Bar. The majority of the guests belonged to the same profession, and for at least an hour after the ladies left there was an unin- terrupted low of anecdotes. One that was new (and doubt- less invented) was told by a learned judge, and related to the present Lord Chancellor. Lord Selborne's town house is in Portland Place, close by Regent's Park. Returning home one evening in the present summer, the Lord Chan- cellor found all his family out. Inquiring where they were he was told that the favourite parrot had got out of its cage and flown away into Regent's Park, and that the ladies of the family had gone in search of it. His lordship thought a stroll in the park would not be disagreeable, and he accordingly went in quest of his two younger daugh- ters who had gone in search of the parrot. Presently he discovered a crowd round a tree in the park, and in the centre of it was one of his daughters holding out a cage in- vitingly open, whilst the other was trying to induce the par- rot to enter it. Bat the parrot was very comfortable and went on offering irreleva,.. re- ...mks, to the great amusement of the crowd. As coon as its eye lighted upon its noble master, and, according to the story-teller, familiar with his prevailing habit, on presenting himself in the evening pre- vious to dinner, the parrot, ,t.ocking its head on one side, said, "Let us pray." The shilling offered the other night to the Sergeant-at- Arms by a stranger anxious for admission to the gallery of the House of COW/WM is not the flrst transaction of the kind which has taken place. When Mr. A. M. Sullivan was still member for Louth he SAW in the lobby a young man, evidently from the country, whe desired to get into the gallery. Mr. Sullivan, with his well known urbanity, I showed him through the usual round of the library and the reading-room, finally landing him at the door of the Speaker's gallery. Hereupon the young min took out a leather purse, and, carefully extracting sixpence, offered it to his guide. It was evident from his look that be regarded tfhewis da yasn, andextravagance. musthe was up in London for a gote pacs. Mr. Sullivan declined the money, anet the young man, thinking more of him than ever, returned it to his purse. Sir John biker took a more practical view of a similar case which came under his notice. A friend asked him to look after one of his constitu- ents who had entered the lobby and wanted a place in the gallery. Sir John having obtained admittance for him the stranger pressed a shilling in his hand, which Sir John with a " Thank von" transferred to his pocket, and was fond of showing as the most easily earned fee he had received for many years.

Mr. Toole is something like the historic clown who, stricken with a fatal disease, died on the stage, the audience roaring with laughter at the exquisite fan of his contortions. Everybody laughed when, bidding a temporary farewell to his theatre, Toole said he had some notion of turning it into a tea garden on the model of the Healtheries. The fact is, as already noted, the theatres are suffering sorely from the competition of the Health Exhibition. In all years het weather affects the theatres. But formerly people having nowhere else to go, and feeling bound to go somewhere, braved the stiEing atmosphere and sat out the play. Now they can go to the Healtheries, stroll about amid a fairy scene, sure to meet plenty of people whom they know And

having the opportunity of listening to some of the finest band music in Europe. The consequence is that they go in thousands, and the wail of the theatre mananers is becoming painful. Someone asked Bancroft the other night how bus*. flees was with him. He paused for a painful moment and with an appropriate contortion of the face uttered the single word " Ghastly!"

The autumn session grievously interferes with the hell. day arrangements of our legislators. The passion for travel IS always growing in England, but nowhere are its develop- ments fuller than in the House of Commons. Formerly a trip to Switzerland, the German Baths, or late in the year, to Italy, was the fullest journey contemplated. America is now about the nearest goal, and New York is regarded only as a starting point for the remotest parts of the great COEI tinent. Even San Francisco is not now eufficiently remote for our M.P.'s. Last October I had a rendezvous at San Francisco with Professor .Bryce, mereber for the Tower Hamlets. When I arrived at the Palace Hotel a note was handed to me, in which he expressed his regret at not being able to keep his engagement. "lam just going over to the Sandwich Islands," he wrote. Presmtly it will come to finding on calling on a friend a notice on the door' Gone to Greenland. Back in an hour ;" or "Off to India. Return to-morrow.

There is some talk of Lord Randolph Churchill going to Ainerica this autumn. His wife's relations are very anxious to receive him, but I doubt whether he cares to go. Sir Lyon Playfair, whose wife is also an American lady, is more faithful in his attachment to the country that secured him the blessing of a wife. He has not since he was mar- ried missed a single autumn without visiting the States. Apart frein the necessity of being in town on the 20th Octo- ber, members already find themselves deeply engaged in connection with the political meetings. One of the mem- bers for a division of Lancashire tells me that be has now engaged himself for the next six Saturdays to attend at public meetings in various districts of his constituency, which is brimfull of indignation against the Lords anent the Franchise Bill.

HOUSE OF LORDS.-MONDAY.
The Hottse-en.ei-ai-fo-u; -011-o-c-k-,-wh'en-i-h-e-Royal assent was given by Commission to the Fisheries (Oyster, Crab, and Lobster) Act Amendment Bill, and a number of (Eller bills. • '' '

Trot PItaIeCITTSX Btr,L.—Lord WEAITSS gave notice that on Thursday he would move that the House is prepared now to proceed with the consideration of the Franchise Bill, on the understanding that an humble address be forwarded to Her Majesty praying her to summon Parliament in the early autumn, for the purpose of considering the Redistribu- tion Bill which Her Majesty's Government was prepared to present to Parliament at the earliest possible moment. He explained that he had drawn up this resolution with- out any communication with any member of that House or the other HOUPO of Parliament.—The Marquis of SALISBURY protested against the in- convenience of the course taken by the noble Earl. The resolution was one cancelling the resolution which the House d-liberately came to on Tuesday after two nights' debate. The House had solemnly recorded that far certain reasons it would not give the bill second reading, and until that resolution was formally rescinded it was not competent for the House to reconsider the bill.—Lord Ross- EV.ItY did not understand that the resolutioniwould supersede any resolution previonely arrived at by the House. He feared with regard to the noble lord (Salisbury) that what he had said left little doubt as to the attitude he intended to observe , towards this resolution.—Lord GRANVILLE said he should think primet facie the motion perfectly in order. He be- lieved all they resolved the other day was that the bill should not be read a second time that day ex- cept under certain circumstances. The bill now remained on the papers for second" reading supposing there should be a majority of the House of opinion that the Bill should pass. Her Majeity's Government were quite , prepared to support the proposal of the noble lord. At all events, during the conrso of November the Government would be quite prepared to undertake the very great task of considering the Redistribution Bill, but, of course, on coneli- tiotathat the Representation of the People Bill passed this session. Lord JERSEY expressed a hope that the leader of the Opposition would see his way to accepting the proposal, and so averting the crisis which was impending. The mat- ter then dropped. The House adjourned at 6 50. HOUSE OF CONIMONS.—MoNnay. The Speaker took the chair shortly before four o'clock, and. on a summons from Black Rod, proceeded to the Home of Peers, where the royal assent was given by Commission to several bills. THE CLEATOR MOOR RIOT.-,—Mr. SEXTON gave notice that he would ask the Home Secretary what information he could give as to the rioting at Cleator Moor.—Sir W. HAR- COURT at once read the ofticial report, which said that on Sunday the Orange party, armed with pistols, Bawds' and spears, &c., dressed in the Orange costume, and with flags and limners, were taken to Cleator Moor by special trains. On their way from the station they were met by a large crowd of Roman Catholics, who attacked the Orange party. Several blows having been struck oa both sides, the Orange party fired several shots and struck persons with their swords and spears. A letter carrier at the Cleator Moor Post Office was shot dead on the spot, and six others were wounded. Many more were struck by swords and spears. The Orangemen bad been at last got to the railway station, where the attack was renewed by many persons, men and women, who had reached there by circuitous routes. Several shots were fired by the Orangemen at the crowd who had occupied the railway bridge, bat no one had been injured. Ts NISERO —A number of notices of motion having been put in, Lord E. Ferwermenica, in reply to Mr. Gibson, said other attempts were being micle to communicate with General Gordon, and reports bad lately reached Wady Haifa that he was making constant sallies.—Mr. GOURLEY asked wkether intelligence had been received of the death of another of the crew of the Nisero, that others are suffering trorn lever, and that the whole require additional clothing. —Lord Fereeteurerca was aware of the facts as stated in the question. The remainder of the crew were reported well. Medicine had been supplied by the commander of Her

„ Majesty's ship Pelicut, who bad made arrangements for letters to b. transmitted.—Mr. GLADSTONN moved that this Howe will inamediitely resolve itself into the Committee of Supply, which, after some discussion, was agree i to, and the House went into Committee of Supply upon the Civil Service Estimates. .

...... BILLS ADVASCED.—The Sheriff Courthouses (Scotland) Amendment Bill was read a third time, and the Naval Dis- cipline Act (1866) Amendment Bill was read a second time. The Royal Military Asylum (Chelsea) Transfer Bill, and the Great Seal Bill were read a second time. The Strensall Common Bill passed through Committee. The Trusts (Scotland) Bill, the• Reformatory and Industrial Schools (Manx Children) Bill, and the Newcastle Chapter Bill were read a second time. The House then went into Committee on the Poor Law Guardians (Ireland) Bill. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TVESDAY.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter past four o'clock. TUE FRANCHISE BILL, &c.—Replying to the Earl of Milltown (who Lord GRANVILLE gently hinted, in putting a question made a speech prepared for the recent debate on the Franchise Bill). Lord Granville said he had nothing to add to the statement made after the notice given by Lord Werayss. He much regretted to learn from what had fallen from Lord Salisbury that the motion was likely to be op- posed by him to-morrow.—Several bills, including the Hours of Polling Bill, were advanced a stage, and at ten minutes te six their lordship% adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. Mismsr.r.stueons.—Some time was occupied by discussion of the Lords' amendments to the Edinburgh Northern Tramways Bill. These were disagreed with without a divi- sion. Mr. Gladstone declined the invitation of Mr. Ashmead- Bartlett to inform the House at the present time of the ckaracter of the financial proposals submitted to the Con- ference.—The PREMIER moved that for the remainder of the session Government business have priority on Wednes- days.—Sir H. Woury thought, before this was agreed to, information should be givea by the Government as to the

progress made with the Conferance. Was the House to be kept sitting awaitisg the decision of the Conference P—Mr. GLADSTONE pointed out that there was "three-weeks' busi- ness on the paper," and when they reached the close of Supply the question pu: by Sir H. Wolff might fairly be raised. The Government had no reason to believe that any incenvenience to the House would arise by the prolongation of the Conference.—The motion was agreed to.—The Premier next moved that the Rule providing that the House shall foithwith go into Committee of Supply on Mondays and Thursdays be extended to Tuesdays and Wednesdays. —Stone conversation ensued, and eventually the House divided, the motion being carried by 185 votes against 46. SUPPLY.—Tbe House then went into Committee of Supply, taking tap the Navy Estimates. These were dis- cussed for some hours by members en both sides, the Con- servatives leading off with criticism. Mr. Campbell- Bannerman, rising to reply, found stretched before him an absolute waste of empty benches, not a single member of the Conservative party being present. The hon. gentleman, with great presence of mind, preserved the fiction of the attendance of the Opposition, referring to Mr. W. H. Smith as "the right hon. gentleman opposite," and expressing his appreciation of the general tone in which the debate had been carried on. It was not till midnight that votes began to be taken, and the House remained in Committee till a late hour.

BILLS ADV&NOED.—The Royal Military Asylum, Chel- sea (Transfer) Bill passed through committee, and was read a third time. The Great Seal Bill passed through commit- tee, and was read a third time. The Strensall Common Bill was read a third time. The Prisons (Ireland, Cost of Con- veyance of Prisoners) Bill was read a third time. The Salaries of Magistrates in Ireland Bill passed through com- mittee. The order for the second reading of the Land Im- provement and Arterial Drainage (Ireland) Bill was dis- charged. The Shannon Navigation Bill passed through committee. The Reformatory and industrial Schools (Manx Children) Bill passed through committee. The Newcastle Chapter Bill passed through committee and was read a third time. The Naval Discipline Act Amendment Bill passed through committee. The House went into committee on the Poor Law Guardians (Ireland) Bill, and tbe bill passed through committee. The Oyster Cultivation (Ireland) Bill wr read a third time. The Canal Boats Bill Amendment Bill was read a third time. The House adjourned at 20 minutes past two o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker o'clock. took the chair at 20 minutes past twelve

Pwirrross 7Petit:ons were presented in favour of the Manchester Ship Canal Bill by Mr. Stagg. GENERAL CipeDom.-:—Mr. J. LOWTHER asked if the Go- vernment were in receipt of any news respecting General Gordon's position at Khartoum ?—Lord Fitzmatirice was not present.—Sir W.
