Committee of Supply (Civil Service Estimates), and on the first vote proposed, of £32,622, for the Civil Service Com- mission, Mr. SEXTON threw out the suggestion that fees should not be exacted from candidates for employment in the lower grades of the service.—The vote was agreed to, as was also £58,338 for the Exchequer and Audit Depart- ment. —Some other votes were agreed to, and progress was then reported. MISCELLANEOUS.—The Natal Discipline Act (1866) Amendment Bill was read a third time.—The order for the second reading of the Sale of Int)xicating Liquors on Sunday (Durham) Bill was discharged, and the bill was withdrawn.—The High Court of Justice (Provincial Sit- tings) Bill passed through committee.—Mr. HIBBEET brought in a hill to remove debate as to the powers of the Secretary of State in relation to the altering, enlarging, re- building, and building of prisons, and appropriating any building for a prison.—Mr. GEORGE RUSSELL introduced a bill to continue certain turnpike Acts, and to repeal others.
The House adjourned at five minutes to six o'clock. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TunEtSDAY.
The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack shortly after four o'clock.
FRANCHISE BILL-THE COMPROMISE REJECTED:

There was a large attendance in the House when Earl WEASYSS rose to move that the House was prepared to pro- ceed with the consideration of the Representation of the People Bill on the understanding that en address should be presented praying Her Majesty to summon Parliament to assemble in the early part of the autumn for tue purpose of. considering ,the Redistribution Bill. The noble Lord refer- ring to what had occurred in the House of Commons on Fri- day night, remarked that the Prime Minister seemed to be guided ky a spirit of conciliation. The door was open, and the Conservative side of the House might very reasonably pass through it without stultificstion and without loss of honour, and so avoid the danger, supposing the coming agitation to be successful, of a more sweeping and drastic Franchise Bill. In addition to his proposal auother course open to their lordships was to allew the bill to be read a second time and proceed with it in committee, sus- pending the third reading until the Redistribution Bill was before them. He counselled the Conservative party not to take their stand on mined and rotten ground, but to remem• ber the magnitude and gravity of the occaeion.—The motion was seconded by the Earl of SHAFIESBURY, who felt that if their lordships came to a decision adverse to the Franchise Bill it would lead to a breach of peace and order through- out the country. He urged that the bill should be passed, and that they should provide the secerities they deemed necessary in committee or on future stages.—Earl CADOGAN moved as an amendment that the House was of opinion that it would be desirable that Parliament should assemble early in the autumn for the purpose of considering the Franchise Bill in connection with a Redistribution Bill. He contended that the withholding of the Redistri- bution Bill was A deliberate plan for forcing Parliament to accept whatever scheme of redistribution the Prime Iginieter might choose to frame —The amendment was se- conded by the Earl of Dunne:Tex.—After remarks from the Duke of Somerset, the Duke of Norfolk, and the Earl of Aberdeen, the Marquis of SALISBURY said, after the plain announcement of the Prime Minister, he saw no room for compromise, and he did not see how those who voted with him ten days ago could withdraw from the assertion of the principle that redistribution and enfranchisement must pass together. The bill wa,s still alive, and as far as his party was concerned it would not be killed. The act of proroga- tion, a weapon that was in the hands of the Government to use at their discretion, would if it was exercised kill the bill. It was said if the bill was Rot now passed it would be sent up again in the autumn. He protested against such a course, which would in effect be preventing the franchise being carried out till the Government cauld give effect to their despotic design of using the Franchise Bill as a means of coercing both Houses of Parliament. —Earl GRANVILLE utterly disbelieved that the noble Marquis NVAS in the least in earnest either for the extension of the franchise or for redistribution. He qu3ted words of Lord Salisbury in the country against the extension of the franchise, and main- tained that Mr. Gladstone, on the contrary, was most earnest on the subje.ct. He hoped noble Lords would not go about tieing such clever but mischievous language as Lord Salis- bury had used.—After some remarks from Lord FEYERSHAN, I Lord Wemiss replied and the House divided, when there appeared For Lord Wemyss'e motion l3l Against

Majority against The numbers Ware received with loud Ministerial cheers, the majority being nine less than last week. Lord Cado- gan's amen4ment was then put and agreed to without a division. The other business having been disposed of their lordships adjourned at 25 minutes to eight o'clock. HOUSE OF CONIMONS.—TtIORSDAY. . . .

The Speaker took the chair shortly before four o'clock.. MISCELLANEOUS.—Lord E. FITZMATIRICE communicat?d the substance of a despatch received from the Hague con- veying the assent of the Dutch Gooverliment to the propos Ils made by Her Majesty's Government to secure the release of the crew of the Nisero. It stated that the Rtjala had been. informed that unless the crew were released the G overn ments of Great Britain and the Netherlands would hold him responsible and proceed jointly to secure their release,but in the event of compliance with their demand his p orts would be reopened to trade, and he would receive a small meney payment.—ln reply to a question by Mr. Chaplin as to our forces in Egypt, the Marquis of HAIITINOTON stated that Sir F. Stevenson had asked for one battalion as a rein- forcement, but he made the demand rather as a matter of precaution than of actual urgency. The Government had deckled to send one battalion now at Malta to Egypt. and another battalion now in the Ntediterranean had been ordered to hold itself in retdiness if its services should be required. —The PRIME MINISTER having sttted that he and his col- leagues conslitred that it was a matter of urgency that there should be fur Sr reforms in procedure, but that there was no available time for the purpose at present the right hon. aentleman proceeded to make a statement respecting the Conference.—Mr. GLADSTONE stated that the Commission had completed its labours, and the decisions which now had to be given were exclusively matters for the Conference. He expected that the Cor farence would meet early, and Lord Granville would take the initiative, though net au- thoritatively, in summoning the powers. There would be an opportunity for Parliament to discuss the decision of the Conference.—ln reply to Mr. M'Coan, Lord E. FITZ- HAURICE stated that it was not true that the British au- thorities at Aden had annexed Berbera, on the opposite coasts. A further reference was made to the Cleator Moor riots, the HOME SECRETARY repeating that so far as he could see there was no ctuse for blaming the magistrates. The mob, said the right hon. gentleman, who attacked the armed ptrty were four times more numerous than the party they attacked, and because a party was armed that was no reason why they should have been attacked, as the carryinz of arms was not unlawful in this country. The House again went into Committee of Supply en the Civil Service Estimates.—The vote for Woods and Forests was, after dis- cussion, agreed to, and progress reported. Some other business was transacted and the House ad- journed.

MANCERSTER SHIP CANAL BILL. The Select Committee began their second week's inquiry into the merits of the Ship Canal Bill on Monday morning. Mr Sclater-Booth presided, the other members of the Com- mittee being the Marquis of Tavistock, Mr L Fry, and Mr J A Campbell. Mr James Abernethy, past president of the Institute of Civil Engineers, and consulting engineer to the scheme, having mentioned the river improvements with which he had been connected, expressed the opinion that the proposed works would not be injurious to the Mersey; that they would not lead to the formatien of banks and shoels in the estuary; and that the training walls would not be conducive to silting up. The cutting of the channel would accelerate the time at which the tide would arrive at Runcorn, and there would also be an increased volume brought into the upper part of the river. These results woeld have a beneficial effect, because they would give an increased scour at ebb tide. He was of opinion that the canal works were well laid out for the purpose intended. Since last year there had been considerable improvement in the plans, many curves having been lessened, and the interference with the tide above Warrington had been prevented. On Tuesday morining the evidence of Mr. James Fowler, engineer to the Tees Conservancy Commissioners, was re- eutned. He expressed a decided opinion that after the for- Teatime of the new channel no new deposit of silt could take place between Dingle Point and New Righton.—Mr. Bindon Storey, F.R.S , who has been the engineer to the Dublin Port and Docks for twenty eight years, and who is consult- ing engineer to several tide and harbour trusts in Ireland, was next examined. After a careful examination of the plans he had come to the conclusion that the channel would he in no ways injurious to the bar of the river, but tend to i improve it.—Mr. Shelford, an engineer, whose experience included works connected with the Learn Valley drainage and improvement, and the improvement of the Humber and Tiber, said he did not think the proposed werkscould have any influence on the bar—Mr. W. H. Wheeler, who bad been engaged as a civil engineer at Boston, Lincolnshire, for the last 25 years, and had an intimate knowledge of the opera- tions which had been taken to improve the navigation of the Wash, said the effect of the training walls which had been put down there had been highly beneficial ; and he was con- vinced that a similar result would fellow on the Mersey.— Mr. Giles, engineer, Southampton, produced surveys of the Mersey, which were made by his father in 1819, which showed variations in the channel just in the same way as now..

On Wednesday the committee heard the evidence of several witnesses with regard to the quantity of land which would be vequired for the canal and all the newsary works. Evidence was also given as to the rates of freight on the canal as compared with Liverpool, the rates of insurance, and the feasibleness of navigating the canal by steamers of consid.rable tonnage. The case for the promoters was closed. and evidence was then given in support of Sir H. Da Fret- ford's opposition, when tffii committee again adjourned. In the Ship Canal inquiry on Thursday evidence was given in support of Sir H de Trafford's case against the bill. Mr Fox, medical officer of health for Mid-Cheshire, gave a shocking account of the condition of the Irwell and the Bridgewater Canal. EAR LE S ft) W.N.

ASSAULT AT EARLESTOWN.—George Adams was sum- moned at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, with assaulting Mary Coleman, at Earlestown, on the 28th June. —The evidence showed that the defendant owed the com- plainant a half-crown, and when she asked him for it he struck her on the eye.—The defendant, who alleged that the complaiaant etruck him first, was fined 20s and costs. PITCH AND Toss AT GOLBORNE.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, before Messrs. 14. Houghton and A. C. McCargaridele, John Berke, Michael Joyce, James Med- ley, James Quinn, Michael Garrity, John Horrigan, and John Callighen, were summoned for playing at pitch and toss on the highway at Golborne on the 6th inee—P.C. Whiting stated that he saw the defendants with a number of others playing at pitch and toss, and he saw money pass between them several times.—Each of the defendants was tined is (includi are coats.) THE TrtErr BY A JOINER.—For hevieg, at Heydock, on or about the 24:h et May last, stolen two chisels, a pocket- book, and other articles belonging to Willi etn Whitefield also One saw and four bracebits.the property of Richard Ran- son and one hand hammer, the property of Richard Evans and Co.; likewise, at Sutton, on the 220 d of the same month, having stolen two augurs, one chisel, one saw, and one monkey wrench, the property of John Cross, a joiner (23) named William Jones was sentenced to two calendar months' imprisonment at the Liverpool Quarter Sessions on Wednesday. HAYDOCE COLLIERS' TRIP.—The anneal trip in connec- tion with the Haydock collieries (Messrs. Richard Evans arid Co I took place on Saturday, the place of destination being Blackpool. Notwithstanding the unfortunate dispute with regard to the wages of the colliers, about 2,000 persons availed themselves of the opportunity of visiting the "Brighton of the North." They were conveyed in three special trains, which left Earlestown in quick succession shortly after six o'clock in the morning. Great praise is due to Mr. Young, the stationmaster, and the other officials for the manner in which their onerous defies were performed. CAPTURE OF A HURGLA.R.—At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, James Richardson, a labouring M3O, was brought up for breaking into and entering the dwelling- house et George Barrow. at Winwick, and stealing a quan- tity' of provisions, confectionary, dzc., to the value of 3s 9d ; and also with breaking and entering the dwelling-house of George Lawson, at flartonwood, and stealing a quantity of sugar, butter, and sweets.—Superintendent Jackson stated that he had to ask for a remand in that else. The prisoner had been convicted four times for felony, and he would ulti- mately have to be committed for trial. He therefore wished to ask for a remend for six days.—The Bench granted the application, and the prisoner will consequently be brought up at the Warrington county police court. ASHTON MINERS AND THE HOUSE OF LORDS.—At a mass meeting of 'Mama, about 4,000 being present, held on Wednesday on Ashton Heath, to consider the wages ques- tion, the following resolution was unanimously adopted : "That this meeting of miners has seen with much astonish- ment the action of the House of Peers in throwine out the Reform Bill of 1834, which passed the representative House of Commons with overwhelming majorities. This meeting protests in the very strongest manner against such nncoaeti- tutional action, and hereby urges upon Mr Gladstone's Go- vernment (now that the opportunity is afforded) to give effect in the most efficient manner to the often expressed wish of the United Kingdom to put into operation at once such a mode of procedure that will bring about a speedy die- solution of the House of Lords." The resolution was moved by Mr S Woods, ex-president of the Lancashire and Cheshire Miners' Federation, and seconded by a work- ing man. LADS CHARGED WITH DRUNZENNESS.—At the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday, George Cosgrove and George Lewis, lads, were charged with being drunk and disorderly on the sth met, at Earlestown. The defendants pleaded not guilty.—P C Lloyd stated that he saw the two defen- dants drunk in Viadect-street, Earlestown. They were kicking the door of the Viaduct Inn, and aboat 50 people were round them. Witness got hold of Cosgrove and found him bleeding from the mouth. The landlord then Came out and said he had had to turn them out and had to lock the door as they were drunk and wished to be served with drink-Tae Chairman (Colonel McCorquodale), said the B etch were glad to find that the landlord had not served the lads with drink—Superintendent Jackson intimated that he would take care that the landlord was intormed of the expression of opinion by the Bench.—The Chairman said the Bench hoped that case would be a lesson to the defendants and that they would never be placed in such a position again. The case would be dismissed on that occasion.

, ANTI-VACCINATION PROSECUTIONS: EXTRAORDINARY PROCEEDING'S. At the Newton Town Hall, on Saturday, before Colonel George McCorquodale, Messrs. R. Houghton. C. Pilkington, and A. C. McCorquodele, Mr. J. C. Sutton (clerk to the Warrington Baird of Guardians), rose and said that he was authorised by the 13 •ard of Guardians to make an applica- tion with reference to the decision of the court in certain oases that had recently come before them.—Mr. Thomas Dukbury, of Blackburn, then entered the defendents' box and slid that as he represented the defendants in those cases, he asked the privilege of again appearing on their behalf.— Mr. Sutton replied that it was a matter which referred purely to the decision of the court and was a question affecting the re-issue of a summons. It was clear that Mr. Duxbury had no authority whatever to interfere at that stage of the proceedings.—Mr. Duxbury : Mr. Sutton has no right to--The Clerk ( Mr. Buckton), interrupting: Will you be quiet—don't interrupt.—The Chairman : Who is this man ?—The Clerk: I don't know; he has not been called upon.—Mr. lluxbory r I was the defendant in the cases to which he refers. The Clerk: You must not interrupt the proceedings. Mr. Sutton then proceeded to state that a man named Pres- cott was summoned with a number of other persons to produce his child in order that the magistrates might make an order upon him directia4 the vaccination of the child. 'At the instance of Prescott himself the hearing of the case was adjourned until the following Petty Sessions, when a difficulty arose. Inasmuch as Mr. Gillespie, who had signed the summons, wee not present, the court considered they were without jurisdiction and practically dismissed the case. Mr. Gillespie, however, was present when the summons originally came on for hearing, and as the defendant had asked for the case to be adjourned for his own convenience he (Mr. Sutton) thought it was quite competent for other magistrates to hear it in the absence of Mr. Gillespie. He submitted that a summons issued by one magistrate could be heard by another, and asked that the summons in the case to which he referred might be re-issued. It was a very important matter, and the Guardians were only de- sirous of enforcing the Act of Parliament which the,' were required to carry oat—The Clerk intimated that there was a note in Stone's Manual to the effect that the same magis- trates who signed the summons must bear the case.—Mr. Sutton replied that under the vaccination laws solely that might be, but their incorporation with the Summary Juris- diction Act had done away with that necessity.—The Clerk: You contend that notwithstandihg the note the Summary Jurisdiction Act applies?—Mr. Sutton: It is expressly so by the words of the Act themselves. I say It was in the nature of a nonsuit, and it is the most convenient to ask you to re-issue the summons instead of seeking for a man- damus to compel you to bear the case.—The Chairman: The Bench are quite prepared to give you every facility in the matter —The Clerk: Have you given the defendant notice ? —Mr. Sutton: —Mr. Doxbury : As! represent the defen- dants, may I ask—Mr. Sutton (interrupting) said that , until the defendants were called upon by summons neither they or any person in their name could interfere in the

matter. It was purely a matter between the Bench and the Board of Guardians.—After a little further conversation the Chairman said the Bench were quite prepared to give Mr. Sutton every facility for carrying out the Act of Parliament. —Mr. Sutton said it was respectful to the court to show that the previous decision was wrong.—The Chairman: We are quite satisfied, and will grant a new summons. Mr. Sutton thereupon said that be had to address their worships on another matter with reference to the discharge of the summonses at the previous sessions on account of the notices. Although the year was not mentioned on the notice he (Mr. Sutton) maintained that it was impossible for any person to say that the notice was not a form of the eft ict set forth in the statute. Such a technical and trivial iflatter would not receive a moment's countenance in any court of law in the country. He understood there was also some objection to the notice on the around that the vaccination officer's address was not stat-d.—Tne Clerk: We don't think there is anything in that.—Mr. Duxbury : I represented the defendants in the cases to which Mr. Sutton has referred, aid the points in question will be heard again this morning in the other cases that have to come before you, and I think in all the cases your decision should be at least reserved until the cases are heard, as it is more thin likely that the same points will be involved in all. I totally dissent from the renderinx of Mr. Sutton on many points —At this point the Clerk intimated that owing to the length of time that the cases were likely to occupy a second court would be sitting in another room. Mews. E. Houghton and A. C. McCor- quodale then adjourned to another room, and heard a num- ber of police cases, while the proceedings in connection with the vaccination eases took place before Colonel Geo. McCor- quodale and Charles Pilkington, Env. David Garnett, of Earlestown, was then called, and Mr. Duxbury said he appeared for him. The charge against him was "that being the father of a child named Ada Elig- gins, under the age of 14, did uelawfully omit to carry into effect a certain order made by Thomas John Gillespie, Esq., dated 31st May, 1884, made in pursu- ance of the Vaccination Act, whereby the justices water that the defendant should cause his child to be vaccinated within 21 days; such child not having been vac- cinated, and the time expired, the said child not having been proved unfit for vaccination."—Mr. Dnxbury said he mustask first of all by what authority or right Mr. Sutton appeared in those cases that mornine.—The Clerk : You must wait until you have heard the cases.—Mr. Du shiny : If the application had been made by the Vaccination Officer it was perfectly right, but in deference to your ruling I mnet quastion the right of Mr. Sutton to appear here. If he is willing to appear on sufferance I will not object, but if he claims a legal right I must object —The Clerk: Its has Mr. Duxbury (interrupting): Do the magistrates rule Mr. Sutton has a right to appear here this morning 2—The Clerk: Mr. button will duly give his rights.—Mr. Sutton said ha did not want to exhaust the p atier.ce of the Bench, but the appearance of MrDuxbury was in direct contravention of the Solicitors' Act, notwithstandg the words of the clause in the Vaccination Act.—Tha Clerk : He has a right to cross-examine the witnesses, but not to make speecees.—Mr. Sutton said he produced the authority of the Board of Guar- dians directing him to appear there and conduct the pro- ceedings under the seal of the Board.—Mr. Duxbury replied that that did not touch his point.—Mr. Sutton said the matter simply.rested in a nutshell. The defendant had been summoned, ad the only defence he could answer was the production of a certificate that the child had been vacci- nated, or that the child was unfit. That was the only de- fence under the Act of Parliament. He would prove that the order to have the child vaccioated had been duly served upon the defendant, and that no certificate had been r,ceived of the vaccination of the child.—P.C. Thomas Hunt was then sworn, and stated that he had left an order at the resi- dence of the defendant.—Alfred Cooper, vaccination officer, said he called upon the defendant, and the latter said his child was not vaccinated. He had not since received any certificate that the child had been vaccinated.—Mr. Daxbury stated that by virtue of

the Act of Parliament he must claim to say a few words in defence, otherwise the case was certainly at a crisis at once. He challenged Mr. Sutton's right to appear there. —The Clerk : The Bench have decided to heir Mr. Sut- ton.—Mr. Duxbury : That does not invalidate me giving my reason why he should not appear.—Mr. Sutton : I must really object to this your worships.—Mr. Dux'eury : Mr. , Sutton is now clearly out of order. He has had his say and must keep quiet. —The Clerk (to Mr. Duxbury): The Bench hal decide 4 against you. Do you propose to call any wit- nesses ?—Mr. Danbury : 1 purpose to question the validity of the vaccination officer's appointment—The Clerk : The Bench have decided that it is valid.—Mr. Danbury said there was then the 31st section under which a parent could offer reasonable excuse for not having his child vaccinated, and he (Mr. Duxburv) could offer one.—The Chairman : We want to know whether this order has been obeyed or not. If it has not, we must make our decision upon it. Do you want to show us that the order has been obeyed or that it has not been obeyed 7—Mr. Danbury stated that a defendant was only liable if he could not show some reason- able grounds for not carrying the law into effect. He maintained that the reasonable ground in that case was that the order was invalid because it was made without the privilege of hearing evidence that might otherwise have actuated the Bench in coming to a decision. The order had been ma le without any evidence that the officer before the court was duly appointed.—The Clerk: That is not so.—: Mr. Danbury replied that it was. He had bad a copy of the cases from a shorthand writer's notes.—The Chairman: We decide that it is a valid order, and therefore you need not go into the subject. Is the child ill or unable to be vaccinated?— Mr Duxbury: lam not obliged to admit it lam not obliged to commit myself in any court —Mr. Sutton: There is really no defence at all your worships. Mr Duxbary said that even then he claimed the right to Arldn.ns the Bench for a mitigation of the penalty. The Chairman No.—The Clerk: Yee, he may address you in mitization of the penaltv.—The 'Chairman: Yes, go on.--Mr Duxbury said the Bench would probably be ready to grant that they had the option of mitigating a penalty even if a case was proved.—The Clerk: The magistrates have a discretionary power.—Mr Duxbury : In most cases clerks are not supposed to give utterance.—The Clerk: You may make a good keeper of a Temperance Hotel, but I don't think you know much about the Vaccination Act.—Mr Danbury in tint ained that the act did not mean to apply to such cases as those.—The Chairman: I have consulted with My brother magistrate and now tell you and Richard Higgins, the father of this eland, that if he will undertake within a reasonable time to have the child vaccinated we will adjourn the case and de- cide our course of action afterwards. We must have an un- derstanding that the child will be vaccinated within a given time in accordance with the order which we c msider valid. Are you prepared or aathorised to do this 7—Mr Duxbury said such leniency spoke well for the Bench, but at the same time the questions had large considerations for the parent and be WAR not prepared to make any each offer then.—The Chairman: Then we must adjudicate upon the cases.—Mr Duxbury- was proceeding with further remarks when the Chairman said: We are not going to discuss the law; we are going to take the law as it is laid down.—Mr Sutton said that in Landon. Liverpool, and other places, and so near as Widnes, epidemic disease was spreading. and the guardians felt that they must put their foot down on the obstinacy at Earlestown, and which, he was •happy to say, was confined to Earlestown only. Of the persons upoa whom orders had been made he thought they were only six who had not had their children vaccinated. He had to ask for the costs in the cases after all the trouble they had been put to.—The Chairman added that the Guar- dians had been lenient, and they knew some people had con- scientious objections to the Act of Parliament, placing a great responsibility on magistrates. Bnt they could not bear of an Act of Parliament being wrong, er an oversight on the part of Parliament. They hid to take the law as it stood, whether it was agreeable or not, and in that case they had determined to inflict the full penalty of 20e and costs.— Benjamin Harrison, of Earlestown, WAS summoned for a similar offence, and on the case being called Mr. Danbury said that all the Cues were exactly similar. The time of the court might be saved if he (Mr. Duxbury) readily granted that fact.—The Bench imposed a fine of 20s and costs.—Alexander Forster, of Esrlestown. was also sum- moned for a like offencs.—Alfred Cooper, vaccination officer, said that he had not received any certificate that the child had been vaccinated.—Mr. Danbury: Are you the officer appainted by the Warrington Guardians for the Earlestown district P—Witness : 1 am.—Mr. Duxbury: Have you the authority for that appointment ?—Witness : Yes; it has been shown before each time I have been here.—He then handed to the clerk a written document, which was sueseemently given to Mr. Duxbury. Mr. Duxbury then said: This has , ,no relation to the question I ask. It is simply his instrac- ' tions from the Guardians; but the question was Was he ap- I pointed officer? I ask for documents as to that appoint- ment. —The Chairman: He has taken his oath that he is so, and we are inclined to believe it.— Mr. Duxbury: The appointment by the Guardians must be canfirmed by Local Government Board, and my question I ask again. Has the appointment been confirmed? e This question has not been before the Bench before, and it is a ground why I don't ad,nit the offence.—The Chairman : We call upon him to vaccinate his child in a reasonable time and will give him an oppor- tunity of doing so. Is he prepared to do so ?—Mr. Dan- bury : Certainly not. Do your worships overrule my point as to the production of his official appointment? It has never been urged before.—The Chairman: Alexander Forster is fined 20s and cosm.--William Gilmour and John Clarke were also fined 20s and costs each in similar cases, Mr. Danbury on their behait declining to promise to have their children vaccinated. Mr. Danbury asked that the option of paying the penalty or having the chil- dren vaccinated might be left with the defendants until Has next sessions, but tne Bench declined to graot the applica- tion,--Joseph Emmett, of Earleetown, was summoned for a like offence, but the Bench said the case would be ad- journed until the next court day, as they had not a copy of the order served upon him before them.
. THE EARLBSTOWN CHURCH DISPUTE. SCM4DALOUS SCENES IN CHURCH. '

There was another discreditable scene in St. John's Church, Earlestown, on Sunday. At the forenoon service there was not a very large attendance—there being less than 20 adults present. The apparitor of the church (Mr Stacey), who was discharged by Mr Matthews, was again present, and before the service commenced the Vicar (the Rev T R Matthews) went up to him and said he had no business there. Mr Stacey replied that he bad not received a pro- per notice to leave, and asked the Vicir why he did not pay him the money which was owing to him. The Vicar said Mr Stacey was going on another subject, and added that he had nothing to do with it. The Vicar subse- quently walked behind the organ. where Joseph stac.y (the organ-blower) occupied his usual seat. Mr Matth.we, im- mediately ordered bite out, and said he bad no right to be there. He had got some one else to blew the organ, and ha

div.head: PATNFUL CASE OF WOUNDING.
div.p: PATNFUL CASE OF WOUNDING.

A very painful case of wounding with the knife occurred at Warrington on Sunday night, under circumstances detailed at the Borough Police Court on the following day, when a respectable-looking man named Jacob Hewitt was charged with unlawfully cutting and wounding with a carv- ing knife one Henry Emmett with intent to do him grieveus bodily harm—Mr. Hunt (chief constable) said that the pro- secutor was a stonemason, a married man with a family, and resided at 79, Buttermarket-street. The prisoner was a stonemason by trade, but of late he had been following the business of a pork butcher at 53, Winwick-road ; he also had a wife and family. Or. Sunday evening, between eight and line o'clock, he left his home and proceeded along Winwick- street until near the Ceetral Station where he met a friend, the prosecutor. The two exchanged the compliments of the evening and agreed to meet at nine o'clock at the Pelican Inn to have a glass or two together. They were the best possible friends with each other. At nine o'clock the parties met at the Pelican, where were also two other stone- masons, all four being particular friends. They remained a while in the public-house and had a few glasses of beer, and then all four repaired to the house of the prisoner, where there was a piece of cooked ham and other things on the table for supper. Emmett said "Now, Jacob, cut me a nice piece, I want a Food supper." Hewitt was at the time sharpening a knife and remarked in a jocular tone "Which side will you have it." Emmett thereupon put his hand to his face and said "This side," and the prisoner, in- stead of drawing the back edge of the knife, made the un- fortunate mistake of drawing the keen edge across his friend's throat. The prisoner's wife said "Jacob, thou's cut him," and prisoner exclaimed "Good God. I have not, have Ie" and then ran off for Dr. Joseph. The wound thus in- flicted was a very serious one, and the prosecutor was then in a sad condition.—Dr. Joseph deposed to being fetched to attend to Emmett, who, he said, he found to be suffering from a wound about three inches in length, and very deep, on the left side of the neck. It had crossed the main artery of the neck and had divided one of the branches. The man was bleeding severely and had lost a large quantity of blood. With some difficulty witness controlled the hemor- rage, and up to that time there had been no further hemor- rage, so that if the patient could get over another 24 hours he did not think that there would be any danger from bleeding. The wound was, however, a very serious one apart from the danger of bleeding, but, Emmett being a healthy man he had every hope that he would come round. When prisoner fetched witness he seemed very much dis- tressed, and was sober enough to know what he was about. No man could have made more endeavour to try to repair what he had done.—Mr. Hunt informed the Bench that the prisoner was a highly respectable rnan, and said that the question was whether he should not be set free on someone coming forward as his surety.—The Mayor said that he hoped no bad consequences would ensue from the occurrence. —The prisoner was then remanded until Friday. I Yesterday morning the defendant again appeared, and prosecutor, who was now present, stated that they were as good friends as ever.—Mr. Hunt stated that the prosecutor was going on favourably, and that the defendant, who was exceedingly sorry, had offered to pay the doctor's bill, wages of the injured man, and other expenses.—On this understanding defendant was simply bound over to appear when called upon.
POLICS RATE.—At the Liverpool County Sessions, on Tuesday, a local pollee rate of 1d was ordered to be levied or PrescoL

(Stacey) must leave, as he had no money to pay him on account of the collections having been so poor. Stacey ,e- -plied that he had not received a proper notice to lease, and he was not going to do so until he did get one. Mr. Matthews replied that if he WAS not going out he would fetch somebody who would soon put him out. In reply to another remark by Stacey that he would not go until begot a written notice, the Vic ir said he would not begin the service until he did go out. It is stated th it Mr. Matthews had two boys ready to blow the organ, but when the dispute occurred between the Vicar and Stacey they re- tired, and the Vicar had to order his own son to blow the organ. In the course of the squabble the Vicar picked up Stacey's hat, and, walking away with it, told the owner to follow it. Mr. Matthews took the hit and placed it on a ' seat near the church door. When the Vic tr's son put in an appearance Stacey left the church, and the service was pro- ceeded with as usual. Mr. Pemberton, of Liverpool, was the organist, and five or six girls again did duty as a choir. At the evening service Mr. Walter Stacey (the apparitor) was again in his usual place, and Joseph Stacey (his son) again went behind the organ. Mr. Matthews told Mr. Stacey that he wished him to remove his son from behind the organ before he (Mr. Matthews) fetched a policeman to remove him. Mr. Stacey replied that he would have nothing to do with him. His son was at his post, and he would stop there until he had received a proper notice to leave Mr. matthews thereupon proceeded to the organ-blower, and again informed the latter that he had better be going as he had no right there. It would he beet for him to go quietly as he had not done with Newton yet. The Vicar added that many a one would have got hold of him by the neck and thrown him out; " but," replied Stacey, "that is against the law. sir." Mr. Mat- thews said You know a bit about the law, then," and Stacey replied that he knew that much. The Organist (Mr. Pemberton) also advised Stacey to leave, and the latter ultimately surrendered the blowing pole to the vicar's son, who again officiated as organ blower. The service was then proceeded with. When the vicar entered the pul- pit to preach he drew forth some letters and pipers and said that before proceeding with his sermon he wished to say that he was not to blame for the recent diepute. Re read letters to the effect that Mr. Smith (the curate, who left under circumstances reported last week) had come male: peculiar conditions, and that the position WAS offered to him as a last chance. If Mr. Smith in anyway mis- behaved himself he would not have another situation. The Vicar said it was entirely Mr. Smith's fault what had taken place in the school; accused him (the curate) of having "wired into "him (the vicar) "tooth and nail," and added that the curate had opposed him in everything he had done in the Sunday school. The curate's qaerrelsoine d position was alone to blame for what had occurred. He then read letters from Mr. Smith. stating that the latter intended to resign long before the school dispute and the vicar added that he had read them in order to show that it was not owing to what had taken place iii the school that Mr Smith had left. Referring to the scholars whom be had discharged the vicir said they had been greatly irregular in their attendance. He w s sorry that Mr Smith had had to leave; but he (the vicar) could not help it as it was Mr Smith's own fault. Mr Matthews went on to say that the papers were always telling lies—there Was no believing them. Whoever wrote the letters to the news- papers were telling lies. He said he was the target at whom they shot, but he did not care so long as he had got a clear conscience—they could shoot as hard as they liked. In con- cluding the vicar added that what he was telling them was the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. After this extraordinary address a number of persons got up and left the building. During the week the attack upon the Rev II E Smith by Mr Matthews from a pulpit where he could not be'replied to has created a painful impression throughout the perish. It has tended to increase the strong sympathy and respect for the late curate which has ever been manifested since he came to E erlestown ; while the action of the viola has been condemned by all parties. PUBLIC MERTING OF PARISHIONEES.—PETITION TO REMOVE ran VICA.R. The proposal to erect an iron church for the scattered con- gregation of St. John's Church, Earlestown, has received a fair amount of support, and on Thursday evening a public meeting of the parishioners was held in the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, to decide upon what course should be pur- sued in reference to the matter. The business of the meet- ing, as stated on the handbill, Was "to take into considera- tion the spiritual destitution of the district of St. John's, and devise means for the erection of a new church. lire right. thing portion' of the scattered congregation are requested to attend." In response to this invitation there WAS a very large attendance. Amongst those present were NI-83ra. B. Corlett (late people's warden), M. Birkhead, G. Owen. E. Scott (late sidesmen), H. J. Durman (late organist), Henry Bradshaw., Henry Waywell, George Wright and the principal members of the congregation and choir. The meeting commenced about helfaast seven, when Mr Birkhead, speaking from the platform, said they would all know for what they had met that night, but be- fore the business commenced he would go a little out of the way to explain one or two letters that had appeared in the newspapers. He alluded to one written by the Rev Gustavus Carson, of Liverpool, who, he said had interfered in a neetter about which he knew nothing. (Hear' hear.) '1 he parish- ioners had been very anxious and had hoped bygenee would have been allowed to be bygones, and they hid striven as much as ever they possibly could to bury the hatchet. They all knew what they did when they went to see Canon Hop- wood, and they all knew the result of the arbitration that had taken place. But the very first thing after that arbitra- tion that the vicar did was to go and set that arbitration at nought. (",hharne.") The parishioners were not to blame about the matter. The Reverend Gustavus Carson had written a lot about the matter, but in replying he (Mr Birkhead) could say that fools rushed in where angels feared to tread. (Applause.) The rev, gentle- man in his gushing zeal for his dear friend the persecated vicar—(laughter)--had taken up the pen to champion a cause of which he was totally ignorant. His only informa- tion he bad gathered from the esirarte statement of the vicar, which at the best was a doubtful source. Tne only favour that the church people of Earlestown asked of Mr. Carson was that he would mind his own business—(applatrie) —and if he had any spare time on his hands to visit the hundreds of poor, starving, dying wretches in his own parish, who had not yet heard his voice or seen his face. The reverend gentleman had given them 3 Scriptural quo- tation, but he (Mr. Birkhead) did not think much of that. The devil could do that, and yet he was only the devil when he had done. (Laughter and applause.) What they wanted at Eirlestown was a man who lived a scriptural life, even if he did less at quoting. The class of worshippers Mr. C er- corn and the vicar of Earlestown would like would have to bear all things, believe all things, en- dure all things, pay for all things, and ask no questions. (Laughter.) The parishioners of Eerlestown were not quite reduced to so low a depth, but claimed the right to judge for themselves in things pertaining to religion. When the squabble was in its infancy, had their Vicar had Christian men for counsellors insteed of the luminary from St. Augustine's, Liverpool, the dispute would never have assumed such proportions. (Hear, hear.) When the nine summonses were issued, and the officers of the church were prosecuted, the Reverend Gustavue C ersen appeared at court in all the pomp and circumstance of law, minus the wig, and acted as chief prompter and deputy proeecutor. The poor vicar and he had together sown to the wind, and were n iw reaping the whirlwind. " The galled jades wince; In vain they try To pipe all hands; its all my eye!" —(loud laughter)—and Mr. Carson might yet learn that a fool meddling with strife not belonging to him was like a man taking a dog by the ears. All men were not gifted with the egotistical presumption that Mr. Carson was endowed with ; not that. they were ashamed of their statements, but simply wished to avoid notoriety; and many people thought it would have been more to Mr. Carson's credit and to the character of the " cloth " if his letter had been written under a nom de plume of some sort. (Hear, hear.) It was a dirty bird that fouled its own nest, and why bring Ireland into that miserable con- troversy ? Had they no clerical cowards, no pulpit meal- sins in this country that he must needs go and sully the fair fame of the land that gave him birth ? (Laughter.) To talk about their grand old church was all bosh. As a rule her teachings were good, but would to God he could say as much for her teachers. (Applause ) In the third paragraph of his letter Mr. Carson showed himself in his true colours. It amounted to this, that Mr. Carson had set up an image, and unless they fell down and worshipped that image the bread should be taken from them. (" Shame.") He (Mr. Birkhead) thought the directors of the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany were too much of gentlemen to listen to such " cant " as Gustavus Carson came out with. (Hear, hear.) There was no respectable parson in Lancashire who would help to form a deputation with Mr. Carson to go to them. The spirit Mr. Carson showed in his letter woe that of the old Bishop Bonner, and it he had power they who rebelled against him would have to go to the stake. It was a pity Gustavus Carson was not born 200 or 300 years ago, for the spirit he manifested in his letter showed that he would have made a down right good inquisitor. (Applauee, and cries of "Shame upon him.") Yes, it was a shame; and if Mr. Carson would only attend to his own duty be would have plenty to do without meddling with things he knew nothing about. (Applause.) Perhaps some of them would have read the letters written by their poor persecuted vicar. (Laughter.) He (Mr. Birkhead) thought the working ,men of larlestown were in the habit of calling a spade a spade, and a man might tell a big lie by leaving out a bit of the truth. (Hear, hear.) It was not quite necessary to say, "You are a liar," but it could be implied quite as much, and very easily. The Vicar's letter omitted a bit of the truth, and the most important part of it ; and a man who would read from his pulpit part of the arbitration and leave out the most important part of it was just the man who would leave out anything from a letter that was against him. In the letters referring to Mr. Smith, which the Vicar bad given to the papers, he had left out the most important one, and he did not think a man who did that and tried to villify the character of another to answer a purpose of his own was worthy the name of man. (Hear, bear.) Refer- ring to the discharge of the scholars by the Vicar, be (Mr. Shithead) thought the Vicar ought to discharge his family from the church for the same reason that he had discharged the scholars, namely, non-attendance. When the dispute began one or two of the Matthews' said they would never attend the church again so long as Mr Donlan presided at the organ, and they had religiously kept that vow. ("shame.") If young people kept away from the school while the dispute was on and had to be dismissed for It, then he thought Miss Matthews and Master Jahn Matthews ought to be dismissed from the chard, because they had not attended

for six months. (Applause.) Mr Smith was charged hi, 111( Matthews with having an iron chnrch in view, but Mr Smith never knew one word about the iron church, and it was a most deliberate falsehood to say that he did. (Hear, hear.) Mr Smith never had anything to do with it, and he (Mr. Birkhead) could give a downright denial to the state- ment, which was a false charge against hiin. (Applause.) It was not right to try and damage the character of a young man in that way. ("No," and "Shame,") They hid met that night to hear the opinions of the parishioners, and be would propose that Mr Corlett (the late people's warden) take the chair. (Applause ) They hail to consider whether they would have an iron church, whether they should for the present meet and hold a service elsewhere, or whether they should petition the bishop for the removal of the poor persecuted man. (Cries of "Remove him" and please.)

Mr. H. Waywell seconded the proposition that Mr.B. Core lett be chairman, and the motion was carried. Mr. Corlett said the meeting had been called to consider the advisability of erecting an iron church, for they certaisly wanted something of the sort. ( Hear, hear.) It was a shame, to see the congregation of St. John's sent to the winds, and it was only on Sunday last that he had seen members be- longing to the Church scattered about from one place to another. ("Shame.") That had been going on for the Past seven months at least, and it appeared to him it was geing from bed to worse; therefore the time had now arrived when they should take immediate steps to have a place of worship et their own. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The matter would require a grett deal of consideration, but as far as he was concerned he did not think it would be wise for them to ge into it at present. They ought not to have done with the ohurch—(hear, hear,)—they had erected. They ought not te throw it over for the whim of one man, but they ought to stick to it. They had paid for it and paid for everything about it, and they ought to stick to it like men. (Appl,tuee.) Before they went any further they ought to make one grand effort for the removal. of the " encumbrance " from Earlestown—(loud applause) If ever there was an encumbrance in Etrlestown it leas the vicar of S: John's, and if ever there was a man who had upset the place it was the vicar of St John's. .They cenld not tell him one grand act in any shape or form that he had done since he came to Eerlestown. (Hear, hear.) He had never done one, but they had found him upsetting and ob- structing everything and anything that the congregation had brought forward. (Applause.) They therefore should stick to their church, and, before throwing it over, should get UP a petition for the retnovel of the vicar, and place it before , the Bishop of the diocese. (Hear, hear, and applause.) When he (the speaker) attempted to put an end to the scan- • dal at the beginning, the vicar turned upon him and said, " It is not your business, and I shall not have your interfer- ence." He considered that an insult, because he WAS present • at the meeting as the people's warden to carry out their in- structions, and he was there also as the representative of the money that they found to carry on the sinews of war, and - they had a right to see to the spending of it. They had en- dured that thing lon, enough, and they ought to try by all the legitimate means in their power to remove that obnoxieue man. (Loud applause). Mr. Birithead stated that the best thing they could do Was to get someone to exchange livings with their vicar.. • (Voices: " Who will have him ?") He had once suggested ' that he should be sent out as a missionary so that if he c mld not convert the heathens they could eat him. (Laugh- ter.) Whatever might be the result of that meeting, it was only right that they send to the Bishop a petition res- pectfully worded and signed as numerously as possible. praying that the Bishop would look into the matter. If the Bishop took no notice of it then they would have done their duty, and although the vicar classified them as an "ungodly clique," he (Mr. Birkhead) woald say like the Pharisee of old, "Thank God I am not as the vicar." (Applause.) He did not pretend to be any better than his fellow-men. but be stood as well in the estimation of the people of Eerlestown as ever the vicar did. (Loud ap- plause.) Mr. William Mandeley (from the body of the hall) moved a resolution to the effect that a respectful memorial be pre- sented to the Bishop of Liverpool, as numerously signed 0 poesible, with the view of having their vicar removed from the district. (A Voice: "I don't think he has any power to remove him; the el= holds him at defiance now.")-- Mr. George Atty, who during the recent disturbances had been a warm supporter of the vicar, seconded the resolu- tion amid prolonged applause,—The resolution was then put to the meeting, and carried with acclamation. The following gentlemen were appointed a committee to draw up the petition :—Messrs. Wm. Meudsley, Robert Har- rison, Henry Bradshaw, Henry Wersiey, George Atty, ' Henry Waywell, M. Sickbed& B. Corlett, and Lewis Jones. Me. Birkhead subsequently remarked that it had been suggested that they should interview the Viaduct Works r Committee to see if they could not get the use ot the large , room on reasonable terms where they might assemble for prayer, and he did not see why they should not have as hearty a service in such a place as ever was held in any church. (Applause.) He believed it would be possible to keep the old organist, Mr. Durmen—(applause)—the old choir—(applause)—and most of the congregation as well, and he thought he might say that they would be able to have as good and better sermons, and on as good terms, too. (Leughtsr.) They, wanted a minister who would lead his fleck and advise them properly, and not one weo would bring the Bible in one hand and a whip of scorpions in the other. (" No," and ap- plause.) He asked them if it was their wish that the com- mittee should try to obtain the Viaduct Institute, in which to hold services. (Laud cries of " Yes, yes.") The com- mittee knew after that expression of opinion what ;hey were to do, and they should try to mike as favourable arrange- merits as it was possible and have their services as attractive and as beneficial as ever they were. (Applause.) The present position of the Church of St John was a complete farce and burle-que on religion, and he defied any man to go to that place of worship and be a better man for attending. The proceedings concladed with a hearty vote of Minks to Mr. Corlett for presidine ; and in resoondink Mr. Corlett stated that to show they meant business they had had plans drawn up for an iron church, and they were ready for pro- ceeding with the work at any time. He had conducted his part of the dispute honestly and fairly, and if the Vicar bad done the same they would have been saved the scandal that had occurred. (Applause.) THE VICAR AND THE CURATE. The following letter from the Rev. T R. Matthews ap- pears in a Liverpool contemporary for Wednesday last : Sir,—ln your issue of the 10th instant I find the following falsehoods added to their numerous p edecetsors. viz. :—That " the Rev. IT. E. Smith (my citrete) has left the town, not being able to work with the vicar." , has not left the town. bot is hers doing—he koows what, it is true that Mr. Smith did leave the towo earns time ago, and it was on this wise: On Mae 31st he had a quarrel with a parishioner, an elderly man, and on the next day. Whit-eund ay. was unable to cep duty, left in the aft trnoou for Liverpool, and did not return until the sth instant, During his five weeks' absence from Earlestown I received the tollowinz ietiers from him:- 3d, Gledstene-street, Edgehill, Liverp eal, June 26, 1884.— Deer Mr. Matthewe.—l have been trying to come back every - Friday, but hove heel) very unwell. D a you want me for Sun- day? 1 think I Lave made up my mind to leave Barlestown before the end of the year. Heweeer, upon this matter I wilt speak to you. I hope poll wil, not consider these my bolt lays, for I want them in August. With kindest regards to you all, believe me. dear Mr. Matthews. vary sin .erely yours, 0. ELWELL 811ITS.—Thyugh Mr. Smith was to unwell to return to his own wok, he Was advertised to preach and did nreach• in a certain church in Liverpool on the 15th of June. (Second letter.) June 27, lett —Dear afr. Matthews,—Thank you for your immediate reply to my letter, which I received at dinner time. lam obliged for your allowing me to Stay away over next Sunday You will let me know the day you wish me to return. We can talk about the other matters to- gether. and no doubt, arrange all things rightly —With kiodest regards, very faithfu'ly yours, H ELWELL (Third leiter )—July 3rd, 1834 Dear Mr. Matthews —I have been wadi g and expee ing a letter fr an you every day this week to tell me what, day .0 return. lan a little better in health. I am thankful to say, but I have almost quits made up my mind to retire from ministerial la- lo,urs for a little time shortly. Due notice, however, will be given both t the Blsh-p and to you Await- • Mg the favour of your reply with kindest rtgerds from . us all, ever sincerely yours, II EIWELL this looks like preparation to take his departure from Elarlestown. and why? Net in c msequenre of my ;Wiwi in the school last Standee. as it, is now stated (and the statement must have been furnished by hlm-e4), but in c meequence of his having failed to keep his contract bom with the Bishop and myself. Passing on to what Mr. Smith says about the school. I may state that in looking over the register for the last half-year. I foand that many in gr. Smith's class, as welt as in other classes, had been absent from 30 to 44 times ; and while I IFNI telling these youths that, according to our ;Anted rules, they had excluded themselves' from the school Mr, Smith (not the fret time) most violently obstrueted me in the execution of ay duty, thereby setting a very bad example to these youths. most of whetn are not the best behaved at any time. But, of course, Mr. Smith had a purpose in all this. He did not wish the real cause of his leaving Ear'estown to be known, and so. In a most unmanly way, sought to create another seeming cause to escape from a dint:lady in which be had so unwisely placed himself, to a more congenial sphere in the shape of an "iron Church" which has been talked of In Earlestown for several weeks past, and the.efore is not the result of last Sundae's events, as your article would make It appear. But this will not be Mr Smith's fi. et, ses-sion from the Church rf England. if it does take plane. In Feb, 18113, I nominated Mr Smith in the face of ve^y strong a trice to the contrary, and have been rewarded with ingratitude and disloyalty, and • I cannot but think that had it been.better known by t/ae public what material I have had to deal with in choir and curate, shout I rot have been ma freely blamed as I have. air Smith, rt.:, knows well the conditions upon vitt.% he came here' and yeteet, he failed to fulfill them by tot going up for priest's orders on. - Trinity due esy last. He is still a deacon, ordained in 1377. and has on several occasions in my absence done what, as den-- eon, he ought not to do; and his vecil ages, has been most re- prehensible throughout the disgrace ut scenes which have taken place here, and for a great deal of which I •• • with many others, cannot but think he is retponsible, having e allowed himself to get into the nwebes of an ungodly e ique. Hitherto only one side of this questi ,n has been before the public, and that a most shamefully fame one, as those who have given it very well know but the cause which is bolstered up by a tissue of falsettoods, uttered by unscrupulous anony- mms writers, must be a bad one indeed.—Yours ke„ T. IL MATTHEwS.—The Vicarage. Bartestown, July 12, 18E1. The following reply to the foregoing appeared on the next day aEI pained that Mr. Matthews should make such false statements in your issue of to-day about my leaving Series- town, When I wrote to him 1 was at home very 111, and quite unfit for ministerial work. I was afraid that I would have to take some nsqnths' rest, for L was thoroughly un- manned. I have sedulously endeavoured to keep myself from all the unpleasantness here, and lan grieved to teink that he should, after my resiging my poslsinn tinder hl-n, elm* me so Cruelly. At Mancherter on Saturday the match between England v. the Australians resulted in a draw; the Englishmen at the finish bad a wicket to fall and were 93 runs ahead. The visisors scored 182 in the single inninas, ano . the first innings England made 95, running up 180 in their second when play was finished.—Owing to the inclemency of the weather the match Eton v. Harrow was abandoned on Saturday as a draw greatly in favour of Ifetvow, wh t, with four wickets to fall in their second innings were already 195 runs on, the Etonians with thsir innings only having so sited 82 as again t 126 in the first innings of their opponents. who, In their second innings put on 152, with four wicket• to spare —The match Phila- delphians •. A two-days' match was commenced at Aigbiwth on Monday between Staffordshire County and Liverpool. the viiitors win- ning the toss and making 115 in their first innings. The home ' team ran up 130 and Staffordshire went in again and ran up 51 for the loss of one wicket when time was called. On the second day Staffordshire completed the innings tor 301 and Liverpool followed for 207. the full scores being. fitaffor4shlre. 116 and 301; Liverpool, 130 and 207.—The return match be- tween Lancashire and Yorkshire which commenced on Monday at Sheffield was for the benefit of Alan Hill, the fast bowler, who has &arty earned a recognition of his past services as fir a considerable period he was one of the most valusble members of the Yorkshire eleven. His performances in the cricket field have been remarkable and he has been one of the most popular of professional players. Yorkshire went in first and put to. gather 128. and at the rail of time the Lancashire team were only 23 behind, with six wickets to fall. On the following day Lancashire proved ammessful, winning by elx wickets, about about the most conspicuous victory that has fallen to the county for come time. During the day some tine work with the ball was witnessed, twenty wickets falling for only 118 runs. In all Barlow took 13 wickets at the co.t of 66 runs Briggs and Mr A. G. Steel did some good batting. Be re— Yorkshire, 128 and 72; Lancashire, 170 and 31, with six wickets to spare.—At Letilister on Tuesday, the county eleven failed to follow up an advantage they gained on Monday, and suffered a crushing defeat by 10 wickets at the hands 3f the Australians. Blore—Leloestershire. 143 and 64; Australians, 175 and 33.—When stumps were drawn at Loras on Monday, Middle,eX had all the worst of the game against Surrey, as ey had lost four wickets in their second innings for 18 runs and were s 11l three runs behind. On resuming on Tuesday. however, runs came quick y and the match subsegoently ended in favour of Surrey by ,even wickets.—At Derby on Tuesday. the game. Derbyshire Gentlemen v. Philadelphians, ended in a draw in favour of the visitors. Score—Philadel- phians. 157 and 243; Derbyshire Gentlemen, 141 and 60 for five wickets. On Wednesday, at Gloucester, the last four wickets of the home county fell against Notts for the addition of 19 runs to the overnight score, ens Notte were only set 77 rifle to get to wit. This seemingly light task, however, occupied two hours and cost four good wickets. Notts winning the match by six wickets. 0, Thursday 'about 4.000 persons witnessed the match he- tween Lath-smite and Surrey at aigburth. The feature of the daN 'splay was the fine stand made by la wous. Sinner and Kay for Surrey. The visitors were very unfortunate at the com- mencement. five wickets falling for 23 runs, but these two bats completely altered the state of affairs, and before they were separated a resptctable score had been put on. It was a mis- fOrtuoe to Lancashire when Mr. Hornby let off Wood as be had only then scored four, and when the innings was flushed he was 34 not out. At the close of play for the day the scoie I stood :—Sur ey, 163; Laneashire. 102 for seven wl kets —The Australians me'. Div dleses at Lords on Thursday. and at call of time the Australians were 126 runs on, with one w'cket to fall. Be re—Middlesex, 53; Australians, 179 with one wicket to spare —At Nottingham on Thursday Nmts met Yorkshire. IIUYTON.

I JIUTTON CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH. The quarterly juvenile missionary meeting was held in the above church on Sunday afternoon; Mr. J. Jones in the chair. After Mr. W. D. Stoba had read the lessons of the day, Mr. R. C. Richards gave an interesting address on the Congo Mission In Central Africa, illustrated by diagrams. A collection was made on behalf of the London Missionarl Society. FUNERAL OIP THE LATE Ma. It. BARKEIL—The remains of Mr. Richard Barker were interred on yesterday morning 'week at Flay brick Hill Cemetery. The funeral cortege in- cluded, among a large number of Matives and friends from Liverpool and Birkenhead, the Revs Canon Penrhyn (Huy. ton), A. Knox (of St. Ann, Birkenhead), and Mr. Preston (Stipendiary.) The service was conducted by the fore- named clergy, and the dead march was played on the organ. The deceased was the eldest son of the late William Barker and senior member of the firm of Richard Barker and Co., brewers, tarrying on business at Huyton and Liverpool. Be died on the previous Tuesday after a short illness, at the age of fifty.five, and leaves a widow and family of three asms and four daughters.

The Meeley Relief Expedition has found the seven stir- ' vivers of Lieutenant Greeley's party. Sir Charles Mike has presented to .the House of Com- mons a petition praying for the reform of the House of Lords. Intelligence received at New York from San Domingo an- nounces that General Bellini had been elected president of the Republic. It is stated that the Prime Minister will visit Edinburgh and take part in a great Liberal demonstration towards the end of September. The Egyptian police at Cairo being disaffected, the strength of the British military police force in that city, is , to be largely increased. At Surrey Assizes, Guildford, on Thursday, Ellen Shep- herd, aged 35, was sentenced to death for the murder of her youngest son by drowning him in a water butt. Yesterday morning Messrs Elder, Dempster, and Co., of Liverpool, received a telegram stating that Mr. H. M. Stan- ley, the noted African explorer, is a passenger by their steamer Kinsembo, which they expect to arrive at Madeira any day. . A SUPPOSED DYNAMITER ARRESTED.—Late on Mrisday night a man began firing a revolver in Gairbraid-street, Glasgow. He then drew a knife and threatened to state the passers by. On being arrested documents were found en him containing the names of suspected dynareiters living in Glasgow. He gave the name of James Walker. div.head: FRIGHTFUL RAILWAY ACCIDENT NEAR PENISTONE : _
div.p: FRIGHTFUL RAILWAY ACCIDENT NEAR PENISTONE : _
23 PERSONS KILLED AND MANY INJURED.

1 A frightful lallway accident happened on Wednesday afternoon near Penistene, on the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire line. Nineteen persons were killed on the spot. , twenty-two were seriously injured (four of wham afterwards died), and a number were hurt in a less degree. The train which met with the disaster was the express for Lon- don which left Manchester at 12.30. The cause of the accident was the breaking of one of the axle-cranks of the engine. 'the engine and tender went off the rails, and, the couplings breaking, the rest of the train dashed over an embankment thirty or forty feet high. The engine and tender and a herse-box attached to it kept on the permanent way. Excluding the horse-box, the train was made up of seven carriages and three brake vane, and contained, so far as can be ascertained at present, over sixty persons. About sixty booked at Manchester, and at Godley, whiela was the only stop the train made, a few more joined it. The for- ward portion of the train, which contained the passengers for Grantham and Loriclon, suffered most. Two of the car- riages in the rear portion of the train remained almost up- right, and in them were nearly the whole of the few persons who escaped with a shaking. ' At the place where the accident occurred there is an in- cline of about lin 80, and the line bends outwards on the side on which the train was running. Roughly estimating, the radius is about three-quarters of a mile. About midway along it the railway goes over the road from Woodhead to Sheffield. The bridge is of stone, with stout parapets four or five feet high. The axle-crank is said to have broken some sixty or seventy yards before this bridge Was reached. As soon as the driver became aware that something was wrong he reversed the engineand applied the vacuum brakes which Were fitted along the train. The speed then was the usual speed of about forty miles an hour. Almost instantly the engine and tender seem to have left the rails. The violent jolting on the permanent, way speedily broke the coupling attaching the brake van to the horse-box, which was nextto the tender. The tr.in was then just coming abreast of the bridge. Instead of continuing the curve it went straight over tha embankment, which falls at at a sharp angle. The brake van, which was then the bead of the train, appears just to have missed the stonework of the bridge, for it was projected some distance into the field beyond the road. As it happened it was empty. The next carriage, which was a composite one, must have caught the parapet. Scarcely any of it was left together. It lay a fiat heap of boards a little distance behind the brake van. Two composite carriages, next in order, fell on to the road, turning completely over in the descent. The fragments could scarcely be seen to be two distinct carriages. The brake van which came after and completed the forward portion of the train was also on the road. The front of it was torn off, but it kept an up- ward position The guard who had occupied it escaped with his life. A cirri Igo with a brake compartment and a corn- pesite carriage, which were the first two in the rear portion of the train, did not quite reach the bottom of the embank- ment, and maintained an almost upright position. The end c ,mpartments in both were damaged, but the other compart- ments seemed intact. Behind these two carriages were a composite carriage, a third-class carriage, and a brake van. All three vehicles had turned completely over. The guard of the van also escaped with his life. Very little time elapsed between the beginning and the completion of the disaster. A man who was in a field half a mile off says he turned roand when he heard the train ap- ,proaching. When it came in sight round the curve the noise of it seemed to him greater than usual. Then a cloud of dust arose about the train, and while he beard the crashing as the carriages came over the embankment, he was able to see scarcely anything of what had happened. When the dint cleared away he saw the heads of a number of people who were looking out of the windows of carriages in the rear portion of the train. Help was at once at hand. Bullhonse Colliery is only a few hundred yards from the place of the disaster, and a number of workers there were at Once on the spot. The accident occurred about ten minutes I Post one, and a relief train from Manchester got to the place shortly before three. In the meantime, ordinary trains from 'Manchester and Sheffield had come up, and their passengers were able to reader much assistance. In the terrible wreck which had taken place the work of extrication was difficult, and took a very long time. Great excitement prevailed. The dead bodies were at first laid out in a field, where an effort was made to identify them. Subsequently they were removed to the Station Hotel at Penistone. The injured were attended to as well as was possible on the spot, and then sent off to Manchester. A number of the passengers—how many could not be ascertained—were so little the worse after their dreadful experience as to be able to continue their journey. Among them were a womae and seven children who bad occupied a third-class carriage. They seemed to belabsolutely unhurt. The engine, with the tender and horse-box, went a dis- tance of perhaps 200 yards after parting with the train. The axle which broke was the one en the front driving wheels. It snapped near the wheel. The driving wheels seem to have inclined inwards after the snapping of the axle, and perhaps this had some effect in keeping the engine on the permanent way. A piece of the rail in some way got twisted round one of the wheels of the tender, and the end of it went through the cistern. The rails were tern up for a long distance The b-idge was, of course, greatly damaged. Every stone cf the parapet was carried over, and portions of the bridge side were also torn off. A breakdown gang were speedily at work restoring the line. New sleepers, rails, and chairs were being put down before dusk cameo°. The traffic will practically not be interfered with. The accident itself was not, so far as can be ascertained, actually witnessed by many persons, but there was speedily a crowd of persons on the spot. It was a melancholy task, searching amongst the ruins, following the groans of the in- jured, and trying to afford relief and extricate the people from the debris. One or two of the less injured left the scene as quickly as possible, and one of the first to arrive at Penistone was unable to give any,particulars of the accident, but most of them stayed and did all in their power to assist their less fortunate fellow passengers. The cushions were removed from the train and placed by the roadside, and men, women, and children, as they were removed from the train, placed there and in the adjoining fields. Restoratives were administered, and the medical gentlemen in attendance rendered every possible assistance ; but, unfortunately, in many instances, the passengers survived their injuries but a short time. In about two hours this work had been ap- parently completed ; the dead and injured had been sent on ; but shortly after five o'clock, whilst the workmen were engaged in moving the carriages which had fallen into the road, the bodies of three other men were found and placed in a field near to await removal to Penistone. There was nothing found upon them which would lead to identifica- tion, though from their dress they appeared to occupy a good social position, and in the possession of one of them was no less than £1,500 in gold and notes. The work of identification was going on all day, and OR Thursday evening only two bodies, both men, remained un- identified. The coroner for the district opened an inquest on the bodies of the victims at Penistone on Thursday after- noon. Mr Underdown,general manager of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway, attended, and expressed the great grief of the officials at the calamity, and their desire that every servant engaged near the scene should be called to assist in the inquiry. After viewing the bmlies the jury heard evidence of identification, and the inquiry was adjourned. The Board of Trade inquiry is not yet fixed. MESSAGE FROM TRH QUERN. The Mayor of Manchester has received the following tele- gram from the Board of Trade Office:—" Mr. Chamberlain has been commanded by the Queen to express her sympathy with those that are injured in the recent accident on the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway, and he will be much obliged if you would kindly, if possible, convey Her Majesty's message of condolence to the injured, and ex- press her sympathy with the relatives of those who have unfortunately been killed."

RESIGNATION OF AN TRISH M.P.—Mr. Blake, the mem- ber for Waterford County, will apply for the Chiltern Hun- dreds. The hon. gentleman, who has done conspicuous service to Ireland in support of the interests of the national fisheries, resigns his seat because he finds it impoSsible honourably to hold it under the conditions of Mr. Parnell's leadership. ALARMING RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT LIVERPOOL.—WbRe an express train, filled with passengers, was standing in Lime-street Station, on Thursday, a number of empty car- riages were shunted down the tunnel and dashed into the express at high speed, cursing the passengers to be thrown about in all directions. Great excitement prevailed, the passengers shrieking and rushing from the carriages. When quiet was restored it was discovered that many had sustained cuts and bruises, but all were well enough to proceed on their journey. WEAVERS' r,TRIICE AT Bunsury.—There is now reason for hoping that the Burnley weavers will return to work next Monday on the basis of the agreement come to between their representatives and the meeting of masters held at Manchester on Tuesday. The question was left to the decision of a majority of district meetings called for Thursday, and of Oleos meetings five were in favour of contipuing the strike till the Burnley employers paid the Blackburn list, or till the "universal " list had been framed, whilst ten voted for a resumption of work under the terms of the Manchester settlement. lanransTrots.—The main cause of nervousness Is indigestion, and that is caused by weakness of the stomach.
