SANKEY BRIDGES NEW WESLEYAN CHAPEL. SPEECEI BY MR. W. CROSFIELD, J.P. 'The ceremony of laying foundation stones of the new Wesleyan Chepel, now in course of erection at Sankey Bridges, took place on Monday afternoon. In all six stones were laid by the following ladies and gentlemen :—The Mayoress of Warrington (Mrs Alderman Harrison), Mrs Criep, of Southport, Mrs Garnett, and Mrs R Garnett, of ;Tenketh, Mr W.Crosfield, J P (Liberal Candidate for War- ,rington), and Mr Stammersgill. The new chapel, which is aitaate on a site immediately in front of the present iron • erection, is the first portion of a series of new buildings con- templated to supply a long felt need. When complete, the Whole scheme will comprise chapel,school, and vestries. The :portion of the chapel now being erected will be 51f1 by 361 t .inaglie, 141 t 3in to the wall plate, 331 t to the bridge and 25ft to the collar ceiling, the roof being open timbered. The front to the road will be faced with red, pressed bricks, and the windows will be executed in red terracotta. The style , -.chosen is late Gothic, and the front gable has been broken up and enriched by pannelling under the windows, and in • gables. The roof is surmounted by a ventilating turret. reaching to arheight f about 551 t from the ground. The contract has been let to Messrs Gibson and Son, of Warring- • toa, and the designs have been prepared by Mr Owen, of Warrington. The total cost, including fittings, will be shoat £1,300. On Monday the neighbourhood of the new bailding was made gay by a number of coloured flags and banners which were floating from the scaffolding in honour Of the occasion, and as the weather was on the whole fine and promising a large number of people attended to witness the intereeting ceremony. Prior to a formal commence- meat being made a considerable number of persons were 1 bewared by being allowed to "lay bricks" upon which tuev placed gold and silver in aid of the building fund. Amongst these present, besides the ladies and gentlemen weo laid stones, were the Revs R W Starr, J Yonge, Hg- Linton, 3 McTurk, and T Rippon; the Mayor, Dr Gornall ; Messrs Eskdale, Summerfield, Hough. Snoddy, Tomkineon, Stough, George, and Prince. The proceedings were for- mally opened by the singing of a hymn, after which the Rev J Yonge read a lesson, and the Rev J MeTurk engaged! in prayer. The first stone having been declared well and firstly laid by the Mayorese of Warrington, Ttae Rev. J. Eoetterog presented to her on behalf of the trustees of the chapel a beautifully bound copy of Wesley's hymns as a memento of that service. He expressed the hope that she and her honoured husband might find those hemns, many of which were eminently beautiful, helps to ctevotiosa and cheering in the devotional exercises of their home life, and that the remembrance of that service would not be amongst the least sunny of the memories which, he Crested, would crown their remembrance of the year in which the Council of this town delighted to honour Mr. Alderman Herrisoa as Mayor of Warrington, (Hear hear, and applause.) The MAYOR, in responding on behalf of his wife, said he found himself placed in a position to which he had always had a very strong objection.—that of standing sponsor for anybody. Many a time be had been invited to take upon himself that honourable position, but he had always regarded it ass matter of too great importance to ba done lightly, and aimless he could faithfully carry out the promises they were called upon to make on an occasion of that kind he bad generally, to use what was perhaps a semewhat vulgar phrase, to" shirk the honour." But in that case as he had tt stand sponsor for his own wife he felt the same objections did not apply. (Hear, hear.) He assared them that it wa:s with feelings of unmixed pleasure to both his wife and him- netf that they came there that day to witness that interest- ing ceremony which he hoped would be the prelude to the erection of a church worthy of the architect and worthy of the body to which it belonged. He could promise them in his wife's name that she would ever with gratitude remem- ber that day's proceedings, and he could tell them that she had a very kindly feeling towards the Wesleyan Metho- dists, and therefore the gift would in that respect be doubly prized by her irrespective of that she bad been permitted to assist in a good work, a work which, he trusted, would bear areundant fruit. (Applause.) The next stone was then laid by Mrs. Garnett, to whom the Rev. J. McTurk also presented a copy of Wes- ley's hymns. In making the presentation Mr. MaTurk con- gratulated Mrs. Garnett on the workmanlike way in which she had laid that stone. It had been a very high gratifice- lion to the trustees of the chapel when they knew that she purposed to take that part in connection with that new chapel. it was an additional gratification that she had been able to ire there that day. It wie but a continuation of the good work in which she bad been engaged in association with her I ate husband for many years. During her many years resi- dence in that neighbourhood she had seen the church of her choice grow greatly, and he was quite sure that that work that she had been engaged in that day would have been heartily concurred in by him who is present with his Great Master, Mrs. Coop having laid the third stone, she was presented on behalf of the trustees of the chap.( with a copy of hymns by the 11. iv. T. Rippon, who said it must be to her a great pleasure and a pathetic Pleasure to lay that stone on that occasion since her late husband preached one of his first sermons, if not his first sermon, in connection with that Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Society. He presented her with that book, and in reading its contents no doubt it would give her peculiar satisfaction to know that she had succeeded her late husband in the good work that he had manifested for that people in times peat. (Hear, bear.) The fourth stone was laid by Mr. eummersg,ill. Dr. Crate. nail said the very honourable position had been accorded to him of offering to Mr. Summersgill, on the part of the trus- tees of that chapel, a copy of Wesley's hymns. He must say tilt he ceuld not express his own gratitude to Mr. Sum- mersgill and to the other members of the Wesleyan body teho worked there, and who had built up that spiritual church, and he trusted that the labours they had commenced that day would come to a sac-easeful issue. (Applause.) The Rev. Mr. EC/LINTON here mentioned that a note had been addressed to Mr. E. Guest, the circuit steward, in which was enclosed £lO towards the building fund of the chapel, the note being signed by Jane Welwortle. (Ap- plause.) The next stone having been laid by Mr. W. Crosfield, Mr. Garnett presented that gentleman with a copy of hymns, saying that if he had the eloquence of Mr. Eglinton and his power to put together sentences he should have beenvery pleased to say I,methin both with regard to the book and to Mr. Crosfield himself"; but time was precious, and there- fore he would siiupiy hand it to him in the hope that in his library it would be esteemed as it deserved. (Hear, hear.) Mr W. CROSFIRLD, J P., who was received with applause, said that contrary to the ordinary custom of society he now et.aok his tarn before the lady who had to lay the succeeding atone had her turn. Remarks would be made by the ladies 'they knew. They knew that these remarks were always kindly made. It perhaps might not be their lot to hear all that they said about them and atout that ceremony, but they hoped that the spirit of kindlinese would be continued in all that they might have to remark about their proceed- 's-Igs that afternoon. (Hear, hear.) He was not unaccus- tomed to ceremonies of that kind, although he must say that e had never taken part in the laying of an many stones on one occasion as had been the case that afternoon. It was aiso the first occasion upon which he had had the pleasure and the honour of laying a stone in connection with the Methodist body. He was more familiar with Congregational atone layings, and indeed during the past six weeks in other parts of this county he had had opportunities of lay- ing two stones similar to that in connection with buildings similar to the one with which they were concerned that afternoon. That reminded him that whatever might be the nenomination with which they were connected, they were all engaged in the extension of Christ's Kingdom. (Hear, hear.) They were working together to construct that great edifice, that spiritual edifice, of which the corner stone was Christ. If he made some remarks about that system with which they were chiefly, he presumed, connected, he would not have them to under- stand that be looked upon Methodism as one of the perfect system of this world. He believed that, like other systems with which he was also familiar, it had its drawbacks. lie thought they could none of them have come to that gathering, and held the programme in their bands, contain- ing as it did the name of the Rev. E. Lloyd Jones, and also be conscious that the time was not far distant when they were to lose that immediate intercourse with which they Lad been blessed daring the last three years of their present pastor without feeling that there were certain inconveniences in connection with the frequent removal of ministers from the circuits in which they had been in many cases eminently useful. (Hear, hear.) These were drawbacks present to their minds, but it was not for him to enlarge upon that topic. In considering the greatness of Methodism one looked back upon a time when the Methodist system commenced, when in the 18th century there was such a different religious condition from that in which it was their blessing to live, when it was said of the Established Church in that day that she was dying of dignity. When they remembered that there was in the Church pulpits, which were then the chief pulpits of the land, a poverty of preaching, not a poverty of preaching in the biblical sense, but in the sense in which they were now accustomed to use that word. Then it was that the Church was above all things endeavouring to stamp out anything like religions enthusiasm. It was to such a condition of things as this that John Wesley set his mind and his heart. It was that condition with which he was dissatisfied, and which he endeavoured, and so successfully endeavoured, to amend. John Wesley was indeed a great preacher, but he was more than that. He was a great preacher with a genius for organisation, and out of that genius of his had come the great Methodist system with which they were most of them identified. The greatness of his preaching was not so much intellectual power as simplicity—the preaching of great truths in a manner in which they could be clearly " under- standed of the people," the preaching of truths so that these truths could be carried, not only in the minds but in the hearts of his hearers. (Hear, bear, and applause.) nw. leg such means as these that the great evangelical revival came about in the end of the last and the beginning of this century, and from that beginning they had now the great, the all-pervading system of Methodism. It was A man-made system, but it was inspired from on high, and that inspiration had given it its great StICCPSB in our land. (Applause.) It was a system wonderful for the economy of spiritual force. Those of them who were in the Methodist system would know how there wasa work for 'them all to do, and how that the power of every man was taken hold of and was made use of; and they knew, he' hoped they all knew, that there was very little chance of idleness for any wan in the Methodist system. It was a great confederation. It was knit together by very close bonds, and they found that this confederation led to great adaptability in missionary enterprise, a missionary enter- prise that was carried on in connection with very close Christian fellowship, for he thought that the Methodist

I system was of all others eminent in that it had the power of 1 pervading our land. Their system of class meetings, their system of local preaching; the many other ramifications in which their plan system carried itself, were singularly adapted to such a work as that which they were about to carry on there. They had small beginnings with cottage meetings—which all denominations were now beginning to sea the force of —(hear, hear,)—commencing with small gatherings in private houses until they adjourned to snore substantial buildings, such as the one they were even now going to leave behind and come to that better building; and ultimately, he supposed, they would have another Bewsey- road chapel on that or some adjoining spot. (Applause.) The flexibility of the Methodist system was such as one couldn't fail to admire. There was indeed no locality to which that System could not adapt itself. However small it miet be, however distant might be the groups of people, the villages, from other religious privileges there were al- ways to be found members of their Methodist connection who were ready at great personal sacrifice, at much bodily fatigue lo undertake the ministration of distant places, and indeed as a result of that system they found that throughout the entire land "to the poor the Gospel is preached.' (Applause.) The Rev. J. EGLINTON said they were very much obliged to Mr. Crosfield both for his services in laving that stone and also for the admirable address to which they had lis- tened. He (Mr. Eglinton) had heard somebody say behind his back that Mr. Crosfield was so fully acquainted with their system that he might be a Methodist superintendent. (Laughter and applause.) He begged to propose a vote of [ thanks to Mr. Crosfield. Mr. SIIMMIIRSOILL seconded this vote, which was carried by acclamation. Mr. CROSPIELD having briefly returned thanks, the sixth and last stone was laid by Mrs. R. Garnett, who mentioned that she had braught a gift of a goat and twelve dozen of files from Mr. Thomas Wilkinson, of Prinketh. Mr. Brougb having presented Mrs. Garnett with a copy of hymns, and a few remarks having been made by Mr_ Garnett, the pro- ceedings were brought to a close by the singing of the dox- ology.

div.head: TEA AND MEETING.
div.p: TEA AND MEETING.

After the ceremony a tea was partaken of in the Bewsev- road Sunday school, at which about 360 persons sat down. The following ladies rendered active assistance at the tables., via.: Mrs. Summersgill, Mrs. George, Mrs. Summerfield, Miss George, Mrs. Bennett, Mrs. Hough, Mrs. Graham. Miss Williamson, Mrs. Snoddy, Mrs. Highley, Miss Stelfoulkes, I Mrs. Mills, Mrs. McTurk, and Mrs. and Miss Elorthn. Subsequently a public meeting was held in the Bewsey- I road chapel and was addressed by several ministers, Mr. R. Garnett occupying the chain—The Rev. J. Merman read a telegram from the Rev. Lloyd Jones, stating his inability to be present. and proceeded to remark that they very much appreciated the kindness and presence of the Mayor and Mayoress at their proceedings that day.—The CHAIRMAN said that they had had a most glorious and interesting day and a ceremony that would live long in the memories of many who witnessed it. It was a red-letter day fee Sankey Bridges—hardly the beginning of small, but of great things. The friends present had been interestal for years in the development and growth of that little plus, and there were many present, he did not doubt, who would date all the good they possessed to what they had listened to and felt in the little old chapel at Sankey Bridges. There were some objections made with reference to Methodist or- ganisation—one heard that day was the frequent change of ministers, and it was a question more Or lees open to diecn sion—'sut they were sure that in the chapel, the foundation stones of which had been laid that day, the gospel would be preached. (Hear, hear.)—The Rev. T. BITPOte then read a financial statement, which showed that the chapel was to cost £1,300. rhey had £205 17s Id cash in hand when they began the stone laying. The cash promised was as follows: —Mr J Guest, £5O; Dr Gornall, £5O; Mr It Garnett, 1,50 ; Mr E T Guest, £25; Mr T Carter, £25; Mr Hall (Monks Hall and Company), £10; Mr Dixon, £10; Mr Isaac, La; Mr T Hayward, £10; Miss Bessie Dutton, £10; Mr McMinnies, M.P., £10; Mr Edwin Brown' £5; Mr Johnl Bennett, £10; Mr D Garnett, £25; Mr ItCook, £10; Mr H Bennett (Padgate), £10; Mr George Crosfield, £5; Mr Edwin Richardson, £10; Mrs Walwark, £10; Mr Thomas Bennett, £10; The Mayoress, £5 ; Mrs Garnett, £2O; Mrs Coop, £5O; Mr W Crosfield, J.P., £5 ss; Mrs R Garnett,l £25; Mrs Suminersgill, £10; Mr Thomas Knowles, £3; Df Mackie, £3 3s. The collec,ion at the stone-laying amounted to £l3 10s 918, and the bricks to £26 is 2d. About 85 children had raised £9 Is 9d by cards. (applause), and the tea tickets amounted to £l6 17e 01. The door money was IN, and the cellectore £4 51 &I. Later on in the evening Mr. Rtmeoet announced that the collections raised at net ,neeting amounted to £lB 7s 611, making a total for the day, including sundries, of £216 2s 91, and a grand total of £770 lie 101—Mr. SUMMERSOILL said that for years they had felt the need of a differeet place of worship at Sankey Bridges, than the one they at present had, and he was gratified that tbe prayers that had been made on behalf of the object had been answered. He then described the progress of Wesleyan Methodism at Sankey Bridges And remarked that their friends there were friends of the right sort, who were ready la do what they could, and who had always been willing to do what they could. They had ale* true friends at Penketh, and he wished to mention that _Mr and Mrs Garnett had always been willing to help them in rams:, matters, and with counsel and advice. They had many dtficulties to contend against, but were that day celebrating a grand success.-Rev R W STARR addressed the meeting at considerable length. Speaking of religion, he sairl he thought that the safest, best, and moat permanent work was that done on denominational lines. It was fashionable now- a-days to take a pride and show zeal in undenominational work, which no doubt was to some extent a good thing, but it had not the discipline of denominational work. Their work was not a jelly-fish, with neither backbone nor brain, but something tangible that they could understand, fixed and certain, which was what he considered most likely to conduce to the spiritual and moral welfare of the people. He had rather have irregular workers than none at all, but he did not want them to be deceived by the glare and ro- mance of which 30 much was seen in the present day.—The Rev Joarr Yosam proposed, vote of thanks to the chair- . _
man, the Rev NV Starr, the friends who had presented gifts towat.it the tea, and those who superintended the teil.ln doing so he expressed his pleasure in agreeing with what . .

had b.ett said in hope of a successful future for the chapel at Sankey Bridges. He hoped that it would prove a free church in the literal sense of the word, that was, free from any pecuniary liabilities. Mr E JEar, BA, Isriedy seconded.—Dr 00111CaLL supported the resolution, expres- sing his great sympathy with the work. The resolutiou having been further spoken to by the Revs T Hippon and J McTurk, the proceedings terminated.

REPORT ON RAILWAY ACCIDENTS. A return has been issued showing the number of persons killed or injured en the railways in the United Kingdom during the first quarter of the present year. No passengers were killed, but 149 were injured by accidents to trains. Twelve servants of companies were killed from this cause and 3.5 injured. BY aecidents from other causes 30 passengers were kilted and 147 injured, and 115 servants were killed and 590 injured. The total casualities were 254 killed and 990 injured On railway premises 14 persons were killed and 1,017 injured. The total number of personal accidents reperted to the Board of Trade by the several railway companies during the three months amount to 268 persons killed and 297 in- jured. Mt:quanta BY A DIVINEEN MOTHER. At Kingeton-on- Thames, on Saturday, Ellen Shepherd, aged 35, of Rbesett. Long Ditton, was charged with the wilful murder of her stepson John, aged eight months, by dropping ,him in a water-bucket,. On Friday the prisoner told another step- daughter, aged eight years, that she would never see Johnnie again. Seeing the body in the water, the child fet- ched her father, whir was working close by, and upon questioning his wife, who was intoxicated, she admitted having put the infant in the rain-water butt. For the previous three days the prisoner had been drinking, and on the night before the occurrence her husband spoke to her about being drunk, when she said she would drown the child like a cit. Prisoner, who had nothing to say, was committed for trial. Tun NATIONALISATION OF LAND.-1. large number of persons assembled in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown, on Tuesday evening, to hear an address by Miss Helen Taylor, of London, on the Land Question, under the auspices of the Land Nationalisation Society. Miss Taylor, who is a well- known social reformer and an active worker connected with the London School Board, spoke with much earnestness, and heraddress was of a thoroughly instructive character. The chair was occupied by Mr. M. Birkhead, who was supported by the Rev. E. P. Jones, M.A., Ph.D., of Mostoni The Chairman remarked that the subject which had cal1e(1 them together was one he did not know very much about. lie had been more troubled with church matters--(laughter)— than the land question. But from his general knowledge of the history of the country he thought the poor people had been deprived of their rights and privileges by rich people enclosing the common lands of the country.—The Rev. E. P. Jones (of Mostyn) was then called upon, ind in a few words he introduced Miss Taylor to the audience.—Mies Helen Taylor was very warmly received. In the course of a lengthy address she said that the whole of the land of the country was owned and monopolised by a few thousands. No man, woman, or child could live for 43 boors without being dependent on the land for his food, clothing, and material with which to build their dwelling, and thus if the few thousands of persons chose the whole of the 30 millions would be their slaves, because they owned that without which the people could not live. She attributed the reason why there was so much poverty in the country to the fact Rot that the people were too many, but that they could not get the products of the land at so cheap a rate as they ought to do. It was a bad thing to bring food from foreign countries when it could be made et:leaner and grown better at tht own doors. (Applause.) Where formerly there were ram. lies of workingmen and women living in their homes com- fortably on the land, now the land was used for game pur- poses, and other such pursuits of the rich men. If they looked into the history of •the past they would find that whenever or whereever a few great men got to own the land that that was the beginning of the decline and fall of the greatest empires in the world. (Applause.) The state of thiags we have in England is just the state ef things that existed in Rome when the great empire began to go to ruin. It was true England was the richest nation in the world, but was it not alse true that it was the nation in which there was the greatest amoent of starvation and misery? Was it not enough. to make each one feel that it was tlielrbounden deity liS Chruitains, nay, as men and women with homes and brain's to rise up and put a stop to so shameful and wicked a state of things. (Applause.) After a few remarks from Mr. John Prescott, a cordial vote of thar!lts was accorded to Miss Tay- lor, and after a similar compliment had been paid to the chairman, the proceedings concluded.

Murray, a young farm labourer, was sentenced to six month's' imprisonment for having wounded Martin Ford, a fellow labourer, at Burtonwood, near Warrington, on the

28th May. William Rose Campbell (23), private in the 2nd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment, stationed at War- rington, for obtainingsa quantity of furniture, of the value of £47 Ss 9d, by false pretences, from John Henry Nor- bury, at Warrington, on the 14th May, was sent to gaol for two moctbs with hard labour. John Grady (18), labourer, was sentenced to three months' imprisonment for having, at Warrington, on the 29 h ult., maliciously wounded Edward Wei-elev, James Johnson (28), shoemaker, was sentenced to nine months' imprisonment for having, at Warrington, on the 20th ult., unlawfully and maliciously wounded Win. Hall. BAPTIST CHAPEL, LATCHFORD. The anniversary ser- mons in connection with this chapel were preached on Sun- day afternoon and 'evening, by the Rev G M W Carey, of Liverpool. Though the weather was rather unfavourable the congregations were good, the chapel being well filled at both services. The collections were in aid of the school and chapel funds, and realised over £25. On Tuesday the school treat in connection with the same place of worship was celebrated, it being the custom to hold the treat after the anniversary services instead of at walking day. The children met it the school in the morning and proceeded in vehicles to the grounds of Mr Percival, at Daresbury, where a day of excellent enjoyment was spent, the weather being warm and sunshiny. The few showers that fell during the day did not in the least mar the pleasure of the children, who, under the charge of their various teachers, indulged in the usual games. The homeward start was made about eight o'clock, and the children were safe at home about nine o'clock. DISeRACEPUL OVERCROWDING: PRECAUTIONS AGAINST TILS CI:COLIMA EPIDEMIC. Mr Norman, inspector of nuisances for the borough of Warrington, has, we under- stand, received instructions from the Sanitary Committee of the Town Council to look cerefully into any cases of over- crowding in view of a possible outbreak of cholera in this ' country. and in consequence a rigid examination has been undertaken of all houses and localities where such cases might be expected to occur. At the Borough Police Court, on Monday, two cases were investigated WI a result of the inspection, and it will be remembered that prosecutions were undertaken and penalties imposed last week. On Monday last the first case beard was one in which John Gibbons, of Bakehouse-yard, Latchford, was summoned for keeping lodgers without having his house duly registered.—lnspector Spinks deposed to visiting the house on the 6th of July, when, he said, there were six men and two women lying asleep on the kitchen floor With their clothes on. In an up. Stairs room 'were two women with their clothes on, and in a seeond upstairs room there was Gibbon, his wife, three children, and a youth with his clothes on. In all there were sixteen persons in the house, which was very dirty and ill- ventilated.—lnspector Norman corroborated the latter state- ment, and added that the house was barely adapted for four parsons. The Sanitary Committee had instructed him to ask the magistrates for a penalty that would deter the de- fendant, as he had been reported before for a similar offence. —The Bench fined the defend tnt 20s and costs, or one month.--In the second case, William Wells was similarly summoned in respect to his house in Glasshouse-yard, off Scotland-road.—lnspector Norman said that he visited the house on the Bth inst, and in the living room down stairs be found a bed containing a lodger. Upstairs were two rooms., In one was a bed containing the defendant, his wife and child, and In the other were two beds, the first containing ' two children belonging to the defendant, and a young girl, a lodger, and the second a young woman. The house was dirty and only adapted for four persons.—Mr Hunt (chief constable) : There are a great deal of overcrowding cases just now—lnspector Normin : The committee has given me instructions to see that all these cases are thoroughly looked up, because there is a possibility of an outbreak of' cholera.—Defendant was fined 103 and costs, or 14 days in prison. PARISH Citnann EXCURSION. The parishioners and friends of the Pariah Church celebrated their annual excur- sion to Blackpool on Monday, the management of affairs being ably undertaken by the teachers of the Boys' Sunday School. It appeared doubtful for some time whetber or not the trip would 113 held, as so many of the works in War- rington now arrange annual trips, and it was thought pro- bable that the numbers which have generally patronised the Parish Church trip would considerably suffer on that ac- count. However, when it was mooted that the trip might ' prove a /allure, and had in consequence better not be held, it was fo-and that numbers of friends expressed their disaP- pointmeot, and encouraged the committee to proceed with the necessary arrangements. Therefore the committee de- cided that the trip should be held as usual. The intending trippers anxiously looked for a fine morning, and they were not disappointed, as the sky was beautiful and clear and promised a fine day. The inhabitants of Church-street and Manchester-road were somewhat disturbed in their rest by the burde call that notified the trippers to assemlsle and by bells of the church ringing out merrily,. The train started punctually at Tam. with about 600 pas- sengere "on board." and made a eyuick run, arriving at its destination at 8.45 a.m., when the excursionists dispersed to enjoy themeel ees by theses or at the various places of amusement, where special attractions had been arranged for their entertainment. Several of the holiday makers of the gentler sex were not content to return home without paying a visit to the Gipsy's Camp on the South Shore. Here they were intheced to enter the tents, and", of course, having entered, they were 'Anther jar:Peed to obtainia glimpse into futurity and learn their various destinies by the simple pro. cess of "'crossing the hands" of the occapants. On emerg- ing from the mysterious habitations their countenances evi- denced that they were satisfied with the pmphecies of the Gipsies. and fervent hopes were expressed' that their pre- dicted expectations might be realised. The train retuned at 7-30 pm. and arrived at Warrington at 94. G; everyone ex- pressing satisfaction with the day's enjoyment. The rail- way company did all in their power to farther the success of the excursion. Jenne Jones preponed " The Pride of Latchford Lodge."—The Secretary (Mr. William Millington), in reply, stated' that although the sickness for the past year had been rather heavy, the in- come had been such as to enable them to meet all claims and to add a balance to their already existing funds. He had that night received the proposition, money a live young men to become members of the lodge. (App(anse.)— The Chairman next gave "The Widows and Orphans and Juvenile Societies," which was responded to by Pro. Cor. Sec. Abel H Mather.—" The health of the Lodge Surgeon, Dr. James Cannel'," was proposed by W.M. Wm. Chorley, who stated that it was a pleasure to him to propose the toast, as he had always found the doctor do all he could for the assistance of members. (Applause.)—The Secretary in- formed the meeting that Dr. Carmel' was unable to attend —. The Honorary Members" was proposed by P.M.Samnel Cliffs, and responded to by Pee. John Hartley.—On the motion of Pre, Cor. Sec. Abel H. Mather, the best thanks of the meeting were given to Secretary Matthew Lomax, Ancient Order of Foresters, for his attendance —"The Host and Hostess" was proposed by P.M. John Murphy —Bro. Ireland, in reply, thanked Bra Murphy for the kind manner in which be proposed Mrs. Ireland's and his good healtb, and also the brethren for the kind manner in which they received the West. They might rest assured that at all times what they could do for the good of Sheplierdry and thel social comfort of its members would be their first considera- tion.—ln the course of the evening songs were sung by Mr. Lomax, Bros. Cliffs, Barber, Jun., and Millington.—Alter the usual vote of thanks to the Chairman and Vice-Chair- man, the meeting was brought to a close by the singing of 'the National Anthem,

WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT : RANILFSUPTCY PROCEED. s9.—At the sitting of this court, on Thursday, an applica- tion was made to the judge, Mr. W. Wynne Froulkes, by Mr. Ridgway, official receiver, concerning the bankruptcy of John Theophil us feeder, described as a brewer's traveller, late of Heatley, but now of Altrincharn. The application was for the committal to prison of the bankrupt for con- tempt of court, he having failed to perform a duty imposed upon him by the court when undergoing his public examina- tion to ale an account of his affairs for the last six years. The bankrupt was now represented by Mr. Hill, of Men- chester—Mr. Ridgway stated the facts of the case to his Honour at some length. He said that he had served the bankrupt with a copy of the order, and at his adjonrned ex- amination- the bankrupt admittea having received it. It was his duty as official receiver to have that statement filled up. —His Honour having made a careful inspection of the ac- counts and, documents handed, in said that from what he could gather the proceedings of the bankrupt seemed to have been recklenafrom beginning to end. He seemed to have tried his hand at a variety of businesses, but conld not give the slightest account to any of his creditors as to how he had been conducting them. He thoaght, however, that the most be could at present do was to order him to file the accounts with the receiver before the next meeting of the court. On the applicat:en of Mr. Ridgway his Honour decided that certain out ot pocket expenses, court fees, dna, ehonld be borne by the debtor, remarking that he saw no reason for leniency. ' ORANGE DEUONSTRATION.—On Saturday the Orangemen of Warrington celebrated the 12th July by a dinner at Culcheth, proceeding, there in various vehicles. The mem- , berm assembled in the afternoon at their different lodges, where they assumed their tokenaof office. At Cclabeth they were met by the members oP a lodge recently formed there. Arriving at the Rectory, they were received by Mrs. Black and ether ladies, in the absence of the Rector, Dr. Black, and they' then walked in procession to the residence of Dr. Sephton; where they were conducted round the grounds Thence the party proceeded to Culcheth Hata the residence or Mr. James, where a number of gamesewere indulged in by the Orangeuien in a field lent by that gentle- man. Subsequently a dinner wasmerved up in tents at the Pack Horse tuna when about 130nat down. After dinner it meeting was held; presided over ley Bro. Bloomfield. The usual loyal and patriotic toasts were honoured and speeches were delivered by several of the members, including Bro. Kean, in condemnation of the policy of the present Govern- ment. A resoihtion was passed condemning the Franc-bin Bill as incomplete without a Redistribution of Seatsf and supporting the action of the Lords in throwing out the Bill, which action, it was hoped, would lead to the intro- duction of a better and more complete measure of reform. A resolation wne also unanimously carried condemnatory of the action of the Government in prohibiting meetings of at Newry, when that part of the country was invaded by a hostile and seditious party. A vote of thanks to the chairman terminated the proceed- ings, and the homeward journey was commenced at about 9-30, Warrington being reached in aft hour. SCHOOL LITROYEMENT. Considerable improneneents have been effected recently at the National schools, church. street, and the Heath Side day school, Warrington. At the latter school (Mr D W Finney head master), the chief improvement consists of the erection of four new rooms, two up and two down, each room. containing two lavatories, making in all eight lavatories. This improvement has been carried out on the recommendation of Her Majesty's School Inspector, as an inducement to cleanliness among the scholars. The lavatories are fitted with patent "careless" taps, which, cannot be left ramming through carelessness, be- cause the seater is shut o when the tap is dropped, ffOne of the rooms is divided into, two parts, one part being inten- ded for e waiting room for the accommodation of any par- ents attending the schools to make inquiries. The lavatories are supplied with town water, and the wastewater is carried from the rooms to a grid outside. In each room there are 300, hooks for the scholars to hang their elothes upon. The woak has been about three 'weeks in completion, and has been done by Mr William Porter, of Leigh-street, under the superintendence of Mr William Owen, architect, Cairo- street. The cost is estimated at about .8200. At the National schools (Mr' Dewhnrst, head master) the old gallery, which probably had stood ever since the school was built, and which was at one end of the building, has been taken entirely away, and a new one twes been constructed near the opposite end of the room. A partition of pitch. pine has been erected, dividing the room into two parts, the smaller of which is termed the class-reorn, and is fitted with Patent desks and forms, presenting a very neat appearance. The old lead lights in the windows have been removed, and large squares of glass have been sabstitnted. In addition to these alteratione, both this school' and the Heath Side sclool have been thoroughly cleaned throughout. The work at the Nanonal school has also been dons detainee the holidays, Mr Porter being the contractor.
THE PENISTONE RAILWAY ACCIDENT.

On inquiry on Friday morning at the Mancheseer Royal Infirmary, it was ascertained that there had been no more deaths, and that the injured there were going on favour- ably. The official inquiry into the circumst mces of the accident opened on Friday morning at London-road station, Man- chester, before Major Marinden, of the Board of Trade. The first witness was M'llermott, assis:ant locomotive fore- man at Sheffield, Who examined the engine directly after the accident. The right outside driving crank of the en- gine was off. There was an old flaw in the web, extending, he should say, an inch and a half or two inches into the metal.

The general manager of the company (Mr. R. G. Under- down) received a telegram late on Wednesday night from Mr. Calcraft. of the Board of Trade, asking for the information of the Queen, for particulars of the condition of the wounded. Mr. Uaderdown replied Much • touched by her Majesty's sympathy for the sufferers. They are all doing well with the exception of two, who are still uncon- scious."

Thirteen of the nineteen bodies lying at the Wentworth Arms, Penistone, have been removed to their homes for in- terment, the railway company affording every facility for their removal. Thebodies of three children named Ber- wick, and Agnes Ekins, were removed in four splendid oak coffins to Salford at two o'clock on Thursday morning. At Barnsley Police Court, on Friday, Henry Bradwell, stoker, and Joe Briggs, labourer, were remanded on a charge of stealing various articles belonging to persons killed in the Penistone accident.

div.p: THE CHOLERA.

TODLOIC, FRIDAY, 16 WA-r.-.=:-Th-ere Were fourteen deaths from Cholera last night in this city and suburbs. The con- dition of the Mayor is improving. M. Basseren, the acting Mayor, is confined to his bed. The panic among the in- habitants continues, and the exodus has increased during the last two days. MartsmcnEs, FRIDAY, 9-35 AM—Twenty-three deaths from cholera were registered here last night. Two DEATHS ON AN ENGLISH STEATIER.—The steamer St. Dunstan, which left Marseilles on the 9th inst, in ballast, arrived in the Mersey on Friday morning. Her coming had been known to the authorities, and the medical officer of health boarded her at once, and found that two. deaths had occurred on the voyage. Commnnicaticn with the shore was immediately cut off, and every precaution was taken to isolate the vessel. She had a crew of 33, but no passengers. MARSEILLES, FRIDAY EVENING. The deaths from cholera since eight o'clock this morning number 34. The mortality at Toulon is still very yeeef and is increasing.

FLOWER SHOW AT LATCFIFORD. On Thursday the Latchford (Christ Church) cottagers' flower *bow was held in the schoolroom, and proved 'very successful. A very attractive collection of plants, flowers, • and vegetables were arranged in the rooms, and during the afternoon and evening a conaiderable number of visitors attended the show, including the Mayor of Warrington, and expressed themselves highly satisfied with it. Mr. Green ably acted as judge. During the evening several selections were given on the piano. The prizes were awarded as fol- lows :—Window plants: Best collection of no less than three varieties, Mrs. S. Smith; single plants: Geranium, Miss Dew; musk. Mr. W. Knight; fuschsia, Mrs. G. Margretts; hydranger, Mrs Margretts ; best collection of any other description, Mrs Tickle ; extra prize, Mr Wallace. Cut flowers: best three varieties, Mr John Monks; extra prize, Mr W Starkey; best hand bouquet, Mr 'Waterhouse; extra prize, Miss J Barber. Fruit: best collection, Mrs Water- liou!e ; best dish of strawberries, Mr W Booth ; red and white currants, Mr Marsh; gooseberries, Miss Dew. Vege- tables: cucumbers, Mr Joseph Gibson; potatoes, Mr W Booth; cabbages (2), Mr Joseph Gibson; beans 0.2 pods), Mr Muskett; peas (12 pods), Mr Peter Walker; shallots the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) and Mr. Soden; onions, Mr .3 Millar; rhubarb, no prize, Mrs Waterhouse, best ; lettuce, Mr Gibson ; special prizes were given for the best specimens (various) grown in the gardens of gentlemen resident in the parish, Mr C Broadbent taking the lead in these exhibits. Extra prizes were given to Mr Thewlis, gardener Mr Ball, and Mrs Harrison. Mrs Broadbent took the prize for the best bouquet, and the Mayor took a prize for cut roses. At the conclusion of the show an interesting address was de- livered by Captain Reynolds, who, having rensarked on the success of the present show, said that he hoped that another year there would be even more cottagers' exhibits displayed In that room. It was admitted that there might be still more.competition, and Ile hoped that they would all help the Vicar to make the show a success. The idea was mentioned last year of having a field, and he must say that he felt very much disappointed in net being able to find a field in Latchford so near the centre that people would not have far to go, where in the evening, after work, the men could look after vegetables on plots of land, as was done in other places with great success. He should be pleased another year if they could find a field where that plan could be car- ried out, so that those who had not room at home might thus cultivate produce in their spare hours. He also threw out the suggestion of obtaining a plot of land that could be used as a recreation ground, and for athletic sports, which would improve the muscular part of the body, and at the earns time interest the mind. He thought they would all agree with him in being proud of Latchford, for it had been said that it was one of the nic,st, prettiest, little villages to be found in any part of Cheshire, and he advised them to still further improve it by making their gardens pretty.—Mr. C. Broadbent said that he entirely concurred with everything that Captain Reynolds had said. He expressed his opinion that there was nothing at the present time so important as a good re- creation ground for Latchford. Captain Reynolds bad cer- tainly a good right to speak about Latchford, for he had done much to make it the beautiful village he desired it to be. The houses that gentlemen had built had increased the beauty of Latchford, and the inhabitants of those houses would be still happier than, they were if they had a good playground and a good garden, He hoped that the show would he held annually, and that it would prove an in- creased success. The prizes were then distributed.

div.head: WHERE ARE RUNCORN'S BANDS?
div.p: WHERE ARE RUNCORN'S BANDS?

Sir,—Daring the summer- incT.M-t-h-li.l-a-st7e:r-t-h; people of Runcorn were granted the pleasure of an open air concert on the Market Ground once each week. The brass bands who provided these entertainments did so without fe• or reward, and simply Gut of pure love of music, and to gratify an ex- pectant public. Why, mat I ask, have these concerts been diScOntinued ? And to whom must we look for their con- tinuance? Last year music stands and other accessories were pnrchased by public subscription. Who is responsible for these things, and where are they now ? An answer to these inquiries is due to the public, and desired by Runcorn, July 15th, 1884. A SUBSCRIBER.

div.head: _IR._BOTTOMLEY'S REPLY TO MR. HOWES.
div.p: _IR._BOTTOMLEY'S REPLY TO MR. HOWES.

--.--.. have just seen Mr. Howe' letter. "No one not ac- quainted with him could conceive it possible for any man to be so dead to all sense of shame as to write such a letter., having a full knowledge of all the facts which preceded it." I have all the correspondence on this subject in my posses- sion, and I am willing to join my opponent at the expense of printing it for gratuitous circulation, so that the public may see Mr. Howes in his true character. The correspond- ence will prove the truth of my assertion, viz., that the delay at Barnard Castle was caused by Mr. Howes not con- senting to defend Liberalism. The acceptance of the chal- lenge to debate the question, "Is the policy of the Beacons- field or Gladstone Government most likely to strengthen our position at home or abroad?" I have never heard of until now, and certainly it has not yet appeared in the Teesdale Mercury, although the correspondence has been appearing there for months past. Whatever action the Warrington Conservative Association may think it policy to take, Mr. Howes will not ha allowed to slip out of the debate at Bar- nard Castle as he has so often wriggled out of others. After he has proved himself a man there by following up words by actions, let him then talk of other meetings, and I shall at any time be pleased to accommodate him either in War- rington or elsewhere. I have met him twice before in debate, ; at Littleboroug,h and Oldham, and "if I can only get the I opportunity of comparing the last Government with the present one, I have no fear of the result."—Yours faithfully, J. H. BOTTOMLEY.
121, Henshaw-street, Oldham, July Bth, 1884. P.B —Your readers see the character of Mr. Howes in writing to a paper that I should never have seen had it not been for the kindness of Mr. Westbrook.
SUNDAY CLOSING.

Sir,—l was much pleased to read "Social Reformer's " letter, because, in the first place, he sets my mind at rest respecting his vote. And again, I notice he declines to starve himself to death, preferring the half-loaf. Now why on earth should he not take the whole loaf? This and a tankard of Greenall's XX would certainly cheer him, and if inebriation followed, why, what then'? Surely for the nonce his troubles would be forgotten, and if morning found Him rather dumpy, why another tankard would set him all right. What a want of good sense "Social Reformer " displays by comparing publicans with the manufacturers, merchants, and shopkeepers. Bless us, these folks are they who help to embitter life ; the first grinds you down to starvation wages, and the latter tempt your wives to spend all, leaving little for poor Boniface. The publican ought to be classed amongst the benefactors of his race. While the builders and property owners seek to make the working-man's home as comfortless as possible, he steps out, and with the utmost zeal provides a bright and shining room ; in winter a cosy fire ; at all times, a cheerful, civil, and handsome attendant. When do you meet with this in a coffee-house P My friend deprecates Sunday boozing because it leads to " playing " on Monday's ; just one of the reasons why it should have our heartiest support. Just Imagine-what a miserly lot of hum- bugs we should but grow into i? these water drinkers had their own way. From Christmas Day to Christmas Day one long intolerable round of toiling and moiling, all for what? Why to save the taxes. It is quite an open secret that those M.P.'s who give in the House of Commons their support to the various water fads, immediately wash the good action down with a bottle of Bass. Of course-the soberer we get the more work we do; and, of course, the better able are our employers to keep their wine cellars well stocked.

"Social Reformer" speaks of educated men falling like Lucifer, I suppose never to rise again. Well, they will per- haps have the pleasure of reigning like Lucifer also. It must not be thought for a moment that teetotalism will do away with misery; it will only aggravate it. So long as we have the abominable system of competition amongst us, so long shall we have that fierce incentive to grind one another down. Employers under-selling one another, workmen underbidding one another, men who call themselves trade unionists taking their money to cheap butchers, cheap clothiers, cheap shoe shops; employers and Tory brewers taking their money to London, and dealing at fashionable Co-operative stores. These would-be "social reformers" are shallow; look only on the surface, and then cry out, " Eureka." Butl am becoming serious, and that is not my bent. I know of no portion in our litrary past than that which is written of our old taverns, that yields so much true pleasure; and I think, Mr. Editor, were Ito give full swing to the pen you would have to cry out stop. Sylvanus Urban pleasantly tells in—" The rights of honest topers were suppressed by King Charles 1., who, for the poor fee of an annual three pounds sterling, granted licenses to tavern keepers to sell wines at what prices they pleased." Fancy the grand doings of those good old times. Jolly 'places these imas must have been. No one thought of "heckling" the member then about Sunday closing. A man might get drunk as a lord, and was thought no worse of.

In conclusion aMow me to suggest to " Social Reformer," and those who think with him, that they turn their attention in another direction—provide better dwellings for the poor. Don't coop thorn an in pigeon holes; put baths in every house, and at once put away the idea that all invested moneys shall bring in seven per cent, or else there is loss. CAPTAIN CITITLE.

MR. GL Poet's TILNURB or OFUICE.—The Pall 711a11 Gazette of Friday had the following 1---" To-day Mr. Glad- stone has been Prime Minister for nine years and one hun- dred and forty-seven days, one day longer than Lord Pal- merston, whose tenure of power, like that of Mr. Gladstoue, was divided into two administrations. The only two states- men who, since polities assumed their present shape— say within the last 100 years—have governed the country for a longer period than Mr. Gladstone are William Pitt (18 years and 10 months) and Lord Liverpool (14 year and 10 mouths.")

Tug STonm.—During the thunderstorm of last eveninfC week, the lightning struck a trolly as it was passing Main Hall. The box underneath was knocked completely of, the horse was thrown down, and the driver was blinded for A moment or two by the brilliancy of the light. SERMONS AT PARTINGTON.—The annual sermons ell behalf of the Eirtington Congregational Chapel and Sotool were preached on Sunday; in the afternoon, at three o'clock, by the Rev A. Mackennal, 8.A., of Bowdon, and in the evening, at 6-30, the Rev. H. Hall, M.A., of Bowdon, Of elated. special hymns and anthems were sung by the chil- dren and choir, which were well rendered. The collections amounted to nearly £l2, a large sum for comparatively a small chapel.

PENKETH. A FARMER IN TROUBLR AT WARRINGTON.—At the Warrington Borough Court on Monday, William Cooke, described as a farmer of Penketh, was charged with being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and cart in Sankey-street on the evening of Sunday, the 6th instant, and also with furiously driving at the same time and place.—lnspector Spinks deposed that at 9-25 on the evening in question be was in Sankey-street, near Bold-street, when be observed a horse and spring cart being driven up Sankey•street at a quick rate. Sankey-street was very much crowded, and witness called out to thirdefendant, who, however, turned the corner at a fast speed, rushing down gankey-street in such a manner that pedestrians had to jump right ad left to get out of the way of the horse. Witness followed and succeeded in stopping the horse, when he found that the defendant, who was in company with 'two or three others, was not sober.—Other witnesses corroborated.—Defendant called witnesses to state that the horse was driven slowly,l but the Bench held a contrary opinion, and fined him 5s and costs for being drunk, and a like amount for furious driving. VVEhLETAN Mt/TUAL IMPROVEMENT ASSOCIATION.-012 Saturday, the members of the above association had their annual plcnic, the place selected this year being Buxton. The members assembled at Sankey station at 12-10 pm , proceeding via Warrington, Stockport, Millers' Dale, dm After a pleasant journey, they arrived at Buxton at 2-30. The party then separated to view the various places of in- terest, such as Poole's Cavern and Pavilion Park, while others had a drive Up Lovers' Leap and Milers' Dale, assembling at the Wesleyan School, Old Buxton, for tea at 4 p.m. Tea was provided, as last year, through the liberality of the president of the association; the number which sat down being about 60. ample justice was done to the ex- cellent things provided. Mr. W. Longshaw moved a vote of thanks to the President for his hospitality. It was seconded by Mr. A. J. White, and supported by Mr. Gar- nett, Mr. J. C. Routledge, and the Rev. T. Rippon, and car- ried with applause. The President suitably responded on behalf of himself and his wife. Amongst the party were Mr. C. Choriey (borough treasurer, Warrington). Mr. and Mrs. Garnett, Mr. and Mrs. D. Garnett, Mr. C. E. Parker (secretary), Miss Parker Mr. E. Cross, Mr. and Mr.. Mainley, Mr. and Mr& I:ongshaw, Mr. and Mrs. White, Mr. R. Hughes, Miss Cook (Hall Nook), Mr. Watson, &A. The return journey was commenced At 8-35, arriving at Oankey at 10 p m., all having enjoyed themselves, for the weather was all that'could be desired.
